We evaluate the decay length of $B^0_s$ mesons turning into $K^+K^-$ pairs,
utilizing a dataset spanning 11.6 inverse nanoseconds in proper decay time
and sourced from $J/\psi j\jet$ events. Our methodology involves studying
the $B^0_s$ meson's invariant mass near the $J/\psi$ resonance, either alone
or in conjunction with an associated $J/\psi$. Effectively decay widths are
calculated as follows: $\Gamma_{eff}^{(0)} = 0.460 \pm 0.010 \, \text{fs}$,
$\Gamma_{eff}^{(2)} = 0.469 \pm 0.011 \, \text{fs}$, and their average
$\Gamma_{eff}^{(ave)} = 0.466 \pm 0.009 \, \text{fs}$ aligns well with the
established $\Gamma_{bs}$ value of $0.461 \, \text{fs}^{-1}$ derived from
global fits of $B^0_s$ oscillation and decay width parameters.

This study focuses on the numerical solution of a specific stochastic regulation problem governed by a parabolic-type random PDE with an irregular Hamiltonian. We develop and analyze a suitable numerical scheme to approximate its solution. Theoretical results demonstrate the convergence of the method, which builds on the existence of a solution provided by Delarue in Adv. Math. 226 (2012). Key components of the analysis rely on the existence of a solution to the discrete random equation, detailed in the reference labeled D1, as well as relevant approximation results for the solution of the continuous problem.

Our analysis of 979 recorded minimum-bias minimum-energy events detected by the Fluorescence Telescope and Surface Detector systems of the Pierre Auger Observatory has revealed significant local fluctuations in the cosmic-ray energy distribution on a scale of approximately 1 steradian at energies above 4.3 EeV. This finding was revealed by comparing the measured energy fluctuation factor (σlogE/σlogγ = 1.57±0.45±0.10) to the fluctuation expected from an isotropic maximum-entropy distribution (σlogE/σlogγ = 1). The measured fluctuation factor is 2.5 standard deviations below 1, signifying a notable deviation from an isotropic maximum-entropy distribution. It is worth noting that due to the limited size of our measured event sample, our results should be interpreted with caution, as they may not fully capture the true magnitude of fluctuations present in the high-energy cosmic-ray population.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) enables the study of particle interactions between protons and large nuclei like lead, which can significantly alter produced particles due to nuclear effects. These effects are crucial to understanding in charged particle spectra and nuclear alteration factors for pPb and pp collisions at root s of 5.02 TeV, as analyzed using ATLAS data and simulations. Various theoretical models, including ABFG, LaQ-LNC, and LEPTON, are evaluated for their ability to accurately predict low and high multiplicity pPb collisions and proton interactions with lead nuclei. The results indicate that while these models generally align with data in certain areas, they diverge in others, particularly in high and low multiplicity collisions and specific transverse momentum ranges. Furthermore, a new model is proposed, based on leading-order nuclear parton distribution functions and NLO QCD cross-section calculations, to better match observed data and be utilized in predicting signal background for beyond Standard Model searches in pPb collisions.

The standard quantum mechanical framework, characterized by the deformation parameter $\theta$ and the commutation relation $[x_i, x_j] = i\theta \epsilon_{ijk}$, exhibits a fundamental flaw as it fails to align with any specific Lie algebra. This issue becomes apparent when considering the dimensionality increase that occurs as dimensions rise from two to three. Furthermore, this problem exacerbates the discrepancy between existing models, particularly severe in three-dimensional space, which has direct bearing on the statistical mechanics of noncommutative stars and clusters, especially when condensation occurs beyond the critical dimension of two. To address this, the concept of "cross-deformation" is introduced to explicitly acknowledge the intrinsic non-associativity present in both star and cluster systems, in contrast to their planar counterparts. Additionally, a simplified model involving three dimensions, referred to as the "trivial star," has been developed, applying specific constraints to facilitate mathematical handling. Through these developments, clear connections can be established between various non-associative algebras used to model quantum mechanical frameworks for both stars and clusters.

In cancer therapies, identifying and categorizing the five types of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes is crucial. This study presents a federated learning approach to classify these cells within digital pathology images, taking into account patient privacy. Two federated learning strategies were developed and compared against conventional machine learning methods. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed federated learning methods achieve comparable performance to conventional approaches, with the categorical K-prototypes federated learning model outperforming its counterparts and traditional methods.

Equalization techniques are utilized to overcome challenges associated with installing fiber-optic communication systems in underwater environments. Despite their effectiveness, these techniques struggle with the type of noise generated during the use of cutting tools during fiber splicing, which can cause a large number of bits to be corrupted in a short span of time. Traditional forward-error correction codes are unable to mitigate this noise due to their memory length limitations, memory that is similar to the length of the decision feedback equalizer used for enhancing fiber transmission performance. In an effort to address this issue, a modified DFEBOS equalizer with the integration of a forward component is proposed, which can undo the detrimental effects of the splice-noise by unwrapping the feedback component, and in combination with a standard code, enables the reliable transmission of data in undersea communication systems. Simulation studies demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in achieving high data transfer rates, in this case 10 Gb/s, in undersea transmission links that are highly susceptible to noise.

Recently, technologies like HC³ and WaveNet showcased the effectiveness of Time-Distributed (TD) layers in Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs). However, the extensive use of convolutional kernels across multiple TCN layers poses a problem, particularly in terms of memory consumption and computational efficiency, posing significant challenges for model optimization. Building on the success of TD, we explore the concept of Trimmed TD (TTD) layers with reduced-order coefficients, thereby preserving the TCN model's performance while significantly decreasing the number of parameters. We introduce a novel optimization strategy, known as Trimming In Time, which involves restructured TCN layers with fewer parameters, combined with an efficient loss function called Group Sparsity. The HC³ network serves as the foundation for our framework, allowing for seamless integration of TTD layers and the use of efficient convolutional backpropagation. The proposed method has been validated on various audio classification datasets, including Fungus Audio Database, Bird Song Classification, and Dataset of sounds in Rich Environments, with results indicating substantial performance gains, including an average accuracy improvement of 88.57% with 5x compression ratio, 86.14% with 10x compression ratio, and 84.21% with 15x compression ratio.

It has been proven that the lower central series of a free zinbiel algebra satisfies the condition $F_{n+1}[F_m, F_k] \subseteq F_{n+m+k-1}$, which implies that its associated Lie algebra is unilaterally solvable. As a result, all zinbiel algears are also unilaterally solvable. Moreover, our research further demonstrates that all zinbiel algebras have the property of being abelian.

Our analysis of the lead-lead collisions at the LHC with a center-of-energy per nucleon-nucleon collision of 5.02 TeV reveals the need to consider fluctuations in the initial state to accurately interpret the observed fluctuations in the v3 stream angle and the ratio of the third harmonic coefficient to the first harmonic in the azimuthal harmonic analysis of two-particle correlations. Specifically, this study focuses on mid-central collisions and examines correlated pairs of charged hadrons within midrapidity and a mid-transverse invariant mass range. The observed fluctuations in the stream angle and the $\frac{b_1}{v_1}\,$ ratio are well-reproduced by hydrodynamic simulations only when the fluctuations in the initial state are taken into account. Furthermore, the results indicate that ignoring these initial state fluctuations would lead to an overestimation of the initial state variance, and thus, a consideration of these fluctuations is necessary to accurately interpret the stream structure in hadron data and the corresponding parameter $ \sigma_{\phi3} $.

Reverse correspondence theorems establish a connection between two models K and J through a function, where elements from model J are paired with subsets of model K. Given a proposition φ valid in model K, the pairing ensures that φ is true in model J given that a certain subset of K, specifically one that also verifies φ, meets the criteria. This guarantee relies on the existence of a closed subset in model J. The concept of the duality between modal and first-order logic has been explored since the 1990s, yet the underlying systems were incompatible due to differing variable management rules. The present study introduces a cohesive framework for semantic dualities within the tableaus of modal logic, grounded in a revised first-order logic called DLE-logic, which standardizes the variable handling rules from tableaus. The presented tableaus of DLE-logic are influenced by the inductive definition of logical operators in traditional tableaus. The study demonstrates the applicability of this tableau-based semantic duality by showing how the reverse correspondence theorems for modal logic can be derived from the fact that tableaus produce conclusive outcomes. The general tableaus tableaus of DLE-logic also enable the extension of reverse analyticity theorems for modal logic tableaus. The study's findings are summarized using the notations commonly found in the literature, which may require a careful interpretation to grasp the underlying logic systems used in the study.

In maintaining accuracy of relational databases, functional dependencies are commonly used. However, measuring their violation in databases with missing values has been a challenge. While previous approaches attempted to address this issue, no clear consensus has been reached on the exact formulation nor did any approach consider context. In a recent study, we explore an alternative approach to this problem by formulating a new method to rank possible solutions to a data cleaning problem. This method takes into account the probability of each possible solution and provides a clearer understanding of how missing values affect the computation of confidence. Additionally, we illustrate this approach with examples and compare it to other methods, including those based on maximum entropy.

This research introduces a novel dynamic linear model for forecasting time series data, which accommodated an expanding set of degrees of freedom without compromising estimation efficiency. A selective variance reduction technique was adopted to estimate the model using both Gaussian and Monte Carlo methods, specifically TVPR and TVPMR. Furthermore, an information criterion was proposed for effective method selection. In a series of simulation studies and real-world applications, TVPR and TVPMR consistently outperformed their traditional counterparts in terms of model fit and predictive accuracy.

We introduce a novel representation called Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) that
effectively captures the identity and spatial orientation of objects, which is
crucial for manipulating them. By separating these components into orientation-
dependent and independent parts, NDFs enable precise object localization from
sparse and noisy data points. This separation also facilitates the extraction of
invariant features, which can be used in conjunction with object poses estimated
from partial point clouds. Our evaluation on two distinct object datasets reveals
state-of-the-art results for object pose regression, outperforming previous
methods that relied on point clouds. Furthermore, our approach shows promising
results in downstream tasks like 6-DoF object pose estimation from single RGB
images.

This paper presents an updated analysis and design for the SiD Sensor concept,
utilizing contemporary silicon detector technology. We have updated the SiD Sensor
performance forecast and examined potential impacts on W-boson mass and heavy flavor
meson ($B_c$ and $D_s$) measurement accuracies. An exploration of alternative design
configurations has been undertaken, and each option's feasibility and impact on
physics goals have been assessed. Additionally, we have reviewed the SiD Sensor's
fabrication requirements and production capabilities, and predicted costs.

We investigated the near-infrared color-magnitude diagrams of the globular cluster group Ton2, which consists of 19 clusters discovered within the Naval Observatory of Tonantzintla in the Tonala-Cenante region of the Milky Way. Ton2 belongs to the inner galactic population and is dynamically independent. By comparing the dynamic and kinematic classifications of its members, we found three globular clusters in the inner galaxy that are dynamically independent but belong to the half-light apex. These clusters, which are rare, exhibit red and normal colors. Based on the approximation of the spatial distribution of Ton2, which was obtained from the exponential model of the Milky Way's nuclear bulge, the half-light radius of the cluster group is 260 parsecs. By comparing the velocity dispersion of Ton2 with that of the nuclear bulge, we found that the velocity dispersion of the cluster group is greater than the bulge, and therefore it is more likely to contain post-main sequence stars than red giant branch stars. These findings suggest that Ton2 may be an example of spectroscopic tomography, which is a method used to identify regions of the galaxy with greater than bulge characteristics.

The rise of automated theorem proving (ATP) in the last two decades has led to the creation of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, a vast collection of verified modules spanning multiple domains. Given the intricate nature of the proofs, human reviewers often rely on the Archive to validate newly developed theories by examining their integrated references. However, adding new features or making modifications to the code can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process from scratch. To streamline this process, a proposed framework would provide the archetypal structure of modular verification, enabling developers to efficiently build upon existing components through simple, reusable modules, similar to units in object-oriented programming. This proposed framework would also contribute to the growth and usability of the Archive by establishing the validity of its contents and providing a solid foundation for the theorems within.

Using the path integral formulation, we investigate the $d=2$ classical symmetry $O(N)$ invariance models by analyzing their zero-magnetic field susceptibility zeros. Through high-precision Monte Carlo simulations, we determine the critical spin symmetries $\epsilon' = 0.5
u-0.5$ and magnetic critical exponent $
u$ for models with small magnetic fields and odd $N$ values ranging from $1$ to $3$. Our results verify the relationship $
u = 2.476(4)$ and reveal that $\epsilon'$ is directly proportional, with a constant of proportionality $2/5$, to a universal position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in two dimensions.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish the concavity of a specific function within a limited range. Our primary contribution presents an innovative, concise proof of the local concavity of the TAP free energy, a key function in the rigorous analysis of mean field models. This proof is applicable to a broad category of models and carries over to essential scenarios such as the random satisfiability problem, where it yields a striking implication: above the threshold, the local concavity of the TAP free energy fails, indicating its inability to account for the unsatisfiable phase. Additionally, our local concavity argument involves a limited assumption, potentially offering insights into the long-standing challenge of establishing the uniqueness of the Gibbs measure in the ferromagnetic Ising model. The proof of the local concavity of the TAP free energy involves employing concentration techniques to demonstrate the desired property.

Modern metasurfaces, which are ultra-thin and highly integrated electronic systems built on top of ultra-large scale integrated circuits, present an exciting opportunity for manipulating electromagnetic waves in innovative ways. However, verifying the computational models of these metasurfaces can be a laborious and time-consuming process when employing traditional full-wave electromagnetic solvers due to their data intensity. This examination utilizes three distinct computational methods to efficiently verify the performance of metasurfaces by leveraging simplified calculations over frequency ranges, which can be easily validated through simple measurements. In a practical application, we successfully predicted and experimentally confirmed the characteristics of a metasurface which mimics an inductor at multiple frequencies and an actual chip which integrates this inductive element in an antenna, demonstrating the effectiveness of this efficient verification approach.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of first integrals near nondegenerate periodic orbits. This validation relies on the application of a general orbital normal form theorem.

Developing accurate configuration interaction (CI) expansions for wave functions is a widely used method in electronic structure theory. However, determining the coefficients of these expansions poses significant computational challenges, especially when combining the configurations exceeds $10^6$. In this context, machine learning has emerged as an effective tool, yet existing approaches struggle to scale effectively to larger configurations due to limited training data and slow inference times associated with iterative optimization techniques. Overcoming these challenges requires solving CI expansions for numerous atomic orbitals across various targets, including different electron count, symmetry, and other properties. This study introduces a neural network-based approach, named the CI Completion Network (CCN), which is capable of generating extensive CI expansions by training on single configurations and delivering electron-correlated electronic properties at a significantly reduced computational cost. When compared to traditional iterative configuration interaction (ICI), the CCN exhibits superior performance in terms of electron correlation recovery and reduces orders of magnitude both in terms of computational cost and error for a range of test cases, including electron correlation, angular momentum coupling, and orbital invariance.

The Large-Scale Structure of the universe is widely studied, yet there's still much to discover. Recent observations from Pan-STARRS1 and 2dFLES have yielded a massive sample of galaxies, totaling over 310,000, which when combined, reveals a striking pattern when viewed from different angles. When observed from the North Ecliptic Pole, an unusually long curve becomes apparent, extending nearly 4 billion parsecs and formed by an overabundance of matter. Further analysis, including graphical representations and statistical tests, have confirmed that this curve is not a result of observational errors or artifacts, but a genuine feature of the universe's structure. Despite its significance, the curve's formation remains unclear, as the sample size and statistical tests suggest it is not due to experimental bias, nor does current simulation suggest it results from foreground effects. Instead, it appears to be a result of universe dynamics, and its characteristics may help refine parameters such as $\Lambda$CDR. Upcoming galaxy surveys will either unravel the curve's mystery or diminish its apparent significance.

While traditional methods using starlight to measure atmospheric pollutants such as volcanically emitted ash and planetary exoplanets have been well-documented, their application in monitoring Earth's aerosols from above is gaining momentum thanks to the new era of wide-field all-sky surveys facilitated by the advent of vast digital telescope arrays. In this paper the scientific principles and data requirements for employing the colour data from these star surveys to monitor and calculate aerosols above the Earth are outlined. The potential of utilizing these datasets to derive total column amounts of key aerosols, such as stratospheric sulfate layers following volcanic eruptions and tropospheric pollution and clouds in the mesosphere, on the Earth's atmosphere are discussed. The potential of utilizing these datasets to monitor and calculate aerosols above the Earth are discussed. The potential of utilizing these datasets to monitor and calculate aerosols above the Earth are discussed. The potential of utilizing these datasets to monitor and calculate aerosols above the Earth are discussed.

Recently, estimating a object's 6-degree-of-freedom pose from a single image has gained significant interest due to its essential role in various applications, such as robotics navigation and virtual reality. Traditional methods based on optimizing 3D models have consistent performance but often struggle with real-world images because of the high computational costs and complexities involved. In contrast, learning-based methods using deep learning networks show improved efficiency, yet typically encounter issues with accuracy because of the influence of viewpoint and the use of 2D image representations. To address these complications, we propose a pioneering approach called Deep High-Moment Projection (DeepHMAP++), which breaks down the pose estimation process into two parts: first, we employ moment projection learning to create robust, compact, and compact 2D shape representations, and then we use an inverse rendering strategy to determine the object's pose from its high-level descriptions. By focusing on the core object-agnostic elements, our method overcomes the limitations of previous learning-based methods and achieves precise pose estimation even in the presence of complex, real-world images, all while significantly reducing the computational costs involved. Our model's performance is on par with state-of-the-art computational methods, yet 100 times faster, making it a highly efficient and accurate pose estimation tool.

Peridynamic theory is a relatively new mathematical framework that models物体 interactions over distances rather than adjacent points, based on a principle of finite force. This fundamental principle has sparked the creation of multiple bond-based peridynamic models tailored to solid and fluid mechanics. In this article, we examine bond-based peridynamic models and explore their connections with other nonlocal theoretical approaches, particularly in the context of fluid-mechanics where many alternative nonlocal theories exist. Although initial bond-based peridynamic fluid models showed interesting mathematical properties, challenges with their numerical implementation have hindered their practical value. Despite this, bond-based peridynamics offers an opportunity for both existing researchers and newcomers to investigate nonlocal approximations and their distinct numerical behaviors.

Graphical Lasso algorithms are commonly used in high-dimensional statistics for modeling dependencies between variables, as they produce a sparse precision matrix that can be visually interpreted through a graph. The GGLasso is a Python library designed to facilitate the calculation of Graphical Lasso solutions, supporting both conditional Gaussian lasso and binary GLLasso models. The GGLasso also includes the ability to export solutions to the DIMACS format, thus enabling participation in the Antclasso challenge. A user guide with code examples is provided to illustrate the core functionalities of the library.

Numerous simulations in chemistry and biology rely on stochastic dynamics to find low-energy configurations within complex landscapes characterized by numerous minima. Despite advances in optimization techniques, gradient-based methods often struggle with highly nonconvex energy landscapes and remain sensitive to initial conditions. In this research, we evaluate the efficacy of Molecular Dynamics with Langevin Dynamics for joint optimization and sampling, using a hybrid approach that incorporates MD-LD into a simulated annealing framework. Evaluations on benchmark functions and small molecules demonstrate that this proposed method consistently converges to lower-energy solutions than Molecular Mechanics, Simulated Tempering, Molecular Mechanics Minimization, Molecular Dynamics with Simulated Annealing, and Simulated Quenching + Molecular Dynamics. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative two-stage molecular configuration sampling and optimization technique - Thermal Equilibration followed by Langevin Dynamics Cooling (TLED) - and show that it outperforms Traditional Cooling (TC) and Parallel Tempering with Molecular Mechanics Minimization (PTMM) in terms of performance and computational efficiency. TDLED leverages Thermal Equilibration and Thermal Relaxation (TER) to rapidly converge to a narrow minimum within a broad energy landscape and efficiently explores its surroundings. Evaluations on multiple molecules show that TDLED achieves molecular conformational sampling and yields more accurate results than TC and PTMM. TDLED is readily applicable to molecules and may offer a universally beneficial simulated annealing strategy for efficient exploration of complex energy landscapes.

We investigate how a dark energy quintessence field with two different scalar field potentials interacts with the gravitational waves produced by merging black holes. By examining the post-collision merger process, merging black holes of varying mass ratios and separations are compared to determine the effect of the scalar field on gravitational waves. Calculations using numerical relativity in a modified quintessence field background are made for spins aligned and gravitational waves detectability in LIGO's sensitivity sensitivity curve is assessed. We observe the impact of the scalar field on gravitational waves and how it affects the detection process.

We employ a delayed feedback control to stabilize an elongated Euler-Bernoulli beam, Euler-Bernoulli type, is a star graph. The control impact point and the delay time are key factors in our analysis. The number of delays introduced affects the system's stability via the control's delayed feedback. The introduction of a delay period enables the system to reach an asymptotically stable state under specific conditions. The delay period also plays a role in determining whether the system can be stabilized.

Tomography systems utilizing acoustic lenses in detector arrays are commonly employed to enhance the scanned area beyond a single line of sight per detector. However, the selected lens material should have a elevated speed of sound in order to minimize axial distortion and maintain a wide detection range. This study introduces the assessment of an exotic lens material known as sulfuric acid-filled polyethylene, also referred to as "fake soft tissue", for application in photoacoustic breast tomography. Although this substance shares similar sound-speed characteristics with human flesh, limiting its previous use for acoustic lens purposes, its unusual high transmission to low-frequency acoustic signals makes it highly suitable for this application. Through the analysis of simulated and real data, the performance of a two-dimensional photoacoustic scanner, utilizing a spiral trajectory and a novel imaging technique, was tested with a 128-detector array, featuring a 256-element near-field linear acoustic transducer and a magnesium fluoride or "quarter-wave" lens, in collaboration with a linear motor-driven table for precise and rapid 2D image reconstruction within approximately 2.5 minutes.

Community detection and node classification are fundamental issues in the fields of network analysis and related fields such as data mining. Recent breakthroughs in this area have involved the development of prominent methods like graph prominence and vector prominence. However, these approaches have not fully considered the complexities of multilayer networks, which consist of multiple interconnected networks linked through corresponding nodes. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of K-layer prominence, a method that integrates the relationships between the component networks to provide a more nuanced understanding of node importance and classification within multilayer networks. The novelty of our approach lies in the derivation of prominence values through a process that combines the application of Laplacian operators to each of the K constituent networks. A key innovation of our model is the use of outer product matrices to explore the interconnected relationships between the K components, thereby enabling prominence values to reflect both the intrinsic properties of each network and their interdependent relationships. To validate our model, we conducted experiments on multilayer networks obtained from real-world datasets, and the results indicate that node classifications derived from our prominence values exhibit significant improvements over those achieved using traditional methods.

In recent years, single-shot computational photography has gained interest due to its ability to recover high-resolution, high dynamic range images without sacrificing image quality or compromising the user experience.  However, these images often contain significant noise and artifacts as they are captured on the image sensor in the form of a raw mosaic image.  To collaborate with the image sensor's inherent collabloratory capabilities effectively, our new approach learns to process multiple intertwined tasks of demosaicking, denoising and deblurring simultaneously using a novel framework called collaborative low-rank matrix completion (CLRMC).  Our framework views raw mosaic images as incomplete matrices with hidden patterns of independence, and introduces a low-rank constraint to guide the model in recovering the missing data.  Our collaborative low-rank matrix completion (LRMC) model then finds the equilibrium between this low-rank constraint and the demosaicking, denoising and deblurring tasks.  Our initial approach is not limited to the specific image sensor being used and can be applied to any image restoration task where multiple missing data sets are involved.  Our experiments on real-world raw images demonstrate the approach's ability to accurately demosaick, denoise and dedeblur images.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

Deterministic frameworks like reinforcement learning, under general conditions, imply that the policy causes the state. However, in stochastic environments, the relationship between the policy and the state is indistinguishable from the vice-versa scenario. This poses a challenge in identifying causal connections from observational data, a problem that arises in machine learning applications. To address this, we propose a set of tools for performing model-free exploration to discern the direction of influence between the agent and its environment. These tools are integrated into the Causal Exploration Toolbox, an open-source library for exploratory analysis. As a demonstration, we show how the tools can be used to determine the direction of influence in a machine learning agent's environment.

To understand how entries of soft viscoelastic fluids change due to their elasticity and fatiguing, we investigated nonNewtonian, spherical entries and found that at lower velocities, a surface seal forms, which also appears in viscoelastic fluids.  However, as the sphere enters faster, the necking instability shifts from the sphere to the stem.  A new, more robust limit for moderate entry speeds is also defined by a modeled relationship between the sphere's radius, elasticity force, and the fluid's viscosity.

A well-known phenomenon in QCD is chiral symmetry breaking due to the non-zero gluon field strength, which is complemented by the topological aspect of gluons influenced by the $\theta$-term. In the context of quantum gravity, particularly Type IIB string theory, we investigate whether similar phenomena occur in the effective field theory (EFT) by generating $\Phi$ and $\theta$-terms through non-perturbative effects such as instantons and SP(2) instantons. Unlike in QCD, where these terms have dimension four, in the Type IIB EFT, they are highly non-local and depend on an infinite number of operators due to the presence of an infinite number of massless derivatives. As an outcome, we find that both terms trigger global $U(1)_R$-symmetry breaking, which is equivalent to breaking the axial anomaly. Furthermore, the $\theta$-term gives rise to a topological current that breaks time-reversal invariance as well.

A significant concern regarding security systems based on hardware is the possibility of undetected, subtle manipulation of the security features through physical stress applied to the hardware. This phenomenon, also known as confidence minimization, can be difficult to identify due to its covert and gradual nature. Despite numerous efforts in creating robust, stress-resistant hardware in the past, finding optimal - and possibly sub-optimal - circuits has been a challenging task. In a breakthrough development, we present a novel, automated approach to confidence minimization that makes use of physical isolation and requires no prior attempts. Furthermore, this method is applicable to any type of security function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach by successfully implementing confidence minimization in isolation-hardware, obtaining comparable results to highly complex, multi-layered designs typically found in such systems.

In the fields of machine learning and computer vision, robustness is a crucial aspect to consider. In contrast, in reinforcement learning (RL), another concept, resilience, emerges as important. Resilience refers to the ability of an RL agent to adapt and recover from sudden, significant environmental changes, such as those caused by severe data corruption. We explore the potential of using policy gradient methods to develop resilient agents. We propose a straightforward policy gradient approach that utilizes robust loss functions to promote resilience. Our studies, conducted in controlled learning environments and in the context of robust communications command learning (RCC), show that this method leads to resilient agents with only a minor mathematical modification and minimal performance loss. Furthermore, our experiments in partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) settings indicate that the policy gradient method yields resilient agents that outperform other resilient strategies.

In the context of quantum mechanics, a distinctive form of magic state distillation known as a box has been recently demonstrated, but with an unexpected requirement of identifying and discarding a specific outcome, or rejection, which hinders its practical application. The purpose of this research is to investigate whether a variant of the box can be achieved through a box protocol using strictly pure inputs, or if the rejection is an unavoidable consequence. Through a series of both classical and quantum mechanical proofs, it has been determined that such a pure-input box is unattainable, thus confirming the existence of a fundamental limitation. Furthermore, the concept of a choice pressure has been introduced to capture this constraint. By contrast, a specific instance of a box that relies on entangled states is presented, along with a corresponding protocol that requires the minimum amount of rejection.

Our high-resolution X-ray experiments and theoretical calculations investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of cupricite, a copper chalcogenide with a narrow bandwidth, N\'eel order at 12.5 K, and a large orbital moment. The copper ions in cupricite exhibit distinct bi-lobed electron clouds due to its unique crystal field. We found that cupricite's N\'eel order and large orbital moment can be attributed to multi-orbital, superexchange interactions within neighboring heterospins, a mechanism not commonly seen in other magnetic materials. The orbital configuration and exchange interactions in cupricite were mapped using label-specific X-ray experiments and a J-effective Hamiltonian, while copper's large orbital moment provides cupricite a potential use as an efficient contrast agent in magnetic resonance imaging.

Pure organic molecules that make up semiconductor crystals can form spin-active neutral particles known as excitons, whose collective behavior can exhibit remarkable long-range correlations. These correlations are vital for developing efficient and flexible organic semiconductor applications. A key challenge lies in achieving strong light-matter interactions necessary to create such interactions. A novel approach presented here involves using highly spin-active excitons to generate active neutral qubits without the need for external influences like magnetic fields or light. This method utilizes large energy gaps between different exciton states and enormous Rabi oscillations as its foundation. Unexpectedly, large Rabi oscillations were found to occur in certain types of crystals when subjected to intense laser fields, a phenomenon that defies conventional understanding. This discovery reveals that certain crystal structures can exhibit remarkable nonlinearity even in the form of spin-matter couplings, a property that lies at the core of this breakthrough.

In two-dimensional electronic systems, Dirac points stand out as a particularly interesting feature. They appear at the intersection of energy bands and exhibit high mobility in charge carriers. By incorporating a non-space-inversion symmetric lattice, we can break the sub-lattice symmetry, yet still maintain the Dirac points. In this paper, using a 2D non-symmorphic wallpaper lattice, we propose a model that enables us to adjust the position of Dirac points within the Brillouin zone. Through illustrating the model's band diagram and confirming it with numerical calculations from the Kubo formula, we show that including a piezo electric dipole moment can help us fine-tune the location of Dirac points. This proposed lattice holds promise for designing 2D materials with specific electronic properties desired in various applications.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states have been extensively studied both experimentally and theoretically. Further developments, however, are hindered by the need to significantly enhance the intensity of the local oscillating coherent component while maintaining the single-photon component. In this research, we propose utilizing quantum-optical catalysis to directly generate these states. A proposed experiment uses a beam splitter with a high reflection coefficient, combining two distinct input states – a single photon and a displaced thermal state. We demonstrate that this method can effectively produce single-photon facilitated coherent states with increased purity and a greater single-photon component, even without enhancing the thermal state's intensity.

In General Relativity, using the Newman-Penrose formalism and the null tetrad method, we're studying complex bivectors in alignment with the electromagnetic field $F_{ab}$ and the Weyl tensor $C_{ab cd}$. These objects can be efficiently expressed through the use of null tetrads, comprising four linearly independent covectors. We focus particularly on a specific configuration of null tetrad known as the canonical null tetrad, for which we provide the derivation of bivectors for both the electromagnetic field and the Weyl curvature tensor. A notable property of null tetrad formulation in null coordinates is its capability to linearize Einstein's field equations. As a result, the electromagnetic Maxwell's equations and the Weyl curvature expression can be resolved for arbitrary sources, leading to a detailed description of null tetrad and, specifically, complex Weyl tensor bivectors, revealed to be directly related to the Newman-Penrose scalars $\Psi_0$ and $\Psi_1$ for the $\Psi_0$ type universe model.

A novel approach for identifying chemical polymer formulas is presented, combining a linear linear model with an optimal integer solution. This method is built on the assumption that a polymer's composition can be modeled as a linear combination of its constituent monomers' compositions. Initially, the error in predicting the chemical formula of the polymer from the monomers' formulas is minimized using a linear linear model. The constraint that the sum of the monomers' contribution weights must equal one is then applied, and a optimal integer solution is found to derive the chemical formula of the polymer. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to correctly identify the chemical formulas of various chemical polymers.

This paper introduces a novel framework for accurately capturing dual-vibrating systems with multiple frequencies by using direct transcription and a state-space model that includes complex, time-periodic motion. We emphasize that direct transcription methods are more effective than traditional linearization in understanding dynamic systems' behavior. We proceed to explain direct transcription with a focus on ventilated patients infected with RSV or varicella-zoster viruses, which can compromise immune systems. We also discuss the potential of these medically induced systems to unexpectedly generate chaotic motions.

A variety of techniques exist for diagnosing and treating esophageal tumors, yet accurate and timely detection relies heavily on advanced medical imaging. CT scans are commonly utilized, though interpreting these images through 2D slice analysis can be challenging and prone to inaccuracies due to the complex and irregular shape of the tumor. To improve neoplasm segmentation from CT scans, a new model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet) was developed, addressing detection issues via an upgraded attention mechanism and reducing redundant feature extraction with a dense block structure. Specifically, two attention modules were integrated to focus on neoplastic regions, while dense blocks utilized effective feature maps from earlier layers to enhance detection and facilitate skip connection integration. To optimize performance, the DDAUnet model utilized the adjoint method for efficient gradient calculation and a dense block structure for updated feature mapping, leading to better optimization of skip connections. Experimental results demonstrated significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, with the DDAUnet model outperforming various benchmark models, including UNet, ResUnet, and DenseUnet, by achieving an IoU of 0.7352 and overall accuracy of 0.8812.

This study introduces a novel approach to well log interpretation and uncertainty evaluation, utilizing a collective learning framework. We replace traditional deterministic models with a probabilistic description of rock properties, utilizing the accuracy of a collective of decisions to assess uncertainty. A key advantage of this method is its ability to provide reliable uncertainty estimates, unlike some machine learning models. We also present a way to convert the collective's output back into the underlying data space. We demonstrate our approach using well logs and well testing data from a Gulf of Mexico oil field, focusing on identifying reservoir quality indicators. We also incorporate well log data to refine our models. We then apply our method to evaluate past well logs and generate accurate water saturation estimates. We also create a 3D realizable water saturation model based on the uncertainty assessed by our collective.

Nested named entity recognition, a challenging task, demands simultaneous
identification of both outer boundary and internal components of named entities.
We tackle this task by framing it as comprehensive structure parsing, where we
automatically detect all nested entities within a given text. To achieve this, we
propose two innovative approaches: the First-Detected approach, which proceeds
from the first to the last entity in a nested structure, and the All-at-Once
approach, which attempts to detect all nested entities in a single pass. During
our experiments, our NNER framework outperformed the best-performing baseline on
three evaluation benchmarks, showcasing its superior performance on general
news articles, World Bank reports, and bio sections of academic publications.

We'll examine the connections between rational and tropical geometry in the context of a smooth complex quartic surface without singularities. A recent study by Guo and Xu has established a method to compute the number of a quartic surface's tropicalization's smooth points in a way that correlates with its A1-count over the original surface's rational points. We've discovered that the tropical points' combinatorial data can be linked to their rational points' A1-count through a specific weighting system. A key theoretical framework, the Nahm-Schopp interface, allows us to utilize this link to demonstrate the equality of their rational and tropical counting methods. We assume a technical condition to prove the rational counting of the surface's bitangent planes matches its tropical counterpart's count. These bitangent planes' relationships to the surface's tangent planes at two points share a specific property, where their intersection lines form a special type of curve known as a rational normal quartic. The approach used to prove this result can be adapted under broader conditions, as long as the surface's defining equation meets certain criteria.

This research focuses on locating a set of target nodes within a wireless sensor network using a two-dimensional coordinate system. We consider scenarios where GPS-enabled reference nodes and ordinary communication nodes transmit and receive signals, and these signals may be disrupted by unsynchronized, high-power transmissions from a mobile device operating on an incompatible frequency. A new algorithm is developed to handle this type of noise, allowing for precise target node localization. We test and evaluate the performance of this algorithm through simulations using a customized NS-2 module. Results show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, delivering sub-meter target node locations with GPS node spacing as small as 10 meters. We also investigate the effect of increasing noise power on localization performance.

Socio-culturally adjacent languages sometimes combine to form a distinct language phenomenon, known as code-switching, which also occurs in multiple languages that people speak. Code-switching across numerous languages is another phenomenon that affects how people communicate. As these phenomena become more widespread, they pose a significant challenge to the development of effective Natural Language Processing systems that can understand people's spoken or written language. In this paper, we examine the characteristics of research across various resources, datasets, and models codexwitched across English and Hindi, producing a resource that can guide future studies and potentially be applied to other language combinations. Additionally, we identify the crucial factors influencing multilingual code-switching research and suggest potential directions for setting standards in this area.

Evaluating the accuracy of automatically generated image descriptions is a crucial aspect of this technology. Currently, commonly used methods involve comparing automated subtitles to human-written references, either individually or in combination. However, considering that multiple human observers can provide varying descriptions of the same image, each with its own set of strengths and weaknesses, simply treating all human references as perfectly reliable may lead to biased evaluation metrics. In an effort to develop a more precise method for assessing automatic image descriptions, we investigate a model that utilizes human reference information by incorporating uncertainty associated with the provided descriptions. In experiments conducted on two widely used datasets, this approach has been shown to have superior predictive capabilities compared to traditional methods.

Recent findings have revealed a new, previously unknown, phase of the tantalum pentoxide material, Ta$_2$O$_5$, and to further understand this discovery, we performed a series of theoretical calculations. Using first-principles methods, we determined the optimal atomic arrangement for various phases of Ta$_2$O$_5$, considering both its stability and magnetic properties. Additionally, we applied Monte Carlo simulations to determine how different factors, including temperature and entropy, influenced the material's entropy. These calculations helped us to rank the different phases of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in order of likelihood of occurrence, but without any external pressure applied, the newly discovered phase was not found to be the most likely.

Social media misinformation spreads rapidly due to its engaging and emotionally provocative nature. Recent research highlights the emotional manipulation in Reddit misinformative accounts and identifies account geographic diversity as a key indicator of emotional manipulation. We examined the emotional manipulation potential in Reddit's large geographic segmentation by dividing U.S. account holders into groups based on their geographic scope. A significant account geographic diversity effect was found, with more diverse accounts per capita experiencing greater emotional manipulation. Notably, this effect varied across different geographic scopes and was concentrated in specific diverse accounts in the U.S., known as "big geographic sort" accounts. These accounts, characterized by highly diverse account distributions, hold the potential to spread misinformative accounts on various topics to substantial audiences.

The intelligence community faces a challenge in detecting suspicious activities due to the limited effectiveness of existing methods, which heavily rely on human resources. Despite significant investments in technology, current systems predominantly utilize traditional approaches based on rule sets and statistical models. These models, however, struggle to cope with the vast data amounts generated by high-speed information sources, such as social media platforms, in real time. To address this challenge, a novel concept, "Suspicion in Time," was introduced, which incorporates a degree of uncertainty caused by noise and data scarcity. This paper delves into a unique noise model, incorporating both a exponential distribution and an information source's capacity, and develops a degree of suspicion formula, which can be applied to various scenarios, including real-time crisis management. This case study demonstrates the model's efficacy in a real-world scenario, specifically during the 2018 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony, and compares it to alternative models. The results indicate that our proposal outperforms them, including a recently introduced suspicion model, and exhibits robustness against significant variations, including those occurring during the 2014 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony. The model's confidence intervals show comparable performance, and our suspicion model's capability to cope with unexpected events, such as the spontaneous occurrence of the50, was evident. The model's reliability during the 2018 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony, however, decreased, likely due to the increased noise levels. Speech serves as a natural and effective means for teachers to explain concepts to students.
Rhythm and intonation are crucial elements of speech that can be utilized to bolster a teaching language's effectiveness.
Despite the significance of these features, they have not been given sufficient attention in research on verbal instruction to robots.
This study investigates whether specific temporal characteristics of speech, such as acoustic patterns, can be utilized to enhance a robot's understanding of commands.
To answer this question, we collected human-generated commands for PCL-based manipulation tasks from multiple participants using both a physical keyboard and a graphical interface.
We observed that both methods yielded comparable results.
We trained a parser on these commands and evaluated its ability to execute tasks when provided with either human-collected or synthetically generated commands.
We found that the temporal features of human instructions did not significantly impact execution success.
However, introducing slight variations in these patterns via a text-to-speech system led to improved task success rates.
This suggests that while content remains the primary factor for successful task execution, incorporating synthetic instructions with varied intonation can also contribute to robot performance.

There is currently no established method for randomly generating full, ordered trees with varying parent degrees, or a systematic way to generate such trees from the beginning. This paper introduces a straightforward, proven method for producing random ordered trees by specifying the number of distinct degrees and their frequencies. It demonstrates this method with examples and a corresponding algorithm, which can be easily implemented. Additionally, it demonstrates the method's effectiveness for creating complex graph structures, including 3-regular planar 3-trees, by utilizing their existing association with ordered trees.

Recent research has revealed a connection between conformal field theory (CFT) and the solvability of critical points of Euler-Arnold equations, specifically at the boundary. This connection led to the development of "spectrum generating sets" for primary CFT states using Schur polynomials. In this report, a broader framework is established for analyzing the critical behavior of the N-body sigma model, and a detailed examination is conducted for the free boson model. The framework provides a method to determine the critical exponent $\Delta$ through a set of coefficients that define a specific polynomial, and the sum of these coefficients directly gives the desired critical exponent $\Delta$.

The advent of a bot economy in our digitally advanced society has led to
the development of various types of chats, but with this progress comes the
challenge of effectively designing and implementing testing methodologies for
conversational assistants. The lack of standardized practices in testing
conversational agents has been addressed in this paper with the introduction of
a novel testing framework called MAPS, along with example use cases from
automated lead qualification. Furthermore, this paper highlights the critical
need for a public benchmark dataset for testing conversational agents in diverse
scenarios to facilitate future advancements in the field.

Easily detectable large-size planets, referred to as Planet X's, have been theoretically predicted for a long time since its original hypothesis was proposed in the 1980's.  However, despite numerous speculative claims about Planet X, the detection of such planet(s) has not yet been confirmed with reliable, scientific data.  While the possibility of detecting Planet X through its impact on the gravitational field of the solar system's inner planets has been discussed, a comprehensive analysis of its potential effects on the semi-major axis of the known planets reveals striking results.  In order to demonstrate the analysis methodology used in this study, a one Earth mass planet was simulated in various positions, and its potential influence on the semi-major axis of the known planets was examined using high-precision data from the NASA JPL Horizons system.  Assuming a future scenario in which the known planets are precisely measured over the course of one decade, and given that the detection threshold for foreign objects is set at a relative error of 10^-7, it becomes apparent that large-sized Planet X's, with a minimum mass of five times that of the Sun, would leave a noticeable and unique signature in the relative errors of the known planets' semi-major axes.  Specifically, such an anomaly would be evident in the relative mass defect of the innermost Sun and in the North-South distribution of excess mass within the known planets.
