Recent discoveries in monolingual machine translation have led to the creation of massive, aligned translation pairs, which can serve as pre-trained knowledge for improving machine translation. Building on this, we propose Neural Machine Interpretation, a new approach that leverages monolingual translation models to generate explanatory translations for a target language. For instance, when translating the phrase, the COVID-19 vaccine has achieved high global approval rates. into Chinese, the monolingual translation model can retrieve a Chinese to English back-translation of the source text and use it to generate an explanatory translation. We evaluate our approach by introducing a new, monolingual translation archive for English to German and Chinese machine translation, along with base systems that incorporate this archive. Our results show that the proposed methodology significantly enhances the base translation systems, outperforming the baseline by 17.33% and 8.57% in terms of comprehension accuracy on the evaluated datasets. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PMIS-Lab/Neural-Machine-Interpretation.

Researchers in the niche community of Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) have put forward the theory that low-frequency radio astrophysical sources from the current universe could leave a trace in the early universe's cosmic microwave background, specifically as two distinct rings appearing as Gaussian noise. However, a more rigorous analysis reveals that these sources would create two different types of anomalies rather than noise - specifically, an large angular scale power suppression and a decrease in the amplitude of the CMB's primary acoustic peaks. Modeling the current universe's radio signals using a modified Laplace spectrum shows that our analysis aligns with these theoretical predictions.

This study develops a continuous Yamabe flow framework within a specific k-Nakamura data category, demonstrating the existence of short-term evolving solutions. The theory behind this framework is further expanded upon in a related paper. The development of the continuous Yamabe flow was first proposed by the first author and the fourth author, building on the concept of fractional curvature introduced by the first author and third author.

Deep neural networks excel at recognition tasks, yet fall short when encountering new categories with limited labeled data. To bridge this gap, researchers have developed efficient methods using substantial labeled datasets. However, these techniques struggle to generalize well with small datasets. To overcome this limitation, our approach focuses on creating representative prototypes for each category from modest training data. These prototypes serve as category benchmarks, combining features of the category while minimizing variability. We achieve this by combining elements of generative adversarial networks and feasible methods within a single framework. Our method requires no modifications to existing neural architecture and seamlessly integrates one-shot learning with substantial training datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing significant improvements in category recognition with limited data.

Multiple sparse-domain recommendation systems have seen substantial improvement through cross-domain knowledge transfer, yet this approach falls short in complex, multi-sparse scenarios. Existing methods primarily focus on pairwise data translation and neglect the integration of multi-aspect user information. To address these gaps, we introduce a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) framework that is adaptable to multi-aspect data. Firstly, we assume each user possesses a comprehensive set of attributes that are independently preferred by different domains for their respective recommendation tasks. To capture the implicit preference of each attribute, we employ a neural network to model the relationship between comprehensive attributes and domain-specific user information, allowing for mutual sharing of information across domains to enhance recommendation accuracy. Moreover, we incorporate an adaptive data augmentation technique that is domain-independent, which not only prevents model over-smoothing but also facilitates the transfer of knowledge across domains. To sum up, MSDCR is an innovative solution that is not only tailored for multi-sparse data but also its modular design enables it to effectively tackle two-sparse data issues. Numerous experimental validations confirm the superiority of the proposed technique over competing methods.

This research addresses the challenges of working with complex natural conic formulations by introducing Hypatia.jl, an interface tailored for second-order cone and rotated quadratic cones. The interface enables seamless integration of various optimization tools, particularly InteriorPointDirectionSetBased, which employs a specific method to solve large-scale optimization problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by resolving multiple challenging extraction problems in the gas industry, including a novel, larger-scale instance.

Using deep learning models for multi-factorial MRI quality assurance presents significant challenges in generalizing across diverse institutions and MRI systems. In this study, we discovered that, unlike traditional single-factorial scenarios, models trained on multi-factorial datasets tend to overfit rapidly, significantly reducing their implicit capacity and compromising their performance. This issue persists and worsens when the data includes multi-center, multi-vendor, multi-sequence, and multi-task elements. Our statistical analysis and visualizations reveal that during training, models primarily rely on memorizing center-specific and sequential patterns, while the models' implicit capacity remains significantly underutilized. This overfitting phenomenon is attributed to the complex, multi-layered structure of data covariance in such scenarios. To overcome this hurdle, we developed a novel, multi-factorial brain MRI quality assurance dataset consisting of 1,800 samples from five vendors, and proposed a hierarchical enhancement data augmentation strategy, which effectively combats overfitting by counteracting the protective influence of certain layers in the network. This method successfully increases the models' implicit capacity and yields substantial improvements in model performance across all tasks.

To maintain the stability of distribution networks during emergencies, utilizing electric vehicles as energy storage is increasingly vital. However, how EVs impact network resilience is still unclear due to the complexity of these systems. To address this, a new approach has been developed that combines the concepts of resilience with market prices to quantify rescheduling costs and recovery times after disturbances, all while considering EVs as part of the system. Furthermore, a novel methodology has been proposed that applies the principles of multi-agent systems to simultaneously optimize load restoration, EV charge/uncharge plans, and power flow, ensuring a balanced and optimal outcome within a decentralized framework. A case study based on the IEEE 33-bus test system demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by illustrating both the convergence of decisions among agents and the factors that influence resilience, including the availability of EVs, in a post-fault scenario.

Cloud-based machine learning models and database applications rely heavily on memory, necessitating frequent training data reloading and requerying upon instance restart. Containerization and orchestration tools, such as Kubernetes, often terminate containers after short runs or in response to system overloads, resulting in retraining and requerying. This reprocessing consumes significant time and computational resources, hindering efficient training and query processing and potentially causing application failures. Our evaluations demonstrate that using in-memory persistent memory can enable containerized applications to retain data across container restarts, thereby expediting training convergence and reachieving database performance within seconds of recovery.

Multi-agent path finding in complex environments, particularly in hospital settings, often requires considering social constraints, as seen in the "meeting" task where agents intentionally meet at a specific location and time. Solving this problem typically involves agents finding the optimal schedule to meet while minimizing total travel distance. However, the greedy approach of making locally optimal decisions can lead to suboptimal solutions, causing inefficiencies akin to a traffic jam. To address this, our proposed solution uses a multi-agent recurrent network to generate paths under social constraints and incorporates a bonus system guided by flow fields to encourage efficient paths, thereby preventing unnecessary delays and ensuring smooth arrivals. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in successfully completing the meeting task for up to 15 agents in a hospital environment.

This paper explores the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.50$, $0.75$) using a theoretical approach, with findings presented through both mineralogical and physical perspectives. Initial structure calculations through first-principles simulations led to comprehensive descriptions of physical properties. Notably, GdSn3 and CmSn3 were analyzed in detail, focusing on their magnetic configurations and spin-orbit coupling's impact. Spin-orbit coupling was essential for accurate total energy and improved band structure and density of states representation. Further DDFP fit revealed effective parameters influenced by SOC. Entire GdxCm1-xSn$_3$ series exhibited half-metallic behavior.

According to the Standard Model of particle physics and observations from the Cosmic Microwave Background, there should be roughly ten times more dark matter than normal (baryonic) matter in the universe. This model of matter allows for density fluctuations on small scales, potentially enabling massive clumps of baryonic and dark matter within one another, also referred to as "onion" structures. These formations should contain not only dark and baryonic matter, but also an abundance of normal matter in the form of various particles, such as extra baryons, heavy mesons, and even black holes of baryonic and non-baryonic matter. While many structures containing these types of matter may go unnoticed, some "onion" structures should be detectable through their distinctive signatures in the emission of normal matter, such as gamma rays and neutral pions decaying, as well as in gravitational waves from merging black holes.

The foundation theorem for Coxeter groups of type B has been generalized to include all group types B(I1, I2, ...). Furthermore, this generalization extends to cover all group types B where the foundation theorem for type B was previously established for the original group G, resulting in a corresponding relationship with the generalized Coxeter group G.

Using the Pantheon dataset, we investigated how gravitational lensing affects the apparent brightness of Type Ia supernovae, typically measured through the reduced surface brightness phenomenon. By analyzing the scatter in the Type Ia data, we found an extra component that could be attributed to the effect of weak gravitational lensing. We determined that the observed reduction in effective shear power, when compared to expectations, implies a certain degree of mass in dark matter distributions. However, further research is necessary to confirm if type Ia supernovae are indeed being lightly lensed and to discern if other factors, such as system-related inconsistencies, might be responsible for the observed results. We discovered that after removing the lensing effect, the remaining scatter resembles the characteristics of noise that appears Gaussian in nature.

These lecture notes are designed to introduce the fundamental concepts of the theory of semilinear stochastic partial differential equations. The target audience comprises individuals with a solid understanding of functional analysis, measure theory, and PDE, but may need a refresher on some probabilistic concepts. The material is based on a presentation given at the summer school in mathematical physics held in Bressanone, Italy in 2019. The source referenced throughout is the book titled "Analyses for Mild Solutions of Semilinear Stochastic Partial Differential Equations".

Modern data centers face increasing challenges in managing power consumption and signal losses in their electrical networks. On-chip photonic interconnects offer a potential solution by reducing losses and allowing for effective heat dissipation. However, integrating high-speed, low-loss photonic components with silicon electronics has been a major obstacle. We overcame this barrier by introducing a novel, low-loss 'T-hybrid' waveguide structure. This photonic component exhibits exceptional performance with less than 0.05 dB of insertion loss and less than 0.3 dB of loss asymmetry at a wavelength of 1.55 micrometers. It also demonstrates minimal differences in propagation velocities between the optical and electrical signals, amounting to less than 0.1 lengths per meter at 20 GHz. These results were verified through both numerical simulations and experimental measurements in a pilot integrated circuit. The low-loss T-hybrid waveguide is a crucial building block for silicon photonic routers, switches, and other photonic interface components that utilize electrical packetization protocols.

3D MRI images serve as crucial medical imagery for diagnosing and monitoring brain disorders, however their intricate nature can pose challenges to human interpreters. Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning techniques along with auxiliary Image Processing tools, the task of analyzing these images is streamlined. This project utilizes 3D MRI images to examine and visualize a human brain, enabling the identification of pathologies such as tumors. By leveraging 3D MRI images, the analysis is made more efficient, leading to improved visualization of the brain. Furthermore, the incorporation of Unet and Resunet algorithms has streamlined the image processing task. These models enable the extraction of features and segmentation of regions of interest, making it easier to visualize and locate tumors within the brain. By utilizing pre-trained models and leveraging the power of machine learning, the analysis becomes more accurate and reliable.

Overall, the combination of machine learning and deep learning models, along with image processing techniques, has made it easier to detect tumors in MRI images. By leveraging the power of these technologies, healthcare professionals can receive more accurate diagnoses and streamlined workflows.

The classical approach by K. Eiseniskis for computationally determining Bernoulli numbers involves extensive calculations with large integers. In contrast, a recent discovery by T. Ohkuma reveals that the mod $p$ Bernoulli numbers can be expressed using specific determinants formed from Jacobi symbols, which can be efficiently computed using Shanks' algorithm to generate cubic residues and yield practical results for various primes $p$. Building upon Ohkuma's insights, we develop an algebraic framework to derive the rational Bernoulli numbers based on these mod $p$ determinants.

The understanding of exoplanet characterisation and yield is hindered by stellar activity that contaminates radial velocity measurements. To mitigate this, the effectiveness of filtering radial velocity data via spectral matching using line catalogs is evaluated for its ability to reduce stellar activity noise. Our study assesses the performance of this approach by analysing the scatter in exoplanet radial velocity semi-amplitudes derived from various line catalogs across the U.S. National Optical-Infrared User Network. Additionally, we explore the potential of improving spectral matching through analyzing the relationship between the reduced chi-square of line intensity residuals and specific parameters of the catalogs, including wavelength ranges, hydrogen donor states, and stellar line profiles' occupation factors. Our findings indicate that while choosing specific line catalogs can provide a marginal gain in precision, a significant improvement over the entire observed wavelength range is unlikely. Conversely, randomizing the selection of line catalogs that exhibit low scatter in planetary parameters may yield a substantial increase in precision. Lastly, we suggest that increasing the signal-to-noise ratio of observations remains the most effective strategy to enhance radial velocity-based stellar activity filtering's performance.

Recent research has developed Hierarchical Scope Sectoring (HSS), a sophisticated bidirectional link caliber estimation technique. However, HSS's advanced design poses implementation difficulties and employs excessive energy in its operational links. To address these issues, we introduce an innovative, energy-efficient variant of HSS that leverages bidirectional link calibers, dubbed Modified Hierarchical Scope Sectoring (MHSS). Our analysis indicates that MHSS offers comparable performance to HSS while offering superior energy efficiency. Furthermore, we present a new protocol, On-demand Gathering with Modified Hierarchical Scope Sectoring (OG-MHSS), that integrates MHSS and a hierarchical node role assignment method, allowing a single node to collect and manage data from multiple disjoint networks using less energy than HSS-based approaches. Our analysis shows that MHSS achieves a 95% accuracy rate in scope sector estimation, while HGSS achieves 90%, and MHSS outperforms HSS by achieving 50% improved coverage and 50% enhanced energy efficiency in network coverage and node degree degree calculations. Moreover, MHSS exceeds OGSS and HOGS protocols by attaining 50% better coverage and 50% enhanced energy efficiency in network coverage, while excelling in data latency and packet delivery performance.

The role of context in facilitating object detection and classification is a
fundamental concept in both human vision and the design of object detectors that
leverage hierarchical representations, such as RBF networks and cortical models.
Despite the well-documented difficulty of object recognition tasks in varied
contexts, current methods mostly assess the ability of DPN-based detectors to
identify and classify objects in unfamiliar settings. They fail to investigate
whether these detectors are actually exploiting contextual cues to aid
object identification or simply interpolating gaps in pattern matching. In this
study, we aim to explicitly test whether the object detector with a deep neural
network (DNN) is capable of utilizing scene context to aid object identification.
To accomplish this, we trained a object classifier and a DNN object detector to
identify objects in contexts, followed by evaluating their performance on objects
and background contexts that were either consistent or inconsistent with each
other. Our results show that the classical classifier performs best on
consistent contexts, while the detector's unique capability to generalize to
inconsistent contexts is comparable to its performance on contexts with missing
parts. A contrastive analysis with linearly trained baselines indicates that the
DNN detector's generalization to inconsistent contexts is context-related. A
control experiment with randomly trained networks demonstrates that DNNs are not
necessary for exploiting context in object identification, but are necessary for
identifying objects from background alone. Our study suggests that context is
valuable for object identification

The research focuses on a system of Kirchhoff type elliptic equations that incorporate a singular Trudinger-Moser potential. An essential feature of this study is the absence of standard growth conditions and compactness assumptions typically found in similar research. The primary objective involves investigating the system's solution under a new exponential potential and a Kirchhoff coefficient $\beta$ while dividing the problem into four distinct scenarios. To achieve this, researchers apply a dual linking geometry method, a mountain pass method, and a critical point compactness method, ultimately leveraging a specific technique to overcome the system's doubling effect.

We establish significantly enhanced concentration inequalities for independent binary random variables that exhibit variance invariance and pairwise independence but with varying probabilities. Our results hold under negative correlation as well, which we define and explore in relation to both physical and theoretical contexts, including statistical mechanics and database management, and demonstrate the broader applicability of our findings in Chapter 2.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the power series ring $R$ in multiple variables over $k$. Assuming the power of the variables is at least three, the fundamental group of the spectrum of $R$ has a sufficiently large abelianization, and there exists an overwhelmingly large finite extension of the spectrum of $R$ whose fundamental group matches that of the original ring $R$.

The proposed analysis method for RHIC's 2023-2024 spin program relies heavily on the double longitudinally polarized semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS) data. A key aspect of this method involves examining the correlation between hadrons produced in SIDIS reactions when the spins of the incident particles are crossed. Currently, the double-longitudinal SIDIS correlation method faces a limitation due to the influence of a specific term, resulting from the interaction of the incoming particle's spin with the transverse momentum of a produced particle, and associated with a specific hadron orientation. To improve the sensitivity of this method, a new strategy is presented that centers on subtracting the contributions caused by this specific term. A detailed theoretical investigation into double longitudinally polarized SIDIS data reveals the contributions of various factors, and illustrates them using a significant example.

We propose a method to construct a mass-deformed, four-dimensional, globally hyperbolic space, topologically equivalent to a mass-deformed sphere, $S^3_\mathcal{M}$. This new geometry allows for the development of a free scalar quantum field theory, which we then examine from both Lagrangian and Hamiltonian perspectives. Our analysis includes calculations of the commutator of scalar fields, solutions to the Hadamard condition, and insights into the physics of massive scalars in a de Sitter-like spacetime, all within a globally hyperbolic, compact spatial background. Additionally, we derive the Bunch-Davies vacuum state for this quantum field theory.

Let V be a vector space over a field that is not characteristic two, equipped with a non-degenerate skew-symmetric form. The study focuses on morphisms between symplectic varieties, which preserve this form. If such a morphism has a scalar determinant, it can be expressed as the composition of a symplectic binomial alteration and a contact binomial modification. This composition occurs within the category of symplectic varieties.

Wikipedia has consistently been a reliable source of high-quality content, making it an ideal platform for entity extraction and suggestion. However, traditional entity extraction methods that rely on natural language processing alone often fall short due to Wikipedia's rich hierarchical structure. To address this limitation, we propose a new entity extraction approach that leverages Wikipedia's layered graph representation. By transforming Wikipedia into a ranked list of candidates, our method integrates natural language processing with the document order information, utilizing both Pointwise Mutual Score and Linear Model for Ranking to achieve optimal results. Our system has been shown to effectively recover a high percentage of entities from Wikipedia and seamlessly integrates into the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, yielding a significant improvement in entity suggestion performance.

The concept of ideal incompatible kidney transplants has been introduced to highlight the significant potential of cross-matching incompatible kidneys for improving waitlist patients' access to transplantation. According to a mathematical model, around 17 such kidneys could be transplanted each year with current systems, but this number rises to 52 when incompatible kidneys are swapped for compatible ones, utilizing a pool of approximately 1000 pairs where both the egg donor and recipient test positive for each other.

Kernel methods are well established and the most effective approaches for
solving complex, real-world problems in AI. Their success is partly attributed
to their flexibility, with numerous variants now available. This flexibility is
partly achieved by expressing kernels as implicit functions and bypassing the need
for explicit kernel forms. This paper is designed to provide a unifying framework
for research on implicit kernels, with a focus on their key properties and
current applications across multiple domains, including classification, regression,
and generative probabilistic models, with the aim of summarizing the current state
of the art in this active area of investigation.

This paper delves into whether neural networks use n-dimensional spaces with pre-trained word representations to analyze the semantic composition of news headlines and corporate texts, or if they simply identify patterns in first-order statistics. To investigate this question, we concentrate on sentiment analysis, applying various models to evaluate their performance. The results, however, cast doubt on whether word representations truly grasp the sentiment of texts. Specifically, we discover that aggregating word representations by averaging may hinder model efficacy. As an alternative, we introduce a simple yet effective neural network aggregator, which seamlessly integrates sophisticated representations, yielding substantial improvements. We open-source our methodologies to encourage future n-dimensional space text modeling studies.

This letter provides a set of alternative methods achieving the same optimal results in waveform design for Si multi-element antenna systems and multi-element antenna systems using OFDM, which can be seen as an extension to previous research. Specifically, this research demonstrates that for a given and fixed wideband system using multi-element antennas or an OFDM system with multiple carriers, there exist equivalent simple wideband systems utilizing a single antenna.

A novel approach combining level-set and embedded boundary methods has been developed for resolving interface problems within fluid dynamics. This technique leverages the strengths of both methods, employing the level-set to track the interface and using the embedded boundary method to handle complications arising from its geometry. This technique was adapted for use with the latent heat method to address fluid solidification processes. Furthermore, its effectiveness was demonstrated through various tests including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and problems involving dynamic pinning.

In multiplayer competitions, ensuring a rationally supportable equilibrium among participants can prove challenging. Our proposed solution addresses this by utilizing a learning algorithm capable of guaranteeing a rationalizable equilibrium as player participation increases. Essentially, the algorithm adjusts the game's parameters to ensure each participant has a probability advantage of selecting the equilibrium strategy, using only local information about other participants. Furthermore, we've implemented this algorithm in a experiment with human participants in an imperfectly informed game. Without adjustment, humans seldom achieve a rationalizable equilibrium, yet our algorithm consistently does so upon adjusting the game. Adjustments made by the algorithm include identifying essential participants and detecting their influence on probability advantages. Consequently, our research presents a novel capability for ensuring rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer competitions using only control over game parameters.

A dynamic restructuring process is modeled epistatically to mimic a system's attempt to avoid bankruptcy through reorganization, and this concept is applied to ratchets to examine how the systems' overall performance is impacted. The models reveal that the systems' output is always positive when the restructuring threshold is within a reasonable range, and the restructing threshold directly dictates the system's output. As the restructaring threshold increases, the restructaring frequency initially declines and then increases, forming a curve that can be utilized to explore the restructaring process. Furthermore, a distributed restructaring mechanism is shown to optimize the restructaring distribution to achieve the most beneficial outcome for the entire system.

This research explores the interconnections between Cotton flow and both the structural and geometric properties of a nearly Kenmotsu 3-h-Manifold. Specifically, we identify conditions under which a manifold becomes invariant under the flow, and we establish that invariant manifolds will ultimately converge to a state of being Kenmotsu manifolds. Additionally, we establish necessary conditions for the existence of cotton solitons in relation to the 1-eigenspace of the tensor representing the manifold's conformal structure.

Partonic structure hadrons is crucial for precision measurements in high-energy physics experiments, particularly in processes involving deep inelastic scattering, particle production in proton collisions and the overall momentum distribution within the hadons described by the momentum sum rule. In recent years, with the advancement of global analyses combining data from various experiments, especially with more accurate measurements from electron-proton collisions at HERA and a new dataset from CMS in pp collisions at LHC, the need for a robust and transparent theoretical framework has become evident. This framework is now a prerequisite for incorporating the previous achievements of PDF fitting into the high-precision physics environment of the High-Luminosity LHC era. Furthermore, with the potential for establishing charged lepton beams with energies up to 65 GeV at FCC-ee in the future, even tighter constraints on the internal structure of hadrons could be imposed through processes such as neutral current and charged current reactions. As a consequence of these advancements, there is a growing demand for publicly available code that transparently implements numerical and statistical algorithms for global PDF fitting while ensuring the incorporation of state-of-the-art theoretical predictions consistent with next-to-next-to-leading order calculations including various migration effects, making sure the code is compatible with popular fitting libraries such as Coppela and EiCDF in order to meet these challenges.

In reinforcement learning, accelerating policy optimization is crucial for achieving faster convergence. Notably, introducing periodic variance reduction techniques from numerical analysis into policy optimization processes has the potential to substantially decrease variance and expedite convergence. However, implementing these techniques poses a challenge due to the requirement of random sampling with replacement. This study explores the incorporation of such variance reduction methods within policy optimization frameworks in the context of variance-determined experience replay. Specifically, we develop an algorithm that utilizes variance-reduced value iteration and present theoretical guarantees on the convergence of our approach. Furthermore, in robotics applications requiring substantial computational resources for task simulation, variance-reduced sampling is shown to significantly reduce simulation time while maintaining performance comparable to traditional policy optimization with multiple simulations.

I present libcommute, a C++17 template library that facilitates the efficient construction of sparse matrices from symbolic expressions by identifying the common underlying structure, which often appears in physics and other fields. Additionally, I introduce pycommute, a Python interface to libcommute, which also provides access to high-performance solvers and methods for auto-differentiation, although the latter is not applicable to sparse matrices. This Python interface allows for rapid prototyping and development, whereas the underlying C++17 library offers substantially faster runtime performance, ultimately providing the ideal solution for both initial experimentation and final submission.

Our first-principles calculations reveal that the electronic configuration and insulating nature of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ can be well-reproduced by employing an on-site Coulomb interaction (U = 4 eV) on As p-states. Using this revised, authentic electronic configuration and insulating characteristics, we re-examined the dos-plot and band structure, and re-discovered hole-like pockets near the zone boundary along high-symmetry paths. These findings are corroborated by ARPES data, and we hypothesize that these hole-like pockets may be the origin of the observed arc-like electron-like bands in normal state (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$, and potentially in other related cuprate and iron-pnictate superconductors.

Two different approaches have been employed to apply the supersymmetry technique to matrix variables, specifically the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization method. We demonstrate the equivalence of these two methods, and utilize the superbosonization method to derive the Berezin identity. Furthermore, this method is applied to calculate the average polynomial of the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble matrices.

The study of top quark spin offers significant insights and can aid in discovering new phenomena beyond the Standard Model. Despite their fleeting lifetimes, top quarks cannot decay hadronically without losing valuable information due to final state interactions. To circumvent this limitation, researchers analyze decay products from semi-leptonic decays of the top quark. The ability to measure polarization increases experimental sensitivity to new particles or interactions. In this study, we present a method for extracting the top quark polarization observable, known as the average forward-backward asymmetry, from data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC. Our approach utilizes semi-leptonic events from single top quark production in the t-channel during Run 2 of the LHC, allowing us to estimate the average forward-backward asymmetry anxi using a differential distribution of muon scattering angles. The estimated value of the average forward-backward asymmetry is 0.31 ± 0.08, which can be utilized to constrain new physics models extending the Standard Model.

Evaluating the conductive layer of LaNiO$_3$ within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattice structures has been challenging due to surface sensitivity issues with measurement tools. By utilizing $\beta$-detected NMR and measuring the decay of the polarization of $^8$Li particles, the carrier effective mass was found to be consistent with bulk values for structures with more than five LaNiO$_3$ layers. This confirmed the conductive layer's metallic progression as the number of layers increased odd and was verified with $\beta$-NMR mass shift measurements matching those of bulk LaNiO$_3$. Furthermore, with 3 or 5 LaNiO$_3$ layers, the metallic portion was quantified as approximately 40%-50% based on $^8$Li spin echo decay and T$_2$ measurements of free induction decay. These measurable parameters were made possible by the high sensitivity of $\beta$-NMR to surface effects and were supported by band structure calculations considering the lack of oxygen and mixed valence of oxygen ions near the LaNiO$_3$ boundaries.

In our study, we present MultiTalk, a comprehensive collection of dialogue datasets
targeting multiple sophisticated aspects of conversational interactions, including
simultaneous discussions on diverse topics, the retrieval of specific information,
calculations, multilingual capabilities, and the use of specialized knowledge.
Existing datasets and models are extensively modified and integrated to create a
highly branching dialogue testbed, designed to evaluate the potential of multi-
topic conversations. Through a series of logical connections, we incorporate nine
distinct datasets, allowing for conversations up to eight turns long and spanning
various dialogue elements. This results in over 100 possible dialogue paths, each
with unique characteristics. To demonstrate the capabilities of multi-topic
conversations, we employ a foundational model featuring eight topic models, leading
to over 70 possible dialogue sequences. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset,
retrieval math in English, along with a corresponding model, to handle more complex
tasks within conversations. Our analysis explores multi-topic dialogue patterns,
user preferences for certain dialogue subjects, and the underlying relationships
between different datasets. All resources are publicly accessible at this link:
https://github.com/zhongzw123/MultiTopicDialogues.

Our study provides the ability to make reliable decisions in MIMO systems enhanced by intelligent reflective surfaces, accounting for correlated fading and a key phenomenon in these systems. Specifically, we developed analytical methods to predict long-term system performance, taking into consideration: a) multiple clustered reflections in the IRS, b) a realistic model of phase shifts in the systems, and c) finite bandwidth of the systems. Additionally, our analysis yields formulas for the typical capacity of these systems and can be utilized to develop strategies for optimizing phase shifts in the systems. Our simulations demonstrate that our methods are accurate, and our findings also reveal how various system and environmental factors influence the performance of intelligent reflective surfaces.

We introduce DE-Nbody, an innovative tool for simulating N-body systems under non-standard gravity theories. DE-Nbody adapts traditional Simon-boomerang codes to simulate a wide range of theories, offering benefits like saving computation time, reducing data errors, and facilitating the comparison of various gravitational theories. We've tested DE-Nbody with a dataset consisting of 760 galaxies, producing results that are both efficient (with a computation time of about 1 hour) and accurate, offering equal or better precision than existing simulations that took much longer. The results of our simulation reveal subtle differences in the distribution of matter caused by different gravitational models, which may be detectable with future high-resolution surveys. To obtain these insights, our simulation utilized specific theories known as conformally modified Newtonian dynamics and scalar-tensor theories, with specific parameters for each.

Imagine a scenario where an independent Gaussian free field is combined with a large group of chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution paths, neither influencing nor being affected by each other. Research has already been done on situations involving 'Boltzmann-gas' of SLE curves, whose interactions were modified by a factor of $1/2$. Our work delves into more extreme regimes, specifically those where repulsive forces between the SLEs intensify, potentially making interactions resemble those of a Carnot group like the Heisenberg group, or even stronger. In our analysis, we examine the ASG limit, in which the number of SLEs grows without bound, their dimensions approach two, and their interaction forces decrease simultaneously. Our main achievement is the construction of a novel, highly interconnected SLE path that exhibits fractal and self-similar properties, discovered through mathematical derivations including delicate estimates and transformations. This derived path, which is equivalent to a set-known as the radial Heisenberg-Voiculescu macroscopic path, shares the same structural properties as the path.

MediaWiki's popularity has been particularly impactful in the scientific community,
where its features are well-suited for real-time information sharing and seamless
integration with Python science stacks. Based on this, WorkingWiki has been devised
as an enhanced open-source prototype that unlocks the full potential of MediaWiki's
capabilities. With minimal coding, scientists can utilize workingwiki to enable
seamless synchronization between local and remote wiki versions, import/export of
data in preferred formats, version history restoration, and more. Have has been
demonstrated to be particularly useful in the context of multi-person astronomy
image analysis, though the platform's applications extend beyond this to any science
task that leverages MediaWiki's capabilities. Have has been shown to be particularly
beneficial in situations requiring a collaborative approach to data analysis, enabling
teams to recover from system failures, integrate with existing MediaWiki systems, and
more.

This study investigates the explosive responses of turbulent jet flames in response to acoustic vibrations at various frequencies. In order to replicate these conditions, an experimental setup was created using a water-filled active flame chamber that allows for flame control through heated steam injection. Upon reaching a critical point, the reaction can be modeled using a simplified control system with adjusted steam temperature and flow rate. An accompanying mathematical model, based on Heo's active flame theory, simulates the dynamics of the reaction by incorporating the principles of thermodynamics and heat transfer. Furthermore, a machine learning approach known as the stochastic neighbor embedding is utilized to reduce the model's complexity for more manageable computation. The simplified model is then integrated into a generalized-epsilon linearsed Navier-Stokes model to investigate the impact of turbulent fluctuations. The combined computational approach yields predictions that closely match the observed experimental reactions, including the amplitude and frequency of oscillations.

Stereoscopic measurements of stellar oscillation frequencies and stellar surface properties can be used to determine the internal structure and composition of stars through linear inverse theory. This approach yields a set of orthogonal functions known as modes, where any surface quantity can be represented as a combination of modes weighted by corresponding coefficients. It has been shown that the modes and coefficients exhibit distinct interpretive significance. Furthermore, a numerical procedure has been developed to compute these modes and a specific linear combination of modes can be identified, where the associated coefficients are equal, facilitating their observational determination. This study examines the characteristics of these functions with over a hundred thousand variations in stellar parameters across various stellar types and finds that modes generally display characteristic structures, including functions with multiple extrema during stellar evolution and changes in form when crossing convection zones. With around a hundred thousand computed modes, it is also demonstrated that surface index changes during a star's evolution correlate with variations in its dominant internal structure. The study also explores the connection between index steps and stellar components and identifies groups of stars with similar index values. Additionally, this research fits observed stellar oscillation periods using linear combinations of modes and demonstrates that model-derived coefficients of fundamental modes provide an accurate and efficient method for fitting data with significantly fewer parameters than the full mode functions.

A type of collective behavior in dynamical systems known as a traveling chimera state combines coexisting synchronized and desynchronized dynamics. Due to its hybrid nature, it has long been challenging to fully characterize. Here, we introduce an entirely different approach to identifying traveling chimera states, one that is both exhaustive and applies to a wide range of network configurations. Our method also leads to a classification of all possible dynamic patterns in networks of interacting oscillators. As an application, we use our approach to design a strategy for identifying traveling chimera states that are robust to changes in network structure.

A comprehensive analysis of two-dimensional cluster kinetics on a square lattice has been carried out for species that interact at neighboring sites using a modified version of the Potts model. We examined how varying the strength of the inter-site interaction and temperature affect an equal initial mixture of two such species. Our findings, presented as phase diagrams, reveal three distinct regions: a high-temperature and high-density area where two separate temperatures are needed to achieve phase separation within a reasonable timeframe, as well as two areas where separation occurs both quickly and slowly with a single temperature. At lower temperatures or higher densities, however, separation requires a specific critical value which can be influenced by the inter-site interaction. Our simulations were also conducted with initial conditions representing a sudden change from a fully mixed state, resulting in the development of characteristic dynamics and evolving morphologies governed by the evolution of interface curvature.

We investigate the impact of ultralight dark matter on neutrinoless double beta decay, Neutrino DM halo forming a background that may interfere with experimental signals. The frequency of halo particles at Earth's location depends on ultralight DM properties and the position within the galaxy, leading to oscillating modulations in the Neutrino DM flux. This could provide insight into the mass and decay constants of DM particles through analysis of neutrino data. In addition, we consider the effects of Neutrino DM interactions on Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the Cosmic Microwave Background, which place stringent constraints on the neutrino-DM interaction strength. The level of these interactions also influences the structure formation of dark matter halos, potentially providing further constraints. However, we find that in regions of high matter density, such as the galactic center, neutrino reactions can be so intense that halos transition to mixed phases of neutrino gas and dark matter clumps, affecting structure formation in those areas.

Observations of solar synchrotron radiation in the UHE frequency range have been detected, and to understand this phenomenon, we modeled the contribution of ultra-high energy photons arriving from the same direction as the solar flow. Given that these high-energy particles are confined by the solar magnetic field, their contribution to observed synchrotron radiation depends heavily on the energy and magnetic field parameters. As a result, some sharp peaks in the modeled energy spectrum may not be characteristic features, and instead, the shape of the spectrum is likely influenced by the distribution of cosmic ray protons on Earth.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a modified version of general relativity that aligns with the equivalence principle and Einstein's field equations. In this research, nonlocal gravity theory is reformulated using tetrads, which provides the basis for analyzing fractional derivatives within the theory. This tetrad-based approach reveals that the equivalence principle necessitates nonlocal connections to be defined in terms of their own lower-order history, which is similar to defining local connections in terms of their corresponding lower-order tetrads. Furthermore, the choice of nonlocal connections represents an additional degree of freedom in the theory. When equivalent to the standard derivative connection, the action's nonlocal coefficients lead to a specific nonlocal relationship between the tetrads and their corresponding nonlocal connections.

Conflicting updates pose a significant challenge in replicated storage systems, particularly when maintaining the same operation order across multiple locations is impractical or too costly. To preserve consistent state and prevent the operation stack from growing indefinitely, systems must either discard some operations or notify users of the conflicts. The Eliminate-Win design framework ensures operations are never deleted nor pending, allowing for high availability, low latency, and strong durability. This framework's core principles are as follows: first, the system partitions operations into two categories - accepted and rejected; second, it decides the acceptance or rejection of an operation based on a quorum-based decision process; third, the system ensures the same decision is made at each location by providing a partially ordered configuration to users' applications. Due to its simplicity, ease of analysis, and versatility, the Eliminate-Win framework is applicable to a range of systems, including CRDS, CAS, arrays, and maps. Notably, our research demonstrates the systems based on this framework can ensure eventual consistency, through techniques like versioning, can eliminate 50% of conflicts without pending operations, and provide at least 10x better availability compared to systems requiring total order configuration.

To better understand the functional composition of genetic variants associated with different traits, we used high-throughput genomic data from the Functional Genomics Genotype Expression Consensus Project in a wide range of genome-wide association studies across 18 different human traits including height, weight at birth and adult stature, as well as 15 other conditions. We compared different measures of variant association with these traits and found that in at least 13 out of 18 cases, CNV-GTE scores were able to accurately predict association patterns. Furthermore, we used high-throughput sequencing to compare the results of genome-wide association studies with those of genotyping arrays and found that these sequencing samples had higher resolution in regions with high functional activity. This improvement in prediction ability was also evident in raw association signals obtained from both genome-wide association studies in European and African populations. We also found evidence of non-linear relationships between genotype and trait in approximately 40% of explored regions.

This study discusses the significance and technical aspects of using minor collision events in hadron physics experiments, with a focus on improving physics capabilities, and explores how this approach can be employed to detect heavy particles or study rare phenomena in searches using leptons or jets at hadron colliders.

Observations of low-mass X-ray binaries within the Milky Way and magnetars within the galaxy have shown that their recurrence intervals vary from under a year to over a decade. A key feature of these X-ray binaries located near the center of the galaxy is their significantly longer recurrence periods, often exceeding a year. A new theory proposes that their recurrence patterns are influenced by an external factor yet to be identified. According to this theory, there are two distinct populations of these X-ray binaries, with shorter periods likely overflowing on their own, while those with longer periods, especially near the galaxy's center, may require an additional trigger. Notably, the distribution of recurrence intervals of these X-ray binaries located near the galaxy's center aligns with that of the pulsars population known as the "Hulse-Taylor pulsars," suggesting a possible similarity in their underlying physical properties. As a result of this, the proposed model predicts a similar intensity in the high-energy emission from these X-ray binaries as observed in other wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation. However, thorough searches for such high-energy emission have so far yielded no confirmatory evidence.

A new proposal is made to expand the ADEV line for characterizing time variability in gravitational detectors by including data from multiple tests. Specifically, the line is defined as the average time variability across tests when adjusted for their respective sensitivity volumes. The concept of the ADEV line with a multi-test approach is introduced and its advantages are discussed, including the ability to combine data from tests conducted under different conditions to identify patterns that affect the detectors in various environments. This new line can also detect variability that may not appear in all tests and supports future developments of gravitational wave detectors by allowing for a broader range of tests and the use of different frequencies. The method is then applied to current atomic clock and pulsar timing array experiments to compare the performance of these tests and discuss their potential for detecting patterned variations on the ADEV plot.

We investigated 84-107 $\mu$Jy radio sources in the Southern Sky Survey using LOFAR, covering 6000 square degrees of the sky between 115 and 165 MHz. A new dataset is now available consisting of 2-bit intensity maps which are ideal for stack-infinite techniques. To reveal features that are not visible individually due to instrument sensitivity or resolution limitations, we performed a series of stacked analyses using various frequency ranges, spatial scales, and polarization components. Our findings show an unusual frequency distribution characterized by two separate power laws separated by a breakpoint in the range of 4-8 Hz, consistent with previous low-frequency findings but also supported at higher frequencies. A broken power law model fits our data well. We observed source compactness to decrease with increasing frequency resolution but stabilize at higher frequencies for sources compact at lower frequencies. The source compactness appears unrelated to source brightness when observed over a wide frequency range. Source ellipticity seems unaffected by frequency but exhibits a distinct pattern when examined at different spatial scales. Source compactness and ellipticity are also uncorrelated. Our research indicates a possible weak correlation between source compactness and total intensity in a specific scale range of 0.1 to 1.0 MHz at frequencies below 150 MHz. Additionally, sources with similar compactness seem to exhibit comparable morphological features. Astronomical phenomena such as supernovae, massive star outbursts, and luminous outflows from massive stars often result in the rapid release of energy, which can create intense shocks and affect the surrounding environment. To better understand this complex interaction, researchers used three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations to investigate how radiative and ionizing feedback influences the behavior of outbursts and surrounding stellar winds. Their findings revealed a critical role of ionizing radiation in enabling the propagation of outbursts, which become stalled due to solar-like feedback when this source of energy is suppressed. They also discovered distinct morphological patterns, such as finger-like and spherical shapes, that depend on the size of the outburst and the surrounding wind. These particular shapes may be relevant to understanding cosmic phenomena such as supernovae with irregular light curves and asymmetric explosions.

We introduce a family of objects known as geometric modularity spaces, which link to paramodular modular varieties and provide a link to proofs of geometric modularity for certain families of p-wild modular representations of finite group type. We demonstrate that geometric modularity holds for these representations by geometricity of modularity spaces, which in turn follows from good reduction properties after suitable semisimplification. Additionally, these proofs of geometric modularity apply to mixed motivic weights, including an new insight into the nature of a family of mathematical weights called Hodge--Tate weights.

Under specific circumstances, the electron-phonon and spin-vibration interactions transform into effective dynamic processes when considering the derivatives with respect to time. This phenomenon arises due to the incorporation of mass into the Hamiltonian model, which generates vibration-induced electron hopping variations and subsequent retrieval. As a consequence, next-generation materials that emit sound could experience time-dependent electron-phonon coupling, ultimately leading to induced energy and spin transformations.

$\tau$-tilting theory, a relatively new area within representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras by Iyama and Reiten, has quickly gained significance and we aim to provide a concise yet comprehensive overview of this theory in this introduction. Specifically, we will discuss the combinatorial aspects associated with $\tau$-tilting theory, as well as its connections to other areas, such as cluster tilting theory and Galois corings.

Understanding how to map natural language sentences into the correct meaning is a significant challenge in the field of NLP. Due to limited annotated data for this task, researchers often rely on using Natural Language Understanding (NLU) predictions from general-purpose models to evaluate the correctness of semantic mappings. The objective of this study is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the assumptions made about the NLP system in the Zero-shot Code Search (Zecs) task. The Zecs task involves linking source code to its corresponding natural language description among a set of alternative sources. We utilize Natural Language Inference (NLI) models to assess the NLP system's outputs in this context. The results of our experiments reveal that employing an probabilistic framework to model the distribution of outcomes, rather than just selecting the single best match, yields a substantial improvement in model performance. Furthermore, we show that the use of code-semantics pairs that are marginally scored is also beneficial. These findings suggest that searching for the natural language description that perfectly matches the source code's meaning is an inadequate approach to solve the Zecs task, prompting us to propose a new method called Margin-informed Zipfian Descent (MZD). Finally, all code, natural language descriptions, and detailed results are made available online.

Automated driving systems require the ability to predict dangers from short video clips during lane changes. Using computer vision, we can extract dangerous actions by analyzing video footage and predicting how other vehicles might move. To achieve this, we developed a framework that uses deep spatiotemporal neural networks to analyze video clips and identify hazardous actions like braking, speeding, and maintaining a steady speed. The framework includes three approaches based on flow fields that transfer segmentation masks. By evaluating these approaches, we found the SuperPoint+Lightweight-Mask Transformer network to be the most effective. It outperformed other methods and achieved an F-score of 0.839, demonstrating its efficiency and robustness. We also optimized the network by reducing its size and improving real-time performance while maintaining its accuracy.
