To enhance the connection between theoretical calculations and experimental measurements in quantum field theory, accurate amplitude evaluations must incorporate the effects materialized in such measurements. While rational approximations theoretically assume idealized, massless particles with perfect energy directionality, actual measurements are complicated by the presence of massive ones and scalar virtual particles within quantum field theory frameworks. As a result, new formalism is required to apply these assessments to practical, measurable situations. In response, the generalized quadratic approximation (ZIT) is introduced as an effective tool that accounts for the theoretical assessment of quantum field theory frameworks and field correlators in this context. Furthermore, the approach's capabilities are showcased through the quadratic evaluation of Higgs boson production through gluon fusion with transverse momentum smearing, yielding a significant improvement in agreement with direct diphoton decay threshold estimates.

Observing high-energy photons, typically done with satellites like Swift/GRE, plays a crucial role in classifying Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs). To explore this further, we analyzed 44 GRBs to examine the relationship between high-energy photon durations and the optical afterglow brightness, denoted as $t_{\rm peak}$, after normalizing their values. Through this analysis, we discovered a distinct correlation with four distinct phases, each following a parabolic trajectory in a log-log plot. These phases can be mathematically expressed as equations for $\log_{10} T_{\rm p}^{\rm norm}$ in terms of $\log_{10} T_{\rm p}^{\rm norm}(0)$ and $\log_{10} T_{\rm p}^{\rm norm}(1)$, where $T_{\rm p}^{\rm norm}$ represents the normalized peak time and $T_{\rm p}^{\rm norm}(0)$ and $T_{\rm p}^{\rm norm}(1)$ are scaling factors representing transitions between phases. To better understand these findings, we proposed a dual-density wave model that envisions a burst as two opposing shock waves expanding within a medium, each shock producing a high-energy photon and a afterglow, respectively. This model revealed that the transition from one phase to another is marked by an interaction between the pair of shock waves at a critical point of overlap

A bipartite vertex division of a graph $G$ occurs when its vertices are separated into three groups, $V_1$, $V_2$, and $V_3$, such that the two subsets, $V_1$ and $V_3$, form a specified subgraph type $\mathcal{H}$, with $V_2$ making up the remaining vertices. When restricting $V_1$ to be strictly smaller than $V_3$, we denote this as $V_1 \prec V_3$. This paper presents a method to divide certain classes of bipartite graphs, specifically those containing a path of length five, a cycle of length six, or both, into graphs with the same size subsets, using parameters that are productive in a limited number of variables related to the graph itself. This approach does not, however, apply to graphs that contain only a path of length four.

Our research targets improving the performance of deep neural network models across a range of scenarios in incremental learning settings. We observe that standard retraining methods, while commonly used to adjust model decision boundaries, can lead to significant accuracy drops and potential security vulnerabilities. We propose evaluating less intrusive alternative approaches for feature-space modifications. We specifically examine three methods: Contrastive Learning, Metric Learning and Contrastive Free Approach, in relation to multiple dataset expansions. Each method's resilience to overfitting and their influence on feature space characteristics in relation to class distribution are analyzed. We particularly focus on instructive space features. Our assessment shows that the Contrastive Free Approach, despite its basic nature, delivers the most balanced and diverse feature space, resulting in enhanced space efficiency and overall model performance.

This research delves into the development of a bipedal locomotion system, assisted by propellants, for a two-wheeled robot. Utilizing a simplified 7-degree-of-freedom kinematic model, we applied a minimum-jerk trajectory planning method to generate natural joint trajectories for the robot's bipedal movement. To ensure a gait that maintains balance and adheres to constraints, our established contact phase stability condition was used to validate our results. Through simulative tests using MuJoCo, we demonstrated that the designed leg system can execute a variety of dynamic movements, assisted by propellants, and respond to external disturbances effectively, while also conserving energy. Furthermore, our joint position control system's ability to achieve optimal joint positioning was confirmed by comparing it to open-loop execution, while also detecting and compensating for significant motor friction losses, enabling the robot to perform complex maneuvers and traverse various terrains with ease. Our propellant-assisted locomotion system not only exhibits improved efficiency but also exhibits the ability to execute a wider range of dynamic movements and recover from significant losses, while also exhibiting fuel consumption levels comparable to other state-of-the-art leg systems.

Let $K$ be a field and $V$ be a domain valued in $K$. We investigate conditions under which the set of maximal ideals in $V$ corresponds bijectively to the set of residue classes in $K$ under a specific ideal completion, and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for this to occur, also exploring its implications in valued domains.

To bypass Titan's memory wall, a new technique called HyperDegradation is proposed, which involves intentionally reducing the CPU's capabilities in order to enhance its performance. By moving the CPU out of the superscalar, high-frequency realm and into a simpler, single-threaded, low-frequency effective CPU model, HyperDegradation achieves significant performance improvements, in some cases up to 5x better than traditional degradation models. A novel code transformation algorithm and a straightforward execution simulation are developed to facilitate HyperDegradation, which surprisingly requires minimal additional effort, in some cases just one straightforward execution. A diverse set of real-world benchmarks are used to validate the universal applicability of HyperDegradation, and its potential to overcome Silicon scalability limitations in the future are explored, in conjunction with degradation models suited for neuromorphic and many-core systems.

Building on previous research, we examine the possibility of a two-Higgs-doublet model with a singular singlet component, in which the neutral singlet Higgs boson interacts with top quarks. Employing an effective theory approach with the assumption that the particle corresponding to the scalar sector is heavier than the current LHC limits, the model allows the neutral Higgs boson to explain the g-2 anomaly while avoiding detection through the di-Higgs boson process measured by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Considering the 14 TeV heavy-ion collisions at the LHC, the prompt photoproduction process could potentially detect the charged Higgs boson through its decay into a top quark and a photon, as the radiative decay of the heavy scalar Higgs boson to a bottom quark and the neutral Higgs boson is inaccessible due to color conservation, thereby restricting the parameter space of the model.

Using the formalism of stochastic differential equations, we derive a method to estimate the intensity of gamma rays from data that does not require a model. This approach is applied to data from the Fermi-LAT, specifically from 2008 to 2018, and we find no significant evidence of a gamma ray belt in the all-electron spectrum. However, assuming a model where dark matter annihilates into quarks, we do have the ability to place constraints on the annihilation cross section based on data that does not require a model.

A knot or link can be transformed into an unknot or unlinked state through a sequence of Reidemeister type I and II moves, exclusively for classical knots and links, in a thorough analysis of their arrangement diagrams. We introduce the concept of the minimum crossing number, defined by the lowest number of crossings in an n-stranded framework that represents a distinct minimum crossing number for any number of strands. A newly formulated minimum crossing number property is then presented, consisting of four conditions. By defining the thickness of a link based on its ability to represent an unlinked state with its component threads, the minimum crossing number property can be simplified to verify whether a link is unlinked. Utilizing this revised definition, the unlinked state of several previously reported pseudo-knots and certain other knots or links can be confirmed, including 11 of 24 torus knots or links unlinked, and a fraction of Flows' pseudo-knots unlinked in the book Flows on Knots and Paths (II). Additionally, multiple newly identified unlinked pseudo-knots and pseudo-knots families are identified based on minimum crossing number characteristic.

We prove that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve $\Gamma$ over a semifield $K\langle t\rangle$ is a finite dimensional $K$-tropical vector space whose semifield of endomorphisms is isomorphic to $K\langle t\rangle$. This implies that the rational function semifield of $\Gamma$ behaves like a finite dimensional $K\langle t\rangle$-tropical vector space.

We demonstrate that both the length and complexity of a Vassiliev characteristic of order three for the Fox-Hatcher loop in a thickened surface can be precisely determined by a single closed curve on the underlying surface. This finding also enables us to replicate a result by Lebedsky for the standard knot in a thickened annulus using our method. Moreover, we provide a closed-form equation for the third coefficient of a series expansion related to a 2-parameter family of loops in a thickened surface. This equation can be interpreted as reflecting the combined effects of length, complexity, and genus in a specific direction from the Fox-Hatcher loop. The third coefficient's value in a thickened surface is purely geometric and holds true for any parameterization. We further establish a correlation between this coefficient and a variation of the Hopf invariant derived from a map between two 2-spheres.

New research by the KATRIN team has established rigorous measurements of neutrino mass consequences in beta decay, yielding stringent constraints on the electron neutrino mass spectrum at very low energies. These constraints can be reinterpreted to set a minimum threshold for neutrino masses, leveraging the well-understood relationships between neutrino oscillation parameters and mass. Based on Koshiba Astrophysical Neutrino Observatory data, the minimum mass difference for neutrino and antineutrino states has been determined to be at least $0.12\,\con{eV\,c^{-2}}$ at a $3\sigma$ confidence level, with a corresponding mass spectrum that could potentially influence the expansion rate of the early universe. In the radiation-dominated era of the universe, neutrinos might have existed in a semi-classical state, subject to general relativity and possibly detectable through future experiments like CONNEXITY.

As matrizes são ferramentas amplamente utilizadas em diversas áreas, como computação gráfica, onde uma unidade gráfica pode calcular um produto de matrizes de 4x4 com 64 elementos de forma extremamente rápida. Com base nessa eficiência, este trabalho propõe utilizar um processador integrado à unidade gráfica para realizar cálculos de matrizes em contextos educacionais. A abordagem envolve adaptação do código da matriz sequencial para um programa paralelo, que faz uso de threads, com o objetivo de demonstrar como o processo de paralelização pode ser implementada de maneira prática. Este trabalho foi realizado no ambiente Windows, comparando as duas abordagens através de medições de tempo de execução com um cronômetro de alta precisão. Os resultados obtidos foram coletados para cada teste e permitem avaliar a eficácia do processo de paralelização na aumentação do desempenho do programa.

Our proposed method enables a group of robots to work together effectively in a dynamic and unpredictable environment. Our system works by having each robot identify possible roles, with the most suitable robot being selected to perform a specific task. A pre-determined hierarchy of roles is used to choose the leading robot, with any remaining robots following the leader. This system has been successfully implemented in a simulation of a search and capture scenario, where one agent acts as the leader and the others follow, consistently outperforming other collaborative approaches in terms of success rate. Furthermore, our role-based leadership protocol is the first of its kind to achieve consistent results across a wide range of team sizes. With only five agents, our approach was found to be nearly as successful as other methods, but outperformed them significantly when team sizes increased to 20 agents or more. With these results, role-based multi-agent systems have been shown to be a reliable option for collaboration in complex scenarios, with our method providing role assignments that are optimal from a computational perspective.

To bypass the limitations of tree-level amplitude calculations in quantum field theory, our group developed a method using world-line paths to incorporate both real and virtual corrections, which yields a comprehensive series of 'IR-enhanced' corrections beyond leading order while maintaining unitarity. This novel approach led to the discovery of an additional type of enhancement, referred to as the 'super-leading colour' effect, absent in traditional perturbation theory, resulting in significant scattering patterns producing highly energetic intermediate states connected by soft gluons. Consequently, standard perturbative QCD theories may fall short in describing processes within proton collisions driven by these effects, notably impacting the theoretical predictions for Higgs boson production through boson boson fusion, and possibly other processes such as top quark pair hadronization, where our group's IR-enhanced methodology offers an alternative perspective, and we will discuss a few case studies. Moreover, we aim to explain the connection between our world-line formalism and effective field theories like SCET, in the context of multi-loop factorization structures, and discuss the necessary conditions that any effective theory design must satisfy, specifically the geometric properties of nested and hierarchical loop integrals.

In this report, we examine the vulnerabilities of vertical federated learning VFL protocols to two types of privacy breaches committed by an adversary with access to a single row of data. The research focuses on three prominent VFL protocols utilizing machine learning models for row-based prediction. The research reveals that without sufficient defensive measures, these protocols are susceptible to accurate privacy assaults in a error-free setting. The investigation spans both deterministic and probabilistic VFL protocols, and we demonstrate that assault accuracy can be significantly improved by incorporating randomness into the protocols. The research primarily targets assumptions made about the adversary in VFL, and our findings may guide users in assessing the risks and benefits of employing specific VFL protocols.

Nonparametric density estimation techniques, specifically kernel and kernel density estimation (KDE), provide crucial insights into understanding and visualizing large datasets, yet they struggle with scalability when applied to them. Traditional KDE faces additional challenges due to its O(n^2) computational demands, making three-dimensional visualization of vast datasets particularly difficult. To address these issues, we introduce a novel, innovative approach for high-dimensional data visualization and analysis consisting of two primary components. Initially, we employ a set of orthogonal and pairwise independent pseudo-random fourier traits to map data into binary values, thereby reducing data dimensionality by a factor of n and enabling efficient processing. Subsequently, we utilize linear kernel estimation on this transformed, reduced dataset to create an accurate and efficient representation of the data's underlying structure, allowing for rapid (O(n)) calculation of the estimate at any given point. Our method showcases remarkable advantages over traditional techniques including smooth histograms, strip plots, and KDE, providing a level of precision and speed previously unattainable when working with vast datasets, and demonstrating particular utility in visualizing and analyzing time-series data in the context of financial applications.

We propose a new approach using Cartesian Partitions to achieve the representation of a product group in a wreath framework, specifically for $G^n \tau_m$ where the permutation group $G \tau_m$ is a wreath product of two groups $G \tau_1$ or $G \tau_2$. Our method extends previous results, as it can derive the representation of $G^n \tau_m$ from the representation of its constituent parts, $G^n \tau_1$ or $G^n \tau_2$.

We investigate conformally flat hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ by defining a M\"obius structure using the M\"obius conformal factor and principal curvatures, and by demonstrating that a lower bound for the M\"obius scalar curvature implies a lower bound for the M\"obius normal curvature, particularly in the case of $\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ symmetry.

Automated cardiac magnetic resonance (MRI) image segmentation is an essential initial step in analyzing MRI data. Traditionally, MRI images have been segmented accurately, making analysis straightforward. However, there are rare heart defects as heart diseases, making MRI interpretation complex due to poor image quality and unusual anatomy. Furthermore, MRI scanning can be costly and time-consuming. Utilizing MRI images for surgical Scheduling, although beneficial, also has its drawbacks. Therefore, identifying the best surgical scheduling strategy is crucial. In this investigation, we evaluated how magnetic resonance (MRI) data functions for surgical scheduling, focusing on three primary aspects: (1) MRI image quality in rare heart defects, (2) magnetic resonance (MRI) images' ability to accurately predict surgery duration in patients with rare heart defects, and (3) MRI images' ability to provide insights into surgery complexity. We conducted this study by using U-Net to scan MRI images and obtain the results. Ultrasound network unit is used to obtain the required result. It was trained by using 119 patients with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy data. It was then scanned on 24 patients with transposition of great arteries data. It was then correlated with surgery duration and surgery complexity. It was found that the U-Net model performed well in adult cardiac conditions but performed poorly in rare congenital heart conditions. It was also observed that the magnetic resonance (MRI) data did not seem to include relevant information to predict surgery duration and surgery complexity.

A new class of function spaces, named $W^{1,q}st$, is defined with respect to a given metric and collection of functions that satisfy a specific condition known as strict inequality. These new spaces are shown to be equivalent to a previously defined space by Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré when the underlying measure has no singular components. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the space $W^{1,q}st$ maintains the same closure properties and can be independently characterized through a specific norm inequality. The characterization of these spaces leads to an established and practical inequality involving the norm. In addition, the paper provides the required conditions for the continuity and semicontinuity functions within the $W^{1,q}st$ space. Finally, the concepts of subdifferential and distributional derivative are introduced.

A novel SWIPT-enabled wireless system, which utilizes energy-harvesting capable receivers, is investigated in this paper. In order to enhance overall network performance, a total energy maximization problem is formulated by considering a vector objective function. The resulting optimization issue, which aims to optimize allocatable subchannel and power resources, results in the development of a priority-based energy allocation scheme. To solve this problem, a tailored penalty method, which employs a convex approximation technique, is proposed. In addition, a suitable energy-utility utility function is suggested, which facilitates an efficient harmonic search algorithm for finding near-optimal solutions. The algorithm's performance is further analyzed through a convergence proof, which demonstrates its reliability. The results, which are validated through numerical examples, illustrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the penalty method and algorithm. Moreover, the results show that increasing priority differences leads to lower total energy, while near-equitable energy allocation can be achieved through suitable utility function selection, regardless of energy-priority levels.

We analyze all-items based reinforcement learning under a Markov decision process framework, a crucial step in developing efficient healthcare interventions through personalized learning. A key challenge in this field is overcoming exploration bias, where patients with poor outcomes experience greater improvement than those with successful results. To address this, we use a standard smoothness assumption from reinforcement learning to create a all-items efficient algorithm achieving $\tilde{O}(K^{4/3}k^{1/3}k^{1/3}\sqrt{ horizon})$ regret. Under stronger k-gram smoothness, we further develop an efficient algorithm with $\tilde{O}(K^{5/3}k^{2/3}\sqrt{ horizon})$ regret. These achievements mark the first efficient all-items efficient results under a standard reinforcement learning horizon setting. Our findings theoretically justify the value of code-based healthcare experimentation at all items. Our code-based learning approach can also be applied under强化 learning general theory. Under linear reinforcement learning assumptions, we show that our method uses $\tilde{O}(d^{4/3}k^{1/3}k^{1/3}\sqrt{ horizon})$ samples. In statistics, researchers often study how certain conditions and probabil frameworks interact to influence the extreme behavior of systems, particularly when focusing on the highest values within such systems. This work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of research on this topic, including studies on how such interactions affect both asymptotic and interaction-driven extreme behaviors in i.i.d. settings. The work also delves into univariate and multivariate cases, as well as applications to random environments and disordered systems. Furthermore, an investigation into how subexponential and rapidly varying tail behaviors influence extreme dynamics in two-layer models is included. The two-layer models, in turn, are examined in light of their relevance to financial and insurance systems, necessitating careful analysis of tail dependencies across multiple levels of influence.

Resolving the discrepancy between words' multiple meanings, a persistent issue in NLP, remains insufficiently addressed, despite numerous advances in neural network-based translation quality. To mitigate this problem, leveraging post-training with high-quality data, we present a new approach that constructs a comprehensive word meaning clarification system, now known as CGlossBERT, by building upon the foundation of the renowned model, GlossBERT. We developed two novel preprocessing techniques to efficiently integrate pertinent post-training data from diverse sources, which encompasses Wikipedia, Google's word2vec, and BabelNet, resulting in a high-quality, multilingual dataset, BMBGloss. Our experimentally validated results, particularly in synonym recognition and word sense disambiguation, demonstrate superior performance compared to the baseline model, GlossBERT.

Multimodal instructional guides are commonly used in everyday life to help people learn various tasks from cooking and cleaning to assembling furniture and repairing vehicles.  In contrast to previous studies that focused on single-mode instructions, modern instructional guides integrate both visual and written directions, accounting for the significant role that these resources play in the typical learning process.  However, there has been limited research on developing and evaluating the effectiveness of these complex, multi-mode instructions.  This study fills that knowledge gap by creating and assessing the efficacy of sequencing multimodal instructional guides through a novel, comprehensive set of 100 tasks involving everyday electronics and appliances.  Our analysis of participant performance and difficulty levels, as well as related metadata, using statistical methods such as linear regression and ANOVA, yielded several important findings: (1) the use of multimodal instructions significantly enhances learner comprehension, (2) the general applicability of instructional guides can be effectively used to assess proficiency in a wide range of tasks, (3) beginning instructions with an overview image is a crucial factor in preventing confusion, (4) the absence of feedback in instructions may lead to misinterpretations, and (5) the presence of sub-steps in instructions promotes better comprehension.  These discoveries not only contribute valuable insights to the fields of human-computer interaction and education, but also inform the development of next-generation multimodal instructional guides.  Finally, our data and set of tools are available to facilitate further research into the creation and evaluation of complex, real

Recently, researchers have developed an improved version of the percolation model to model the dynamics of fire on slopes, known as the quench-percolation model. This new variant incorporates spatial correlations by utilizing a two-dimensional percolation lattice, and in a particular study, a dual-site bond Percolation lattice called the 'honeycomb-tree' was utilized. A novel type of percolation structure has been generated for Cayley trees by implementing the QPB, and it was observed that above the critical threshold, these structures exhibit two distinct phases, or clusters, that separate based on the branch factor of the tree. A theoretical analysis was also conducted to explain the critical values and a practical application was shown by generating these cluster-type structures and confirming the critical values through multiple simulations.

In this study, we derive an explicit formula for a specific class of polynomials, known as the universal Airy polynomials, defined by the recurrence relation and boundary conditions provided. Our findings indicate that these polynomials can be accurately described by a second-order differential equation, and for scaled indices, they satisfy the pure Airy recurrence relation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the universal Airy polynomials are orthogonal with respect to several weight functions, and for certain conditions, their coefficients are real. Our research also reveals a connection between the universal Airy polynomials and the Delangue polynomials, as well as an explicit expression for their generating function.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is limited by the angle at which the laser beam exits the detector's recycling system. A previously proposed method, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, can increase this angle and thus reduce the exit angle limitation. This design offers other potential benefits for gravitational wave detection, including enhancing the detection of rotating black hole mergers' higher harmonic signals. A change of one part in $10^{-4}$ in the detector's fundamental mode can significantly improve the detection of these waves. We analyzed the high-frequency sensitivity when implementing this technique in LIGO and found a 10 times gain can be achieved with a 4 times increase in the detector's circulating power. Additionally, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer may provide stability benefits due to its inherent symmetry, but the coupling of modes can hinder its performance. To address this, we propose an asymmetric design to decouple the modes and achieve mode purity, which also provides decoupled tunability for the detector's fundamental and higher mode resonances.

In high-frequency communications, multiple antenna systems are prevalent, and their performance heavily relies on accurate visibility data. However, traditional methods for obtaining visibility data assume that interference can be effectively separated, which isn't always feasible given the large number of antennas used. Assuming a certain level of unmodeled noise, our research investigates conditions under which certain system areas experience maximum interference without a clear boundary and others always have maximum interference but cannot be distinctly separated. Conditions for these conditions are derived and characterized by key factors including the number of antennas, system frequency, and noise levels. Map of conditions is created to provide guidance for designing new methods for efficient data access in multiple-antenna systems.

Our understanding of how protoplanetary disks lose heat is incomplete, particularly in terms of identifying specific cooling mechanisms. In some regions, especially near the midplane, the disks may not be optically thick enough for re-radiation to be effective. As a result, alternative cooling processes must dominate and could potentially lead to various physical phenomena, like the formation of dense structures. To investigate this, we developed a three-dimensional radiative transfer simulation of a protoplanetary disk using a simplified power-law viscosity model. Our simulation focuses on capturing the selforganizing structures that can form in these environments and we established empirical relations to predict the distribution of dust temperature, sublimation pressure, and midplane density in these regions.

A significant phenomenon observed in the Giant Rhodium-103 as well as in other nuclei is the giant dipole shape vibration, which is missing in most theoretical models. Studies reveal that this mode vibrates the two protons-neutrons clusters within a nucleus, deforming it into an ellipsoid. The energy of this mode is substantially higher than that of its counterpart within spherical nuclei. Theoretical calculations based on time-density functional theory, which employs a relativistic Lagrangian model, demonstrate that non-relativistic two-body forces resulting in the rich spin-isospin structure of the Rhombic Lagrangian lead to an excessively high energy for this mode. Excessively high energy would negatively impact the accuracy of nuclear matter predictions and the neutron star radius. To mitigate this, a relative contact term with a significantly higher stiffness is required. As a result, a distinctive feature emerges in neutron stars, characterized by a dense, compact core with the "Big Apple" structure.

Using spin-based isolated magnetic ions allows for the straightforward, spin-only description of many transition metal oxides via mean-field theory. However, this approximation fails to accurately represent the more complex electronic structure. To overcome this limitation, we used Density Functional Theory + Dynamic Mean-Field Theory (+Crispt-Cluster-Cluster-Exact-Map-Theorem) to more comprehensively examine the electronic and magnetic properties of SrMnO$_3$. This required the utilization of atomic orbitals with overlapping wave functions, which led to subtle shifts in the spectral features that matched experimental data. By using this level of theory, we were able to resolve the in-core spectrum, which revealed white-line and costep-structure features that matched experimental X-ray absorption and emission spectra data, which we used to refine our atomic orbitals + wave functions model. This allowed us to match the actual spectral features, which we used to resolve the "missing weight" issue, which we showed was largely due to coherent low-energy spectral weight, which we used to refine our atomic spectra model, which we showed was due to Hund's rule coupling, which we showed was largely due to coherent low-energy spectral weight, which we used to refine our atomic spectra model, which we showed was due to Hund's rule coupling, which we showed was largely due to coherent low-energy spectral weight.

We propose a new method for generating the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen entangling gate between atomic qubits that operates independently of the specific frequency of atomic interactions and remains stable despite changes in the atomic-mirror cavity. This method involves using a sum of frequencies technique in which a precise combination of microwave fields, each coupled to a different atomic-mirror cavity, causes a distinct atomic internal state to become linked to a different acoustic mode of the chip's phonon field. A key innovation of our approach is a novel sequence of laser pulses called a 'multi-sideband type reverse-Aharonov-Bohm clock', which acquires a phase related to the frequencies and numbers of atoms coupled to each atomic-mirror cavity. As long as at least two frequencies contribute equally, the gate's duration and quality will be largely unaffected by changes in these parameters, thus ensuring robust and reliable operation.

Recent high-resolution imaging techniques have enabled precise measurement of the lattice vibrations and electron movements within the perovskite structure of nanometer-scale particles. A new image has been generated that provides a detailed view of how atoms move within structural templates based on the perovskite lattice in these materials. A specific method was used to record the motion of atoms within these templates in a type of perovskite material that is not ferroelectric, specifically in the form of PbTiO3. A simulation was then used to verify the recorded motion of atoms, which was found to match the theoretical predictions. A more in-depth analysis of this recording has further revealed the existence of mixed phases within the perovskite material, which may have previously gone undetected due to masking effects from data noise, which has been reduced to as little as 10 parts in a hundred thousand. A specific method was used to filter out data noise, which was found to be caused by the random motion of air molecules. This method was demonstrated to be effective for studying the electron movements within the perovskite material, which should help to identify previously undetected mixed phases in the perovskite material.

Dirac metals belong to a category of quantum materials that can be considered as the extended version of quantum spin Hall insulators.  In this class of metals, the external magnetic field and spin-orbit coupling play a significant role in defining its properties, and strong interactions between particles can further shape its theoretical understanding.  A comprehensive model combining this metal's Dirac nature, Berry curvature effects and strong interactions has been developed, and its mean-field solution along with non-abelian and diagonal anomalous Hall effects can be achieved through a circulant matrix approach in this study.  As a result, it shows that strong interactions can cause a metal-insulator transition and give rise to a strongly correlated Dirac insulator which exhibits a large anomalous Hall conductivity characterized by a large Berry curvature in its band structure.

A frequently encountered phenomenon in nature and society is synchrony,
particularly when oscillating entities interact and synchronize their periodic
motions. Our proposed framework for analyzing systems comprising two entities
that exhibit bimodal behavior is the second of our sequential frameworks
previously developed to examine 1-to-N frequency relationships. This framework
is distinguished by its utilization of phase variables to define a system's state,
enabling the description of an 8-dimensional bimodal frequency and phase ratio
(bimodal FPR) landscape. Within this landscape, bimodal frequencies and phase
ratios are represented as distinct manifoles, and a bimodal state is modeled as
a curve defined by a set of parameters. The framework's applicability is
demonstrated through its adaptation to systems as diverse as mechanical coupled
pendulums, electronic circuits, and social interactions between two individuals
prone to mood swings. The discovery of this framework's ability to utilize a
bimodal frequency and phase ratio (Bimodal FPR) system of coordinates brings
about a unification of previously disparate descriptions of systems exhibiting
bimodal frequency and phase behavior. As a result, novel, general expressions
for bimodal periodic motions are derived, and an algorithm is established to
derive the underlying curve of such motions.

This study delves into the potential of the NA62 experiment to set stringent constraints on the neutral lepton, denoted as $N$, which is hypothesized to be part of a neutral lepton with a mass ranging from 125 MeV to 11 GeV. The analysis takes into consideration both production and decay processes of $N$ and is based on projected backgrounds and detection efficiencies of the experiment. The results show the ability of the experiment to confirm or disprove certain hypotheses regarding neutral leptons, even in scenarios where $N$ is not produced in specific decays such as $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. The outcome also highlights the importance of precise measurements in future experiments and can guide theoretical models to ensure they are consistent with experimental data.

In acoustic and electronic systems integrated into optical Sagnac interferometers, spatial asymmetry can lead to spectral shifts affecting ring-back resonance characteristics. These impacts must be considered when measuring the rotation rate using these types of sensors. The spectral shift in a gyroscope with an embedded Sagnac interferometer could be attributed to the 1964 discovery of the moving frame spectral shift anomaly by Gluckstone and Glaser, which was initially considered negligible but has been experimentally validated multiple times since then. This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of spectral shift anomalies occurring within a Sagnac interferometer situated in a rotating reference frame, including previous contradictory approaches to resolving these anomalies and their connection to electromagnetic induction in a moving circuit. A key contribution of this research is the derivation of a unifying spectral shift formula that accounts for spectral shifts caused by both the moving frame and the Sagnac effect, validated with existing experimental data from multiple groups as well as theoretical predictions for additional setups not yet tested in the laboratory. The analysis further highlights discrepancies in previous studies of spectral shifts in moving frames and suggests a need to revisit the spectral characteristics of moving circuits in relation to Ohm's law and Faraday's electromagnetic induction principle.

Kostant's original discovery showed the adjoint action of a differential polynomial on a Lie algebra element yields crystalline $\Lambda$-monomials, a key contribution to finding the Geometric Bracket Polynomial (GBP) in a Lie algebra. In this study, we adapt Kostant's method for semisimple parabolic subalgebras. By analyzing a specific orbit within a semisimple parabolic subalgebra of a simple Lie algebra of type $A$, we apply this method to determine the GBP in that algebra. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the formal power series obtained and the Grassmannian.

The popular N-gram language model is now largely overlooked, but we've discovered it's an ideal foundation for the residual learning technique. By utilizing it as a base, we've found that only minimal, high-level adjustments are needed. We've then proposed a simple yet effective method to create diverse texts with a single model. This approach, called the $n$-gram generator, has surpassed the performance of state-of-the-art models in several tasks such as stylistic transfer, old news revival, and free writing. Our findings also highlight the difficulty of generating diverse texts coherently. In addition, the $n$-gram generator serves as a straightforward yet groundbreaking approach to diversifying the current leading AI language models.

We establish a link between the group of $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties up to isomorphism and the automorphisms of log terminal Calabi-Yau threefolds, specifically relating to the group of Laurent operators.

Creating an efficient, reliable, and versatile 3D face reconstruction and landmark prediction model is a complex challenge in computer vision. Current methods often utilize weakly-supervised or unsupervised training, falling short in accuracy and versatility. In addition, many models struggle with diverse facial expressions, profiles, and occlusions, producing asymmetric outputs. To tackle these issues, we propose a novel, fully supervised approach called SADRNet, an innovative self-aligned dual-face prediction framework that excels in robust 3D face reconstruction and landmark prediction. SADRNet's framework predicts a dual face representation, allowing for symmetric output, and is supplied with ground truth information during training to supervise learning. Furthermore, we incorporate a corrective module to refine errors in faces outside the canonical view and produce high-quality texture colors. Extensive evaluations on the RAF-Occluded and FLAME20k datasets showcase SADRNet's superiority over competing models, highlighting its accuracy, versatility, and performance in processing challenging facial scenarios. SADRNet's results show improved precision in faces with diverse expressions, profiles, and occlusions, and recover occluded structures more effectively than current methods.

We propose a novel class of model frameworks that effectively capture the dynamic behavior of moments of charge under the influence of magnetic fields and Coriolis forces during the process of spontaneously disrupted translations. These models are constructed to be computationally streamlined while maintaining a precise level of accuracy. Our primary focus lies in accurately describing the movement of dipolar interactions as they transform from pinning effects to the emission of gravitational waves, all within the process of spontaneous disruption of translations. Our model effectively captures the pinning of dipoles in the presence of magnetic fields and the blocking of motion by the Coriolis force. Moreover, our model is capable of representing self-interacting fracton systems that emerge from the process of spontaneous disruption of translations.

A wide range of post-inflationary processes, such as gravitational wave production, dark matter condensation, and black hole formation, can result from an highly sensitive sensitive phase transition during the $\alpha$-attractor inflation period. During this phase, a sudden disruption in the $\beta$-oscillation can trigger a resonance effect, leading to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). We investigated whether PBHs can form from a sensitive phase transition, such as the avoidance of a gravitational wave peak. It was found that despite the sensitive nature of disruption in the $\alpha$-attractor inflation, it can lead to the formation of PBHs over a wide range of masses ($10^{-4}c_{*}^{2}10^{3}M_{\odot}$). Moreover, current constraints from gamma-ray bursts, gamma-ray background, and microlensing can be met when the speed of the turbulence $c_{*}$ is set to $10^{-3}$. As an example, we chose the $\beta$-oscillation to be caused by axion moduli inflation, which can lead to the formation of PBHs during its $\alpha$-attractor phase, resulting in a PBH mass range ($10^{3}-10^{4}M_{\odet}$) that correlates with the observed lensing events of Icarus and OGLE.

Given a labeled ordered tree, a depth-based equivalence is established between two vertices. Building on this, the concept of extreme or "deepest" vertices in direction $d$ and集 (set) of such vertices, denoted as $V_d$, is defined. This definition is applied to various types of trees, including binary trees, full binary trees, and general ordered trees. A key property of these deepest vertices sets is examined, specifically in the context of a random ordered tree $T_n$ of size $n$, where the number of pairs of vertices at the same greatest depth in a specific direction is counted. The asymptotic behavior of this count is determined, and it is discovered that as $d$ increases, the set $V_d$ forms a path with probability approaching one. Additionally, the lengths of these deepest branches in $T_n$ are characterized by providing exact expected values and asymptotic variance for the case $d=3$. A connection between $V_3$ and closed walks on a directed triangular triangular triangular triangle is also established, and it is shown that the distribution of lengths of deepest branches in $T_n$ is related to the number of directed triangular triangular triangular triangle closed walks of a specific length. A bijection with weighted rooted trees is also discovered.

In election tallying, ensuring the accuracy of vote counts stands as a crucial challenge. Traditional methods manually compare total votes declared with those individually counted on each ballot to identify any discrepancies. To expedite this comparison, we propose a novel technique that utilizes information from declared totals to correct the count of individual ballots. By incorporating constraint optimization and a specialized variant of Dynamic Time Warping called Informed Time Warping, we aim to produce precise and robust results. Our tests compare various scoring functions, including ordinary least squares, informed regression, inigDTW, and inigTW, against their conventional counterparts, showing significant improvements through better F-scores and mean absolute errors.

Achieving precise interpolation in time series modeling through increased model complexity has gained significant interest. Despite the effectiveness of neural network auto-regressive models in practice, theoretical understanding in the context of over-parameterization remains limited. A key challenge in these models is balancing model complexity with model variability to ensure optimal performance in the presence of noise. A simple linear linear regression model with least squares optimization was analyzed in a high-dimensional setting with independent errors, yielding optimal variance-complexity balance. However, extending this analysis to models that incorporate temporal dependencies proved difficult due to the covariance matrix's difficulty. A novel regression model was proposed that incorporates temporal dependencies in a straightforward manner, allowing for explicit expression of the covariance matrix. It was shown that the same optimal balance can be achieved in this model, and a perturbation argument was employed to show distinct test loss behaviors in under and over-parameterized regimes, resembling global minima and spurious minima respectively. The implications of these findings in the context of over-parameterization were discussed, and the advantages of this novel setting along with potential directions for future research were outlined.

This work is called CABIN, which is an innovative deep learning framework focused on speech enhancement using only a single microphone. The framework employs attention mechanisms to allow the model to selectively focus on relevant parts of the input and utilize both previous and future information from the surrounding context through a type of attention network called Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory. Initially the model uses a time-domain approach to maintain spectral phase consistency before the attention bidirectional long short-term memory layer then handles frequency phase estimation. This hybrid method leads to more realistic results in speech reconstruction. CABIN demonstrates significant performance in this single microphone speech enhancement application through detailed objective and subjective evaluations.

An unaddressed public health threat looms large in the form of bio-weapons being covertly disseminated by wolves hiding among sheep. Unlike previous studies using agricultural metaphors, the inconsiderate behavior of sheep towards one another is now replaced by a far more dangerous neglect towards potential predators. 

When a wolf manages to go undetected, it finds itself in a perfect disguise among the flock, using the covering of sheep to spread a deadly pathogen among the flock with ease. 

Unfortunately, the sheep's natural tendency for herd behavior facilitates the spread of the pathogen, as they either directly interact or come into close proximity with one another. 

Despite the evident signs of lethargy, coughing, and fever in infected sheep, the flock's natural inclination to stay together hinders their ability to isolate the infected, thus allowing the pathogen to spread with even greater efficiency. 

This unfortunate scenario may sadly continue to play out as long as humans fail to distinguish themselves from sheep and instead choose to follow the example set by a wolf hiding among the flock.

We develop a causal policy that enables a battery storage system to partake in a decentralized market by combining an approximate model of future trades with real-time measurements of past transactions. Initially, we examine a scenario where the market operates as an auction, utilizing a learning-based approach to minimize transaction costs. Secondly, we explore a scenario where the market functions through price formation, utilizing first-best social welfare optimization to minimize the combined transaction costs and energy misallocation. In both instances, our method avoids requiring prior knowledge of the probability distribution of future transactions. Empirical results reveal that our algorithm produces efficient outcomes and avoids unbounded energy storage fluctuations. A robust implementation of this method is presented in the form of mixed integer linear programming.

The electronic transformations in atoms and molecules following extreme ultraviolet and X-ray photon absorption have been extensively researched using various spectroscopic techniques. A newly developed method, utilizing attosecond mammography, allows for imaging electron density distributions undergoing transformation by exploiting the attenuation of coherent, broadband attosecond streaking pulses. A previously observed phenomenon, the sudden Absorption edge step, provides an reference point for imaging other electron density features, such as resonantly enhanced structures and the complex dynamics of the Auger decay that ensues after mantle absorption of an X-ray photon. This research offers new insights into the shape of step structure in time and space as well as a detailed examination of electron density dynamics during and following the various stages of the three-body collisional process. A simulated experiment, employing a resonantly enhanced scheme, also suggests a potential method for collecting comprehensive data sets that capture comprehensive electron density dynamics in Time-Resolved Attosecond X-ray Streaking experiments.

Using simplified global circulation models, we've analyzed atmospheric patterns in extreme and moderate temperatures using both toroidal and cubical simulation boxes. We've observed that under conditions of extreme heat, atmospheric rotation follows cyclostrophic turbulence, gradually transitioning to geostrophic turbulence as temperatures return to balance. Notably, these geostrophic patterns resemble the chaotic weather seen in reality, while the orientation of these patterns is determined by the relative orientation of the simulation boxes' z-axis to the axis of rotation.

Most profound changes made by deep learning have been based on static models and vast annotated datasets. In contrast, traditional artificial intelligence systems learn from updated, incremental data. This new approach combines large-scale pretraining with data-dependent continuous learning across thousands of tiers. It also addresses overfitting in high-dimensional spaces, forgetfulness in lower-dimensional environments, and concept interference while leveraging careful system design to prevent catastrophic failures. Tested across 50,000 neural network models and 36,000 tiers of imageNet preprocessing, our approach identified the top-performing architecture, linearized feature transformation, self-focused training method, and 37 unique datasets that illustrate the systems' capabilities via precision-recall curves. The results show that dynamic learning can proceed from pretraining to over-training, from simple to complex concepts, and from diverse to related fields, all without the need for repeated fine-tuning.

This study offers novel analytical and geometrical explorations of the sophisticated concept of algebraic multiplicity, which is crucial in various advanced topics such as the spectral theory of operators and control systems. The definition of algebraic multiplicity, which has significant implications, is defined through a sophisticated structure known as the Kru\v{z}ik functional, appearing in the great spectral theory paradox. Key aspects of this definition are geometrically represented in both finite and infinite dimensional settings, which in turn lead to crucial properties of the algebraic multiplicity, including its upper semi-continuity. Additionally, this framework enables the development of crucial spectral projections and facilitates their further spectral decomposition.

A novel approach to verifying optical phase changes in dipolar atoms is introduced, which builds on the concept of atomic spin. Our method focuses on spin-based measurements of long-lived dipoles, offering a more accurate assessment than previous optical methods. To achieve this, we use a pair of bosonic particles in the spin model and calculate the optical phase's accuracy using quantum Cram\'{e}r-Robeno. At low optical phases, these measurements can reach high accuracy, comparable to optical methods. Moreover, the spin measurement provides spin squeezing for the bosonic pair, which improves their entanglement. This effect is enhanced by a specific type of interaction and can be accurately assessed using bosonic spin sensors. Our framework also allows for the adaptation of this approach to models with multiple bosonic particles.

To build a coherent, two-dimensional quantum computer based on electron spin in the four valleys of silicon, understanding the exchange interaction between electrons is crucial. This study calculates the energy and wave function of up to four electrons situated in different valleys of a single two-dimensional potential well, considering exchange interactions between them. Using a multi-valley effective mass model, we first checked for accuracy by comparing our results with density functional theory using coherently coupled tight-binding models, finding our methods to be sufficiently precise. Then, in our elliptical well simulations, we examined how the ground and first excited states behave as a function of various elliptical well parameters and electron valley indices. Variational decomposition of the wave functions in configuration space provides physical insight into the states' composition, which has significant implications for executing quantum computing operations via spin resonance techniques.

Researchers investigated the conductance properties of HgTe quantum wells, specifically those without a mass gap, and found results consistent with a Dirac particle model. This investigation was carried out for quantum wells of various thicknesses, and the conduction analysis involved measuring resistivity at extremely low temperatures in both transport and capacitive methods. Notably, the findings indicate a significant drop in Hall resistance as the Fermi energy crosses the Landau level, and the level of conduction in the central, negative, and primary transitions can be described using a simple on-site scattering model. Furthermore, scattering from multiple Dirac points in these transitions suggests a shift away from local equilibrium and calls for a more in-depth understanding of landau mixing.

No deep learning techniques have yet been thoroughly analyzed for potential efficiency improvements when used in conjunction with intersection safety systems. This study explores whether any intersection safety system can be effectively enhanced through the integration of collision warning techniques in the context of 5G-enabled cognitive networks and learning-based near-future transportation safety features, specifically Nominal Multi-Point Access Control (NOMA). We developed a novel Nominal Safety System, assessed its performance under various parameters, and investigated whether the system leads to fuel savings, reduced emissions, and nomial speed gains while maintaining a high level of nominal collision prevention.

This paper proposes a novel framework for resolving an imbalance between uplink and downlink traffic in New Radio (NR) or Dynamic Time Division Duplexing. By selectively adjusting the duration of control regions, it fine-tunes downlink capacity to meet upper layer needs. A game-theoretic approach is employed, where the control region's length is treated as a playable factor. The resulting equilibrium provides an optimal schedule for control regions, maximizing system utility. A game is designed with partial information due to the stochastic nature of wireless channels, and a learning algorithm finds the equilibrium in a multi-player game. The algorithm's convergence and effectiveness are validated through numerical results.

A mean-field theory has been developed to explain the Hall conductivity of a superconductor, specifically incorporating a Gaussian distribution of critical heights associated with its vortices.  Our approach yields the mean-field theory's prediction of the Hall conductivity, which can be expressed as $\sigma_H = \sigma_N (e/B)(1/B)(d\langle h_c^2\rangle - \langle h_c\rangle^2)/dh$.  Our examination of thin-film data for a BSCCO superconductor reveals a strong correspondence between our theory's predictions and observed phenomena, including the presence of a normal conductivity term, the peak in the vortex peak and the sharp onset of the superconducting vortices at the point of maximum conductivity.  Moreover, our theory holds the potential to be a flexible and adaptable means of extracting the superconducting parameters from experimental measurements of the peak's position, peak height, and width, without relying on assumptions regarding the shape of the distribution of critical heights of the vortices, or the magnetic field dependence of the normal conductivity.

Using the Renormalization Group, a new non-perturbative and scale-independent method is employed to analyze the 3D Ising model, specifically applying Bayes' theorem to study the model's dynamics from the perspective of correlations. A key finding of this approach is that the essential behavior of the model can be represented by a set of equations, also referred to as cumulant master equations, whose solutions exhibit a set of stable fixed points. It is observed that one of these fixed points accurately matches the critical behavior of the 3D Ising model with a precision of better than 10^-3, which implies a deep universality in the equations of camulet dynamics. Furthermore, small deviations from this fixed point are universal and can be utilized to calculate critical exponents, which are essential characteristics of the Ising model that describe its scaling behavior near the critical point. Ultimately, the study reveals the potential for applying cumulant dynamics to not only calculate critical parameters of the 3D Ising model but also to provide insights into its phase transition behavior and overall stability.

Using the basic objects from quantum field theory, we construct a new type of subfactor, which combines elements from a conformal field theory and a chiral field theory to create a more complex, higher-categorical structure. The constructed subfactor is found to be equivalent to another structure made of the initial objects, or it generates a wide range of quantum field theories as its possible outcomes. Additionally, a couple of more complex conformal field theories are identified, along with a recently discovered example, and it is shown that they all generate the initial combinatorial structure using their local symmetries.

In this work, we evaluate the ability of Hamiltonian Neural Networks to effectively function as a pretrained source for semantic confusion resistance. Our main conclusion indicates that HNNs successfully capture data distribution characteristics, allowing them to provide meaningful gradients through backpropagation, thereby enabling meaningful parameter updates. Our proposed setup incorporates an initial phase during which the network learns an approximate Hamiltonian that models the data distribution. Subsequently, we monitor the capacity of the trained model to provide meaningful gradients when applied to a simple task. Our methodology involves a straightforward task in which the network is tasked with learning to provide meaningful gradients through backpropagation. Our methodology also includes the use of simulations to support these findings.

Deep learning systems depend on automatic data collection, which can be compromised by malicious fabrications, leading to manipulated model decisions. To mitigate this risk, researchers have developed methods to detect and prevent model manipulation through technical detection systems and human judgment. However, these approaches have limitations, such as the need for fine-tuned strategies, human assessors who can be easily deceived, and the high cost of human input. In response, we propose a novel, high-cost approach that leverages human input to simultaneously increase data fidelity and boost confidence in model predictions through two mechanisms: a customized stimulus to correct model overestimation and a human-in-the-loop classification method to redirect suspicious samples to a human assessor, which also leads to automatic model retraining and the generation of reliable data. The results show that our proposed strategy is an effective implicit safeguard against model manipulation, requiring no additional detection methods, by combining human judgment with human-centric data augmentation.

Radiation sources, such as X-ray and gamma rays, are utilized in security inspections to detect prohibited items like explosives, weapons, and narcotics.  An image-based classification model has been developed using deep learning, but current benchmarks lack diversity in terms of data sources, banned item types, and difficulty levels.  To address this issue, we introduce RADI-Sec, a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 570 high-quality samples across 15 banned categories carefully crafted for a binary classification task.  To improve the quality of images and accommodate the limited data available for training, we propose a Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM) that mimics the working principle of image processors and leverages the high contrast between objects and backgrounds to enhance the detection of banned items.  Experimental results confirm that our approach effectively yields high performance in items with high visibility, and the establishment of the RADI-Sec benchmark provides a solid foundation for advancing research in the field of high-precision security inspections.

We introduce a new polynomial invariant for links in $T^2 \times I$ that is based on path counting and satisfies a splitting rule. This invariant behaves similarly to the volume hypothesis found in the classical physics conformal field theory and torus operator mapping technology for links in $S^3$. Moreover, by applying certain techniques, we can show that some values of our invariant are rational numbers.

The dictionary definition context of a target word is often ambiguous, 
reflecting the common phenomenon of polysemy.  To resolve this,  I propose 
introducing additional context - a secondary gloss - to assist in distinguishing 
between different senses of a word.  This additional context can be represented 
as a multi-class classification problem,  and the interplay between the original 
context,  and the proposed additional context,  can be exploited to enhance 
word sense discrimination.  As a result,  the need for co-occurrence statistics 
is no longer essential,  and the proposed approach can be applied to existing 
translation memory datasets.  To validate the proposed method,  context-gloss 
enhancement models are developed and evaluated,  demonstrating significant 
discriminative ability.  Experimental results indicate that the proposed method 
yields a binary accuracy of 77.44%,  surpassing the baseline model's 55.56% 
accuracy.

This study formulates the reciprocal gamma function through the concept of regularized expressions of an integral, which can be applied to the study of special functions including the lower and upper gamma functions.

Our study investigates the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions using both leading-order and next-to-leading-order calculations, enhanced by Parton Distribution Function rationalization to account for heavy quark effects. We examine the influence of various models and examine the expected results for current experimental capabilities at the Large Hadron Collider. Additionally, we analyze the impact of initial and theoretical uncertainties on our findings.

The traditional end-to-lightweight hierarchical approach struggles to effectively manage complex tasks, such as Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL, due to its numerous components, while a fully-endpoint model lacks efficiency and effectiveness. To bridge this gap, a novel Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL linguistic analysis model is introduced, incorporating an auxiliary decoding task to facilitate accurate grammar prediction and enable a simple, direct structure. The experimental results demonstrate its superiority over both standalone models and the hierarchical approach, outperforming them significantly in accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed model's modular design enables easy extension to other complex Text-to-SQL applications.

The vast array of graph-based privacy frameworks encompasses a wide range of applications and objectives, from differential anonymity to differential privacy, and encompasses diverse graph structures and secrecy objectives. In this study, we explore the connections between these frameworks through a unified lens of differential secrecy on graph-structured information, utilizing a game-theoretic approach. Our model simplifies the complexity of multiple theories while preserving key features, and employs game values to quantify the potential for information disclosure. Furthermore, we examine various graph-structured secrecy models within our model and investigate their sensitivity to changes in the underlying graph structure, and our analysis reveals significant variations in their scalability across different graph types.

The upcoming mission Euclid will significantly contribute to our understanding of cosmology, offering high-resolution mapping of the universe's growth and mass distribution. This will provide crucial insights into the nature of dark energy and dark matter. Building on the legacy of Planck and Euclid's science heritage, this opportunity will likely lead to a deeper exploration of these mysterious components that make up the universe.

The auto-alks system is designed to turn left across multi-lane highways when a driver initiates a left across-traffic maneuver. To test this system, a specialized set of road layouts called path networks must be created. These complex, narrow pathways between traffic lanes require precise manipulation of a vehicle while maintaining a safe distance from oncoming cars. In order to create challenging path networks, a method is needed to generate complex routes that an auto-alks vehicle can navigate. This method uses a combination of techniques to create challenging paths that can be used to thoroughly test the auto-alks system. One method involves using a search algorithm to identify the optimal sequence of Beziers that an algorithm can use to navigate a path. This method is then used to automatically create challenging path networks by combining the results of the search algorithm in order to efficiently test the auto-alks system within a reasonable amount of time.

The organization of music playlists, commonly used on streaming services, benefits from effective summary descriptions.  A dedicated music annotation tool needs a robust system to suggest concise and accurate summaries for each song within a given set of music tracks.  This paper presents a pioneering approach to music annotation, focusing on the ability to generate informative summaries that reflect the mood, style, and lyrical content of the playlist.  The proposed method uses a carefully constructed dataset containing over 700 descriptive annotations per track and employs an innovative combination of BERT and summary-generation techniques to create concise and accurate summaries.  Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in generating high-quality music annotations.  Furthermore, this paper demonstrates the potential of NLP-based methods to enhance the annotation of musical data, enabling the creation of enriched datasets that capture the semantic information underlying each track.

A new hydrodynamic theory called random quantum hydrodynamics has been developed
for a class of interacting boson fluids. This theory incorporates quantum fluctuations
into a mean-field approximation and incorporates a stochastic approach to describe
the time evolution of the fluid. As a result, the quantum dynamics can be related to
the Schrödinger equation, while still taking into account interactions. By building
upon existing mean-field approximations, our theory provides a more comprehensive
framework for understanding interacting boson fluids. Furthermore, our theory
incorporates quantum fluctuations beyond the mean-field approximation, which can
be useful for understanding phenomena such as superfluidity and phase transitions.
QHD-based mean-field approximation falls under the broader RH theory framework,
making our theory more versatile. By deriving a set of hydrodynamic equations
from our theory, we gain insights into quantum effects on fluid behavior, which can
be observed experimentally. QHD model provides a more comprehensive understanding
of quantum hydrodynamics, offering potential applications in quantum computing and
quantum communications. QHD theory framework can be applied to develop new quantum
hydrodynamic models, which can be beneficial for understanding complex quantum systems.

Temporal action segmentation tasks require video models to accurately identify beginning and ending points of actions within videos, which can bechallenging due to extensive within-video variation and dispersed semantic information. To address this issue, successful local-global matching approaches have divided videos into segments for global analysis and individual frames for local examination. However, they neglect important temporal connections on both scales. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel DC temporal action segmentation network that separates context into two distinct categories: intra-frame logical connections that capture action similarity within a frame, and inter-frame causal connections that distinguish the influence of prior events on subsequent occurrences. By incorporating DC representation learning to decide the split between these two contexts, our DCAN network excels at partitioning temporal boundaries and leveraging the advantages of DC representation learning also enhance performance on other TAS metrics such as average precision and F-score. Experimental evidence on three prominent datasets confirms DCAN's superiority over existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The long-lived thermal pressure anomalies known as palm tree modes (PTMs) are highly desirable for magnetic confinement devices like the JET tokamak. In the case of L-mode palm tree modes, internal peaks appear on the pressure profile and stabilize at the edge rational surfaces. A unique feature of these modes is their ability to decouple from the magnetic field lines, resulting in peak saturation on specific surfaces while surrounding surfaces show a interaction with the bulk plasma through shear. A unique feature of these modes is their ability to decouple into islands. Using gyrokinetic theory and resistive magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations, the decoupling behavior is attributed to the interaction of slow Alfv\'en waves with the Alfv\'en eigenfrequency. A key parameter for the emergence of PTMs is the difference between these frequencies which needs to be an integer while satisfying maximum conditions for Alfv\'en wave pressure to maintain the islands. A key insight for PTMs is that they only emerge in H-mode plasma due to the sheared Alfv\'en wave shears that cause wave resonance overlap.

This research focuses on creating a collision-free environment for a mobile robot navigating within a factored map of a multi-room space that contains people and objects. To achieve this, a novel approach called the Dynamic Vortex Potential Field has been developed. It leverages a vacuum force to attract the robot to target locations and utilizes vortex forces to repel the robot from obstacles and maintain social distance from persons within the space. The vortex forces are modeled using a logit function that takes into account the orientation, speed, and speed difference of objects or persons, allowing the robot to mimic their behavior and avoid collisions through a follow-the-leader approach. A key advantage of this method is its ability to encourage cooperation among multiple robots by repelling them from areas where other robots are heading for their target locations, as well as its potential for implementing a self-organizing, collision-free system through repulsive forces generated by vortex forces and collision prevention between robots. The proposed method has been successfully demonstrated with a functional prototype robot in an actual space.

The standard model for a random text treats each letter as an independent and equally likely occurrence, which doesn't accurately reflect the statistical behavior of real languages. A more precise model would consider the interdependence of consecutive letters, known as a Markov process. A recent study proposed using a corresponding 'random walk' model for a random text, built upon the interdependent letter sequences. This study utilizes this model to investigate how significant deviations from the expected frequency of each letter can be predicted, by examining the interdependence of letters and applying principles from large deviations. These tests were conducted on English and Japanese texts, as well as on synthetic texts generated based on the interdependent letter sequences for Japarese, to verify the accuracy of the predictions.

Recent advancements in wireless communications have largely treated radio frequency (RF) reflective surfaces as accidental phenomena, analyzing their impact on signal reception.  Our research, however, diverges from this approach by examining these surfaces intentionally, modeling them as controllable and dynamic in response to external stimuli.  A new concept, the intelligent reflective surface, is introduced where these RF reflective surfaces can be adjusted to achieve optimal outcomes.  Focusing on a radar system comprising an transmitter, receiver, and the reflective surface, we explore the potential of this setup to enhance target parameter estimation through careful adjustment of the surface.  Our findings reveal that specific patterns of the reflective surface can lead to more accurate parameter estimation, while deviations from these patterns result in less precise estimates, a phenomenon known as super-sensitivity.  Our approach opens up new possibilities for wireless sensing systems to achieve superior performance.

Discovering vulnerabilities in target applications through fuzzing is a valuable tool for finding security flaws. In recent years, fuzzing has consistently played a key role in uncovering vulnerabilities and enhancing the security of software. Despite its effectiveness, many questions remain about the potential of current fuzzing tools and assessing their performance accurately. This study explores the challenges of evaluating fuzzers, highlighting essential components for a reliable evaluation framework. It also presents such a framework, comprising a set of evaluation criteria, competition-based assessment methods, and criteria for the quality of test inputs. It also discusses the challenges of evaluating fuzzers targeting complex systems, including embedded devices, network protocols, and software-hardware interactions, as well as potential solutions. It hopes this study will pave the way for more accurate assessments of fuzzer performance and guide the development of high-quality evaluation benchmarks in the future.

In our analysis, we challenge the prevalence of complex solutions in deep continual learning by revealing the CL-Baseline, a simple yet effective approach that outperforms more innovative methods in various settings and tasks. Our CL-Baseline introduces a singular, intuitively designed loss function and employs an existing model without alterations. In contrast to various proposed solutions in the deep continual learning literature, our findings suggest that the superior performance of our baseline was underappreciated. As a result, our research reevaluates the genuine advancements made in deep continual learning and highlights the potential for our intuitive solution to be employed in resource-constrained real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we provide additional experiments and analysis in the supplementary section of the paper.

A continuous map from a connected surface to a metric space creates multiple homotopic mappings within a specified open set, leading to the concept of a homotopy regular map inspired by its expansion, contraction, and absence of pinching behaviors. This notion was initially explored by Albrecht in 2007 for its ability to determine a minimal energy configuration in a given open set, however, the theoretical foundation for a surface with minimal energy in a particular homotopy category has not yet been established. In this research, a new definition of a homotopy type-friendly region-minimizing map is defined for a given open set and it is demonstrated that a minimal energy configuration can be achieved by this new definition.
