Additionally, a Dade-type embedding proof is provided for spaces that are able to accommodate a torus with a specific type of map.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive survey of solutions to the generic scalar conservation law $u_t + f(u_x)=0$ on the real line with initially bounded initial data, and initially bounded derivative. The particular focus here is held for the case when the flux function $f$ has variable convexity and the data is not monotone. The key concepts introduced in previous sections now apply broadly to this more complex scenario where the data exhibit more varied asymptotic behaviors.

Our study utilizes a Interacting Shell Model with a large 52-proton space to analyze the characteristics of 64Ni, focusing on its lower-lying states up to an excitation energy of 7.5 MeV. Notably, 64Ni exhibits two distinct ground state configurations that exist within the same spin and symmetry category, resulting from competing protons and neutrons across the f5/2 and p3/2 shells. By incorporating a tensor interaction in the shell model Hamiltonian, we successfully replicate the ground state composition as well as other key nuclear characteristics, including specific collective states, a state with two tensor particles, and various excited configurations. Our successful modeling indicates that forming 0+ nuclear states requires balancing attractive forces from the monopole tensor interaction.

In the context of n-player games with continuous payoff functions, establishing lower bounds for the complexity of finding an equilibrium falls within the class of problems solvable with polynomial time using an oracle. However, previous research in this area has been largely confined to scenarios where the game is played over a finite set of options, largely ignoring the case of continuous games or those involving option sets defined by their boundary conditions, such as those found in economics involving supply and demand curves. A new lower limit has now been demonstrated, showing that finding an equilibrium in a Lipschitz continuous game occurs within the class of problems reducible to the complexity of calculating a specific value known as $\tilde O(\sqrt n \cdot k^{2.5})$ quantum queries, as well as matching classical bounds of $\tilde O(n^{3/4} \cdot k^{3/4})$, where n represents the number of options available and k denotes the number of bits of information that can be obtained from each query.

Machine learning model evaluation and adjustment are crucial for ensuring the accuracy of final predictions. Online systems, utilized by numerous natural language processing and language modeling platforms, heavily rely on these evaluations. Typically, split testing or N-fold cross-validation is employed for this purpose. While standard practices exist for determining the optimal fold in cross-validation, the underlying rationale for the choice of fold remains unclear. To explore the impact of the fold on model variance, this study conducts extensive experiments on the AQuAa data set, testing multiple feature classifiers including Naive Bayes, SVM, and BERT. It is discovered that the coefficient of variation in accuracy can be significantly reduced - by up to 27% with SVM features and a shift from 10-fold to 2-fold cross-validation. Moreover, the introduction of a proposed method, KJF-CV, yields notable improvements in model performance, notably enhancing accuracy by up to 5-7% and exhibiting substantial gains in runtime efficiency, particularly in online environments.

The concept of Multimodal Knowledge Graphs (MMKGs) is relatively new and underdeveloped, with researchers proposing various definitions and applications for it. Despite these differences, the definition and characterisation of MMKGs remain unclear. To address this, we propose the Educator-Pupil framework, a new perspective that unifies existing definitions and helps characterise MMKGs. To explore the current state of MMKGs and their related tasks, we conduct a comprehensive survey on data fusion techniques, MMKG completion, and summarisation. This survey also highlights the potential of MMKGs in enhancing summarisation techniques. To further our understanding of MMKGs, we outline several critical research areas for future work.

The Markov random field and Bayesian network models are graph-based probabilistic models that assist in solving complex optimization problems by making use of their structure for efficient computation. Through their edges and nodes, these models represent constrained optimization problems, which can be utilized to develop faster, graph-based solutions for solving their associated cost functions. By providing a simplified mathematical description of the optimal Markov random field minimum energy method, we propose using a novel notational system to present an advanced form of this description, which makes sense both mathematically and computationally. Utilizing this system, we can propose a significantly streamlined version of a previously published algorithm, resulting in approximately an 80% reduction in its computational complexity, while also providing the algorithm with the capacity to handle an enormous number of constraints, as demonstrated in a computational analysis comparing various methods for obtaining the optimal Markov random field minimum energy within a reasonable timeframe. Furthermore, we can leverage the marked Markov random field energy function for a unique method of constrained nonlinear optimization, as shown by applying it to a number of benchmark problems. By modifying the magnetic field field in a Markov random field, we propose a method of constrained optimization which, when combined with the accelerated min-energy search, provides the best results, surpassing existing top-performing techniques for the optimal Markov random field minimum energy method and constrained nonlinear optimization, as demonstrated in comprehensive computational analyses.

Precision in frequency measurements using light is so high that the recoil caused by absorbing photons becomes a significant concern. Researchers typically mitigate the photon recoil effect on the broad ranges of frequency detection employed in single-beam absorption spectroscopy. However, the impact of the recoil on the narrow ranges required for resonant exchange forces in ultracold atoms research has not been thoroughly addressed. This study investigates the frequency distribution of strand-like structures within cold strontium clouds and reveals their correlation with photon recoil velocities induced by a probing laser beam. By implementing machine learning techniques to analyze the data, the research directly measures the recoil-induced splitting of resonance lines, thereby yielding an absolute frequency in cycles per billion seconds.

Suspensions suddenly undergo a transition from fluid to solid when subjected to stress, with the critical stress exponentially dependent on the volume fraction near the jamming point. To investigate the pre-jamming transition, we employ optical coherence tomography, a non-invasive technique that provides high-resolution 3D images, and analyze the effect of shear rate and particle size distribution on the volume fraction. Our measurements utilize the tomographic approach over a broad spectrum of shear rates and combinations of diameters, and complemented by simulations, allow us to analyze how the shear stress and volume fraction interrelate. Our modeling indicates that shear thickening can be understood through the lens of an effective density, and an universal curve fits both the volume fraction and shear stress data as a function of this effective density.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined through a specific two-parameter family of ideals within the special Glotzmann algebra $GZ_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, the centralizer of the diagonal $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ subalgebra in the $n$-th tensor power. It is then demonstrated that the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$ accurately captures the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ by exhibiting the same dimension and generating degree $n$ homogeneous elements from its naturally identified degree-one subalgebra. The paper also discusses the relationship between the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$ and the polynomial representation theory of the symmetric group $S_n$, and provides a refined version of O's conjecture by establishing that the coefficients of the Hilbert-Poincaré series of $sR(n)$ are strictly positive integers.

Our analysis indicates that within a bilayer honeycomb structure, a specific supersolid phase, encompassing curved fluid and supersolid characteristics, can arise from triplon dynamics in the A-B-A-A type stacking configuration. This becomes possible under the influence of nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor exchange interactions in the A-A layer, as well as interlayer interactions between the A and B layers. Furthermore, we find that an extra A-B layer can be added to this system, resulting in a curved supersolid state that exhibits the same magnetic order within each individual A-B layer but opposite orientations in adjacent layers. The characteristics of this curve-like supersolid characteristic can be modeled through a two-leg supersolid ladder model, and its magnetic order can be explained through mean-field theory.

The crucial role of the incident speed distribution between WIMPs and nuclei in scattering is emphasized missing from traditional two-body model representations. A new three-dimensional model is proposed to emphasize the importance of the angle of recoil in such scattering interactions and provides a more accurate representation. The generalised 3-D model reveals a previously unnoted correlation between velocity and angle of recoil and provides a revised dark matter spectrum of energy recoil that is dependent on the angle of recoil. The implications of this angle of dependence in the dark matter spectrum are explored and the potential for detection using next-generation direct dark matter experiments such as LEGEND-1000 and SHADOW-1000 is assessed.

Google's search engine is integral to obtaining relevant information, yet its personalization features may induce bias by promoting familiar brands and familiar topics. Two studies personalize the experiences of the participants via Google search, using deception to prevent them from recognizing the personalization effect. They were then asked to report on experiences with an unfamiliar social cause, with the researchers using data from Google's actual search engine to monitor how the participants used the service. The findings show the personalization features significantly personalize the participants' use of the search engine, with the latter significantly reducing diverse perspectives by at least 20%. They also demonstrate the continued prevalence of this effect via personalizing the participants' access to new information via third-party services that utilize Google's search engine.

Proposed projects, including Muon-Electron Scattering Synchrotron (MESSENGER) and a Muon-Nucleus Scattering Synchrotron (MuNSS), share a common design featuring a linear input line and a circular synchrotron ring. These projects would leverage existing infrastructure, reducing the need for new construction. By utilizing a linear accelerator or drift tube linerator to produce high-energy muons, the projects could significantly enhance our understanding of nuclear structure and parton distribution functions through deep inelastic scattering, or even without the need for a photon virtuality. Additionally, the projects have the potential to make contributions to Higgs boson research and beyond-the-Standard-Model studies similar to those at the Large Hadron Collider.

Traditional 4D MRI techniques, responsible for generating high-resolution, distortion-free images free of motion artifacts, necessitate breath-holding and result in limited scan coverage. Conversely, free-breathing options exist but frequently encounter issues with scan speed, blurring, and motion artifacts. A novel free-breathing 4D MRI sequence has been engineered, utilizing a reversed, continuous, and symmetric respiratory trigger in combination with a turbo spin-echo sequence to simultaneously address these concerns. This new approach, named RB-TSE, is capable of producing large anatomical scans while precisely capturing different respiratory phases, thereby reducing the burden of multiple breath-holds and breath-gapping on patients. The RB-TSE sequence's efficacy in various applications has been proven, including anatomical free-breathing scans and respiratory motion-synchronized low-dose CT simulations. Furthermore, this new sequence's improved efficiency over the conventional continuous-triggered method has been demonstrated, including the potential for generating high temporal resolution movies from a limited number of phases. The proposed RB-TSE sequence's advantages in terms of temporal and spatial resolution, scan duration, and data efficiency over existing techniques have been highlighted via quantitative metrics and modified approaches in the study.

A novel concept called Input Restricted Control Barrier Functions has been introduced to describe the safe control of dynamic systems with restricted inputs. Our framework makes it possible to synthesize controlled controls for complex systems by utilizing this function. As an example, our method can be applied to control autonomous vehicles within urban environments.

This study introduces a novel approach to area calculation within discrete geometry by integrating linear approximations into traditional sampling theory. An innovative structure, the CF-approximation space, is proposed as a means of representation. Notably, a key identity, the Poincar\'e formula, is proven within this framework, which allows for the decomposition of inner sums into one-dimensional components, thereby facilitating numerical computation of complex integrals and summing infinite series. A specific application is illustrated through the Gaussian integral, and a fundamental result is introduced by restricting the parameter $\alpha$ to $0$, which establishes a connection between two mathematical expressions, the Ramanujan's master theorem and the Residue theorem.

Pairwise testing has long been regarded as a practice to improve the quality of software for its ability to mimic real-user behavior in interacting with applications. Nonetheless, traditional pairwise testing lacks a systematic approach and many researchers view it as an unstructured method. To address these shortcomings, we are introducing a novel framework for analyzing the effectiveness of pairwise testing in detecting defects within complex combinatorial input spaces. In contrast to earlier methodologies that relied on rough approximations, our new framework employs an exact paired-Permutation model to accurately evaluate the efficacy of pairwise testing through a specific test statistic. This enables us to precisely compare the definition-based quality of pairwise testing with that of traditional full-factorial testing, blocking, and random testing through blocking factors representing the number of values per option. Furthermore, we are showcasing the applicability of our framework in a case study involving the evaluation of pair-wise testing quality in interacting with an online ticket booking system.

The shipping industry is crucial to the global economy and the container shipping sector in particular has closely followed the world's economic trends over the past four decades. However, reliable and comprehensive historical data on the container shipping industry has been missing until now. We have assembled the most complete and unified dataset thus far for the container shipping sector, covering vital aspects such as freight rates, shipping volume, new and used vessel prices, and scrapped vessels from the 1960s to 2019. Furthermore, we have investigated the container shipping industry's co-cyclicality with the global economy in various historical periods and found substantial evidence of co-cyclicality in the 1960s to 1990s, as well as in the 2000s and beyond, with industry variables showing significant fluctuations. Additionally, we have found that freight rate and shipping volume play opposite roles in container shipping sector fluctuations, with opposing effects on the industry's co-cyclicality during different periods. The balance of these two factors ultimately shapes the container shipping industry's overall cycle.

We examine the topological properties of a specific fabric space constructed from a triangulation of a metric space. Specifically, if a triangulation $\mathcal{T}$ of a metric space $(X,d)$ ensures that the distance between any two points in the same simplex does not exceed $R$, then the associated fabric space $F(X,d)$ is homeomorphic to $X$. This homeomorphism persists under certain conditions where the triangulation of $n$-balls maintains the same star-radius $R$ for all sub-spheres of dimension $n-3$ or less, allowing $F(X,d)$ to be homotopy equivalent to $X$. Furthermore, we establish a countable lower threshold for the star-radius $\mathcal{R}$ of triangulations of Euclidean $n$-spaces such that their fabric spaces are homeomorphic to respective $n$-spaces.

Graph neural networks have become increasingly popular in applications that rely on complex graph-structured data analysis. While they excel at producing accurate predictions, the black-box nature of these models makes understanding their inner workings challenging. To address this limitation, recent studies have focused on creating transparent graph neural network models that can reliably predict node targets within specific subgraphs. Although traditional explanation methods like Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) have shown promise in this area, they often result in densely connected subgraphs that are difficult to interpret. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a novel approach called Acquired Structure-based Interpretation (ASI), which generates sparse subgraphs by identifying the most critical edges that significantly impact the target node prediction. As a versatile framework, ASI can be applied to various graph neural network models, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), and Attention-based models. Our experiments demonstrate that the ASI method outperforms both baseline and advanced techniques by accurately retrieving top-k important nodes and producing highly precise subgraphs that facilitate efficient and reliable interpretations.

The CountSketch algorithm is a fundamental method in modern streaming and distributed machine learning, serving as the foundation for more intricate algorithms. Its simplicity makes bugs easier to identify and fix. Under specific conditions, it has been proven effective for linear classification and regression. However, its performance deteriorates in the face of adaptive data, which is commonly discarded in numerous machine learning systems. We investigate the count sketch's ability to produce high-quality estimates of linear functions and discover that, despite initial expectations, it cannot provide precise estimates in the face of adaptive data within a polynomial number of rounds. Nevertheless, we develop two revised versions of the count sketch that are robust against adaptive data and require significantly fewer communication rounds to achieve the same level of accuracy as under the stochastic data assumption. These algorithms represent the first methods of their kind for processing adaptive data in streaming and distributed settings.

This research builds upon previous findings, specifically those from the first part of the corresponding series. In the first part of the series, we established the ability to locally represent the scalar curvature in a C^1 way for 2-punctured n-dimensional Riemannian manifolds (n>=4). In this second part, we show that this local decomposition can be achieved without introducing singularities on an entire n-dimensional Riemannian manifold. This result is a key step towards proving the local decomposition of the Schouten tensor.

A liquid containing Nielsen tubes exhibits the Nernst effect, and its magnitude can be related to viscosity through a hydrodynamic framework. By applying this model, we calculate how the Nernst effect and viscosity change as a function of angular momentum and temperature. Our model also predicts a Nernst-dependent entropy per particle that aligns with numerical observations. Furthermore, we determine how this entropy varies with temperature and angular momentum, and we also explore the system's phase transitions using a semi-classical approach.

Advanced prediction and control systems in complex dynamic environments are essential in high-stakes applications like self-driving cars and robotic operations. Traditional machine learning-based predictions and control methods are ineffective for these systems to function properly. Our novel framework overcomes these limitations by developing a machine learning model for predictive control that can adapt to changes in real-time and make updates efficiently. The model's capacity to prioritize and manage multiple objectives at once and seamlessly integrate optimization with machine learning models streamlines the design and modeling processes. Initial testing on the self-driving test drive in Boulder, Colorado, demonstrates the model's performance and efficiency in terms of computational resources and time.

Using deep learning in deep markets carries the risk of overfitting due to the sophisticated nature of the markets that can mimic the patterns of training data. This paper proposes a novel approach, a Neural Generative Adversarial Network, to generate and predict future market trends while filtering out unrealistic patterns. We applied this method to forecast stock prices, utilizing an encoder to analyze real data and an generator to create simulated sequences, both of which are used by a predictor. Experimental results on public datasets and private data show our model outperforms the standard LSTM baseline in accuracy, low prediction errors. However, it's important to note that the margin of improvement is small.

A new shared memory formalism called Shared Envelope Formalism (SCATTER) is introduced, which uses shared objects known as envelopes to combine invariants and actions. SCATTER has a complete verification method that ensures shared memory operations' correctness, considering atomicity and linearization properties. When optimizing for shared cache, these completeness arguments can be adapted to other concurrency guarantees.

This research investigates the production of a pair of Higgs bosons at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC, focusing on determining the number of Higgs bosons produced per event. It emphasizes studying the associated particle spectrum to determine the nature of the interaction between the Higgs bosons. Specifically, it determines the ability to distinguish between type-2 Effective Field Theories and the Standard Model by analyzing the number of top quarks produced in association with the Higgs bosons for a range of top quark masses from 200 GeV to 1 TeV. Additionally, for certain masses, it also studies the ability to distinguish between the Standard Model and Type-2 EFT in additions to producing two electroweak bosons. The analyses assume specific detectors with limited coverage, mirroring those of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC, and include detector effects and background processes. The results indicate that for top quark masses up to approximately 600 GeV, CLIC can distinguish between the Standard Model and the EFT with high confidence, while for heavier masses or two electroweak bosions at masses around 100 GeV, CLIC may not be able to do so with the same level of confidence.

We derive a variety of equivalent Lagrangians for classical general relativity, 
utilizing the geometric framework of the Klein-Groerman bundle. In this setup, 
the gravitational field is represented by the connection form of a principal bundle 
with connection, specifically associated with the group of affine transformations 
of a four-dimensional Minkowski space. Through the application of Noether's 
theorem, we derive the canonical energy-momentum complex and the corresponding 
conservation laws for this connection-form Lagrangian. Furthermore, we extend 
this derivation to include the inclusion of matter fields within the Klein-Groerman 
bundle framework, maintaining consistency with the principle of general covariance.

A highly nonlinear interaction of localized shocks in five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space is examined, using a series of approximations to account for transverse gradients. It is suggested that the expansion achieves greater accuracy when employing second-order derivatives for terms beyond the highest order. A critical issue with conformal field theory on the boundary is the potential pole in the stress-energy tensor correlation function, derived from second-order derivative terms. This issue is linked to a constraint on the initial data, essentially limiting the rate at which the shock front can expand, and may indicate a deeper property of the gravitational theory.

Our research cements the theoretical understanding of anomalous drag experienced by long, thin objects moving through fluids and granular materials. By formulating a new hydrodynamic model for a cylinder moving perpendicular to its long axis, we derived drag coefficients that align with both fluid and granular material behavior. Initially, we validated our model by comparing its predictions to the well-established drag on our cylinder material with infinite permeability, matching Darcy's law. We then experimented with varying levels of fluid saturation within our cylindrical samples and observed the expected transition from grain-scale to continuum length scales. Finally, we experimentally tested the predictions of our general theory with novel materials exhibiting distinct anisotropic drag characteristics.

Using data from CALIFA, we detected large-scale outflows in six star-forming spiral galaxies with notable outflows. In these galaxies, outflows are found where there are prominent signs of recent star formation in the inner regions and can extend up to 10 kiloparsecs in some cases. The energy from these star formation processes is sufficient to ionize gas and create a correlation with the extent of outflows. A theoretical model of radiation pressure suggests that the ionizing processes are a critical factor in controlling outflows. This model reveals that outflows are more likely to occur in galaxies with shorter gas scales lengths. The data also indicate the existence of significant outflows in these galaxies, often exceeding expected limits. Noticing this discrepancy, we found an inverse relationship between gas density within these galaxies and the mass of outflows, suggesting that star formation processes adapt to local conditions to regulate outflows. The data also indicate the existence of significant outflows in these galaxies, often exceeding expected limits. Noticing this outflows are confined to the gas disk burst, and outflows can be visualized as the amplitude of a wave in this burst, suggesting that outflows are not the result of a single galaxy's size, but rather a result of local conditions.

Organizations often grapple with optimizing numerous systems subject to real-world constraints. In tasks such as enhancing server configurations, software settings, or machine learning models, it is essential to experiment with numerous parameters under real conditions and evaluate their effects on conditions closely resembling production environments. As is typically the case, trying out different server configurations or machine learning models is costly in terms of time, making it necessary to minimize the number of trials. In this paper, we introduce Organized BoGraphs, a novel approach to organized reinforcement learning that is built upon record learning and leverages Hierarchical Tree-Structured Causal Models (HTCMs). Organized BoGraphs is an HTCMs that incorporates historical data from previous optimizations of a given system. We detail the features of Organized BoGraphs, an optimization framework based on Organized BoHTCMs, and propose two sampling methods for it. Through a case study on optimizing machine learning models, we demonstrate the efficacy of Organized BoGraphs, and objectively assess its performance via the Learning From Historical Records (LHR) leaderboard.

Our research examined the triangular flow $v_3$ in various high-energy nuclear collisions using the multiphase transport model. By analyzing Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV and Cu+Cu and Zn+Zn collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=32$ GeV, we compared our results to experimental data from the STAR collaboration for Au+Au (39 GeV) and Cu+Cu (32 GeV) collisions. In Au+Au collisions, we matched $v_3$ for hadrons between 1.74 and 3.9 GeV/$c$. For Cu+Cu collisions, we matched $v_3$ for hadrons at 1.94 and 2.76 GeV/$c$. Notably, our model overpredicted $v_3$ for protons in Cu+Cu collisions. However, when analyzing collisions of nucleon pairs with masses around 55 GeV, we found that initial spatial fluctuations alone could not explain the observed flow. To accurately reproduce $v_3$ in these collisions of massive nuclei, initial fluctuations in mass arrangement needed to be incorporated into our simulations. Adding these fluctuations significantly reduced $v_3$ by a factor of two for protons, which aligned with experimental observations.

The growth in size of web data has compromised its comprehension, validity, and utility. To address this issue, constructing high-quality ontologies and semantic webs from raw web data has become a prevalent approach. Nevertheless, evaluating the correctness of web datasets in terms of their structural integrity remains a challenging task due to the lack of explicit integrity rules in data. By leveraging data from the entire World Wide Web, we present TextDojo, a text-mining platform designed to evaluate structural quality at both dataset and individual tuple levels. By comparing data against pre-built schema definitions or ontologies, TextDojo offers a modular architecture featuring text analytics tools that analyze specific attributes. With the ability to process millions of tuples, TextDojo is set to be a foundational element for future research aiming to enhance the evaluation and generation of large-scale, high-quality linked data.

The average response time in computer systems is a critical metric that informs the performance and design of higher-level applications. In practice, response time data is easily obtainable and can provide valuable insights into system performance at no additional cost. The standard method for computing response time includes the sample mean and, in some cases, the sample variance. The choice of these two statistics is crucial as the subsequent analysis often relies on their use. The choice of these two statistics is crucial because the law of large numbers suggests that the sample mean converges to the actual mean response time as data size increases. However, the variance estimator's behavior is less clear under the same conditions and seems to favor either very large or very small sample sizes. The issue lies in the fact that the convergence of the sample mean to a precise value leaves very little variation in the data, which hampers the variance estimator's effectiveness. The proposed method builds upon the established effectiveness measure for estimators in statistical inference and evaluates variance, standard deviation, and median absolute deviation under both theoretical and real-world scenarios, as well as under conditions relevant to typical system monitoring. The study finds that while the sample mean is a effective estimator of the actual mean under both small and large data sets, the variance estimator tends to fail as data sizes approach the common range of millions of entries used in system monitoring. The method also introduces median-based alternatives and shows that they exhibit similar patterns to the variance estimator. The method Monodevia is also proposed as a alternative that

We used high-resolution spectroscopy to analyze a range of optical spectra for a galaxy called NGC 5548, an active galactic nucleus with type 1, located in the constellation of Draco. Specifically, we focused on its spectra between 0.55 and 0.92 micrometers, which yielded a rich set of emission lines caused by a range of elements including C III], C IV, Ne V, N V, Ne III, Ne IV], Ne V], O III], O III], O III], and a range of hydrogen lines. These emissions are characteristic of low-ionization regions, which are typically found outside the nucleus of the galaxy. By calculating the electron density in the low-ionization emission lines, which resulted in a range of values (log $n_e$ cm$^{-3}$ = 10.3$^{+0.3}_{-0.1}$), and comparing this to calculations of the electron density in hydrogen lines, which gave a range of values (log $n_e$ cm$^{-3}$ = 8$^{+1}_{-2}$), we determined that there was a significant difference between the two. This indicated that there are multiple components present in the broad line region of the galaxy, which is not unique to this case.
