To comprehend the complex processes shaping galaxy evolution, chemical cartography serves as a valuable tool by analyzing stellar populations and their patterns. As large-scale stellar surveys continue to grow, the details these surveys provide can break down the complexity of galaxy evolution into simpler components. Building on previous work that analyzed stars within the Milky Way, this study applies similar analysis to rich data sets from the APOGEE-II survey, which covers three massive oblate structures in the M81 group. By examining differences in composition between nearby galaxies and using a two-factor model to identify distinct stellar communities, the researchers found distinct patterns in the data. These patterns vary depending on whether a galaxy shows thin or thick disc characteristics. The most prominent differences between these communities can be understood through simple concepts, such as metallicity, and provide the building blocks for more intricate theoretical models and analyses. The framework this study develops serves as a path forward for future research on the cartography of galaxies.

As severe COVID-19 outbreaks spread, rumor dissemination posing a significant challenge to effective containment. Based on the characteristics of complex networks, we modeled the dissemination of COVID-19 related rumors in online spaces. By examining the infectivity and latency of these rumors, we established a bidirectional dissemination model examining both the impact of health risks on information propagation. Key elements of this model led to the derivation of critical threshold values, which reflect the condition necessary for the widespread propagation of both main scientific and fake information. In addition, data analysis revealed that labeling sources with "COVID-19" in titles significantly accelerates the speed of legitimate information. Furthermore, we examined the impact of rumor propagation by assessing the generation of useful scientific information. Ultimately, real-world data were utilized to validate the validity of the model and its underlying assumptions.

The Fornax3D Consortium is establishing the first 3D maps of several objects within the Fornax cluster, aiding in a deeper understanding of its formation and evolution. This project will generate redshift-based distance measurements for the cluster, focusing on the creation of high-resolution maps of three spiral galaxies, N0327, N0414, and N0606, as well as a comprehensive catalog of all planular nebulae within the cluster. To complete this task, the consortium will analyze the H-band of nearly 70 terabytes of archival data from the VLT's MUSE instrument, which covers the spectral range from 4600 to 9600 Å at a 1.6 Å resolution. A team of six members will design and implement the necessary tools to automate the extraction of spectral data and identify all planular nebulae, which will then be used to measure the exact distances to the cluster itself, as well as any galaxies orbiting them. This project will also establish a fully documented, reproducible workflow that can be applied to other parts of the sky or in different clusters, which will be implemented using the Astropy package and made publicly available, resulting in the construction of precise 3D maps of three galaxies, a complete catalog of all planular nebulae within the Fornax cluster, and a detailed analysis of the stars within these objects, aiding in a deeper understanding of their evolution.

Real-time data processing systems are being widely used in various fields such
as telecommunications, finance, and healthcare monitoring. These systems rely
heavily on stream processing engines that process data one piece at a time,
however, they struggle to handle data being input as updates to previously
collected datasets. Existing solutions like Apache Flink and Spark Structured
Streaming, designed for this kind of dataset management, are inefficient due
to their copy-based processing approach which is slow for single-element
updates. We introduce LifeStream, a pioneering stream processing engine
optimized for systems with hardware accelerators, that处理周期性的数据流. LifeStream provides high-efficiency processing by leveraging the capability of these
hardware accelerators to handle data in the form of contiguous memory blocks.
The engine features customizable hardware that is tailored to the underlying
hardware, providing optimal performance for specific applications. LifeStream
demonstrates significant performance improvements in handling periodic data
processing tasks, providing up to 100x higher throughput and up to 5x lower
latency in comparison to leading hardware-based engines such as Datasketch.

This study delves into the theory of Bertrand curves within time-like manifolds, specifically focusing on submanifolds of higher-dimensional space and examining their relationship with curvature properties. We define a new category of curves called timelike Bertrand curves in this context and provide a detailed derivation of their associated system. As a result, we establish several conditions necessary for such curves to exist and offer proof for a curve in a three-dimensional manifold. Additionally, we offer a series of examples to illustrate our theoretical findings.

Recent research has suggested that altering loss functions in convolutional neural networks may significantly accelerate their performance. Although the proposed alteration involves replacing the target output component with its binary indication, our comprehensive analysis has been conducted on various loss functions and model architectures. The assessment encompasses crookshare loss, binary cross-entropy loss, multi-class cross-entropy loss, and the soft indicator loss, across seven deep learning models including InceptionV3, ResNet50, InceptionV3AE, InceptionV3USV, InceptionV3GAN, InceptionV3VQ-VAE, and InceptionV3VQ-CE. Our preliminary findings indicate that the proposed loss function does not universally accelerate performance but rather produces varying outcomes depending on the specific deep learning architecture employed.

The stability of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations with a boundary feedback control, where the control is applied to a boundary that is not perpendicular to the flow, is analyzed. This study builds on previous research by Y. I. Karshon that proved exponential stability for a linear system with boundary control. Extending these results, we establish the exponential stability of the nonlinear equations under the same feedback mechanism.

This research employs a comprehensive thermomechanical model to simulate material behavior during the rapid heating caused by a laser, which initiates a complex microstructural transformation as the material reverts to a crystalline state. Although existing models address certain aspects of this process, fully capturing its mechanics remains a challenge. To achieve this, a fully discrete material model was developed, incorporating the discrete phase-field theory to map the evolving microstructure. During simulations, a self-organized pattern of cellular dendrites emerged within the resulting grid-like microstructure. Furthermore, modified Allen-Cahn equations, which account for mechanical stresses, were utilized to model the boundary between phases. The simulation was further streamlined through the application of an approximate convexity reformulation, thereby reducing computational demands. As a result, characteristic features often observed in laser-induced material processing were produced, including the formation of an inverted cone-shaped surface and an intricate subsurface microstructure.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on spin-triplet Cooper pairs in a nelematic superconductor, a Pippard generalization of the Landau free energy was developed. The development of the Glorier equation of motion for the superconductor's order parameter under the simultaneous influence of finite momentum, magnetic fields, and nematic symmetry resulted in the calculation of magnetic susceptibility. The formulation of the susceptibility under the simultaneous influence of a finite critical velocity and an external magnetic field in the Ginzburg-Landau approximation was also demonstrated. A simple relationship was found between the magnetic susceptibility and the critical velocity in the limit of small momentum and strong nematic deformation, with the elasticity of the liquid crystal having negligible impact, where the susceptibility exhibits both node-dependent and s-wave like behavior.

Acquiring skilled navigation and manipulation through digital training is a well-established practice in robotics.
One common method involves using feedback from mentors, either from humans or systems, to guide and correct the robot's movements.
In the lab setting, a teacher can guide the robot through a task by physically moving it and letting it experience the consequences of its actions.
The robot learns by experiencing feedback in the form of rewards and information from its sensors.
For complex tasks, having the robot go through each possible situation is impractical, so the goal is to let it experience a limited number of situations and use that to figure out how to complete the task on its own.
To do this, the robot needs to figure out the most useful things to learn from its experience, ask the teacher for help when needed, and combine the feedback it gets with the value of completing a task.
We present a new, flexible method for teaching robots that can also adapt to different types of feedback, and use it to learn tasks like picking things up and moving around within a lab.

The typical differential detection method for continuous phase modulation (CPM) schemes involves observing a difference in phase between adjacent symbols, which can make these schemes vulnerable to increased tolerance for symbol rate spacing. A new differential detection method for CPM was previously developed that operates using data from a single symbol period. In this work, a technique has been explored by introducing an intentional delay within a matched filter to further simplify complex CPM signal detection, based on the observation that symbol-spaced data are derived from a correlation between two shifted forms of an orthonormal set of basis functions. The proposed method enhances the differential detection approach by symbol spacing, at the cost of slightly reduced signal quality due to the delay, however, inserting a delay filter within a matched filter allows for recovery of some signal quality. The proposed technique is particularly beneficial for complex CPM variants such as Gaussian CPM (GCPM), demonstrating its effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and practical or simulation results.

The number of observed black-hole neutron-star mergers is expected to surpass the number of core-collapse supernovae in the LIGO-Virgo-EVEREST detection range. This discrepancy raises a key question: what specific properties of core-collapse dynamics are necessary for the remainder of these events to be identified as merging black-hole neutron-stars? Our primary objective is to assess the synergistic potential between optical and X-ray detectors in distinguishing supernovae associated with low-mass black-holes from typical core-collapse events. Based on this synergy, we evaluate the degree of neutron-matter instability (defined by the parameter $\Gamma$) necessary for a supernova to merge with a black-hole. Simulations show that mergers can occur regardless of neutron-matter instability, specifically when the rate of mass ejection from the system exceeds a threshold of approximately $10^{-3} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot \, \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at the point of low density where the system becomes disconnected from its initial state. Nonetheless, neutron-star explosions (defined by the condition $\Gamma \gtrsim 1$) are far more common than mergers associated with core-collapse.

This paper argues that the compressibility of spacetime compress vacuums, which can be represented by a metric that satisfies the Einstein field equations with a quantum vacuum as the source, leading to a quantum compressibility of spacetime. A derived relationship between surface tension and quantum compressibility indicates that the Hubble constant can be determined by these properties. The surface tension of spacetime can be related to a thermal parameter, which, through statistical mechanics, can be used to determine the thermal properties of the cosmic microwave background radiation. The model predicts a critical thermal zone where the compressibility of spacetime becomes infinite, marking the boundary between expanding and contracting phases of the universe, which aligns with observations of supernovae in a dark-energy-dominated cosmos.

Previous research on rain creation has been unsuccessful due to a lack of guided prior knowledge about the process, which can be thought of as the reverse of image restoration. To address this challenge, we propose a new discrete translation model that utilizes a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to simulate rain creation. By adding an explicit constraint, we enable the VAE latent space to capture rain details. To validate the creation model, we treat image denoising as rain creation with random noise inputs, which allows us to leverage existing denoising models to verify the authenticity of the created rain. For real-world scenarios, we extract the actual rain removal process from the created rain. Our proposed model outperforms baselines on the FSU dataset in terms of rain texture, scene preservation, and overall image quality metrics.

The increasing number of autonomous mobile robots in various settings like delivery services and personal assistants necessitates the development of efficient group coordination methods to reduce operational expenses. One effective strategy is cooperative learning of rewards through clustered rank ordering, though existing approaches struggle with high communication costs and slow convergence speeds resulting from multi-agent gradient-based ranked feedback. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel framework called Visually Aided Cluster Ranking (VACR), which incorporates a cluster-oriented learning algorithm leveraging minimal voting-based ranked feedback combined with cluster data visualization. Our experiments across multiple marbles maze tests and robotic group navigation scenarios demonstrate that the proposed VACR approach successfully learns rewards quickly, outperforming existing group learning methods in terms of speed, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

This study investigates the Q-curvature conformal change problem on a bounded domain $\Omega$ in R^n for n>=5. We prove that for any positive function f in R^n, there exists a metric of the form y^n/4 and with Q-curvature f within the domain $\Omega$.

Research in medicine and pharmacology should consider a person's character, specifically their susceptibility to abuse of prescribed medications. A comprehensive set of 40 questions was used to evaluate a candidate's character across five dimensions, featuring 8 new personality traits not commonly included in such assessments. These evaluations, scored from -3 to +3, were administered to 60 volunteers who subsequently underwent medication susceptibility testing. The results revealed a clear correlation between personality profiles and the ease with which individuals become dependent on drugs, ultimately facilitating the development of a preventive system to identify high-risk candidates before they are subjected to certain medications.

We introduce ATOMIC, a pioneering approach for a reasoning system centered on machine common knowledge (McK) that spans various domains and categories. By drawing from an extensive McK atlas encompassing over one million entities and ten million relations across more than twenty categories, we showcase the potential of McK in supporting if-then reasoning. In a battle-against-state-of-the-art systems on ten benchmarks, ATOMIC either matched or surpassed the performances of the best in class in nine instances. The results of the study reveal the efficacy of McK in if-then reasoning and reveal the value of an extensive McK atlas in empowering the system to generalize across diverse scenarios, thereby marking a substantial advancement for the current base-against-state-of-the-art systems.

The performance of financial systems and services depends heavily on linear algebra operations, specifically the analysis of correlated risks by regulators. This report presents NISQ-HHL, a new risk management approach that utilizes the HHL algorithm, and presents its portfolio application results when integrated with classical computing. Notably, NISQ-HHL outperformed the renowned power iteration method in certain aspects of risk computation. Furthermore, when applied to the EURIDICE dataset of European stocks, NISQ-HHL contributed diversification to the portfolio without compromising returns.

To enhance data efficiency and use of vast amounts of text-image pairs for training speech recognizers, researchers have explored multi-modal learning. However, existing cross-modal approaches fall short due to their reliance on synchronized pairs of data and their inability to leverage large-scale text-audio datasets effectively. In response, a novel multi-modal learning method has been developed, called bidirectional focus training, which overcomes these limitations. This technique grants each decoder equal significance, enables the incorporation of large-scale text-audio datasets for speech recognizers, and simplifies model architecture while maintaining performance through a single additional linear layer. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority, yielding a 3.1-times increase in precision-F1 over previous methods over 10x less pre-trained text-audio data, and achieving state-of-the-performance in speech recognizers.

The concept of average cross section, introduced by Eggleton and over the last two decades various generalized variants have been developed. This paper addresses average cross section in the context of geometric cross sections of mean width and mean brightness. By adapting key lemmas and the main theorem from Eggleton's research, corresponding simplified versions are established. These adaptations enable the proof of two key results: first, average cross section possesses a unique minimum value for convex areas with a constant sum of interior angles; second, average cross section has a unique solution for a constant value when limited to star-shaped, waterdrop-shaped areas with a constant number of symmetric transformations.

For a randomly selected uniform parking function $ \sigma_n $, choose the largest integer $ k_n $ so that the number of initial asymptotic characteristics (for $ i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 $) among the first $ k_n $ elements of $ \sigma_n $ is even. It has been established that as $ n $ approaches infinity, $ k_n $ converges in distribution to an exponential variable with a unit parameter. Moreover, research on the expected initial positions of the second smallest, first element greater than $ n $, and first element greater than $ 2n $ in the first $ k_n $ elements of $ \sigma_n $ reveals expected values of approximately $ 1.17n $, $ 1.37n $, and $ 2.01n $, respectively, in the limit of $ n $ approaching infinity.

investigation into the electrical properties of superconducting nanowires is conducted with emphasis on adding gate electrodes. The gate electrodes allow for the creation of an electric field across the nanowires, which in turn causes a transition from superconducting state to insulating state as the gate voltage increases. The study involves analyzing current-voltage characteristics of a nanowire under both superconducting and insulating states. The critical current of the superconducting state is observed to fluctuate randomly in time and is influenced by the applied gate voltage. The magnitude of these fluctuations is analyzed in terms of the number of electrons trapped in the nanowire. The nature of quantum fluctuations in the number of electrons and coherent quantum phase slips in the Josephson energy are distinguished. The results of this analysis provide insights into the underlying cause of quantum fluctuations in the critical current of the nanowire. The study contributes to the broader understanding of quantum phase slips in superconducting nanowires.

The initial and most studied T-dwarf, GJ 229B, was discovered in the late 1990s and its complex spectrum posed a challenge even with advanced linear retrieval codes. To better understand its atmospheric composition, the capabilities of the APOLLO retrieval code were tested in this study. Unlike previous codes, APOLLO is designed for both linear and non-linear data analysis while incorporating state-of-the-theory for various molecular compositions, the dwarf's surface properties, and the scattering effect on its spectrum. By leveraging APOLLO, the atmospheric enigma of GJ 229B was resolved in as few as 10 minutes, enabling the precise reconstruction of its spectrum from the infrared to the optical range. The code's success in analyzing GJ 229B demonstrates its potential to efficiently explore the atmospheric compositions of exoplanets and other low-mass celestial bodies.

Using the effective kinetic theory, the influence of inelastic scattering on the evolution of an initial-state medium has been studied with a focus on quark and gluon diffusion due to radiative processes. A condition for ensuring that the initial-state quark and gluon gases remain in a kinetic equilibrium state has been established through a quantitative assessment of the five-momentum collision term, which incorporates both inelastic and elastic scattering. Furthermore, an exponential decay solution for this condition has been found and its implications on the development of an initial-state medium have been shown to match results from hydrodynamic simulations. Furthermore, including elastic scattering improves this simulation and supports the hypothesis that a quark-gluon plasma, produced in heavy-ion collisions at high-energy accelerators, could maintain a state of kinetic equilibrium during its evolution.

Predicting how a scene evolves, including how the camera moves, is an essential component in creating advanced video understanding systems. However, this task is challenging due to the variability in real-world data, causing significant difficulties in modeling. To address this issue, we split the distribution into two parts: handling the layout of the scene and the movement of the camera as separate but related tasks. This approach lets us focus on content-related content in one branch of a model, while using a second branch to account for the camera movement. By combining these two aspects, we can use the difference in expected outputs to predict the scene's movement. Surprisingly, this strategy performs well even with a minimal amount of labeled data, enabling us to utilize self-supervised methods to improve the use of large, unlabelled video datasets. We also present a new, publicly available dataset with over one million clips, which we call DRR.

Einstein's principle of exchangeability usually leads to the phenomenon of superradiance, where the most populated quantum state exhibits the strongest signal.  However, contrary to this outcome, the ground state of bosons typically displays little to no density fluctuations.  As a result, the interparticle interaction strength is often gauged by comparing the population of more lightly occupied states.  Here, we present experimental evidence of a different type of interaction - inter-orbital interaction - which describes the energy cost of coupling distinct spatial states.  Our measurements show that a significant inter-orbital interaction shifts the boundary between single- and two-body quantum regimes in specific trap configurations.  The validation of the inter-orbital interaction in this experiment has important implications for the accurate simulation of fermionic systems using bosonic particles and for implementing quantum computational algorithms.

The Ω-baryon, which has been predicted for a long time, was experimentally confirmed in this study through analysis of data collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC. By examining χc0 , χc2 , and JC/ψ0 states containing an s2s' system, researchers established that these predictions lie within or near the acceptable ranges derived from various theoretical frameworks. Additionally, by theoretically modeling the hadronic decays of the Ω-baryon resonances and comparing the predictions with available experimental data, a certain level of consistency was observed.

We've developed a predictive mathematical model for disease transmission on public buses during urban commutes, utilizing statistical modeling techniques and a compartmental model. Our analysis considers the impact of various factors including quarantine measures and the presence of asymptomatic individuals. We utilize statistical methods to estimate model parameters and validate our predictions with data from Los Angeles County, utilizing illnesses caused by SARS-CoV-2 as a case study. Surprisingly, we found that the commutes can be adequately described by a stochastic SIR model due to the large number of asymptomatic individuals. Consequently, we were able to make useful predictions about the spread of illnesses on public buses and assess quarantine measures.

Building on my earlier calculations regarding quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence, I now investigate various possible ways to detect these effects. In the case of birefringence, the proposed detection methods involve analyzing the polarization changes of particle beams as they move through high-speed moving frames that experience the maximal birefringent effect. Proposed proposals include using gamma rays produced from accelerated protons in existing particle beam setups. For sub-nuclear frame birefringence, the suggested detection method suggests comparing the birefringent angles for different energy levels during the reconstruction of invariant masses in electron-positron beam data.

A highly efficient algorithm for listing complete polyhedra of prime transitivity was presented by Eisenlohr and Farris, relying on an algorithm for highly symmetric finite groups. Though the original implementation of the group symmetry algorithm was not open-source, we modified their approach by incorporating the open-charm package for group theory, allowing usage of the closed polyhedra algorithm of Delmozo and using the open-charm package for polyhedra description, resulting in a fully open-source implementation.

The concept of unforgeable encryption, initially introduced by Gertner and Young at POPL 2007, has been explored with significant advancements made by various researchers. Several versions of schemes have been proposed, including those that rely on idealized primitives like one-way permutations and fully secure CPA-secure encryption. Also, some researchers have produced partially CCA-secure schemes under certain assumptions. In this work, we present a fully secure unforgeable encryption protocol in the information-theoretic setting.

Physical layer security (PHL) relies on extracting a shared secret between legitimate parties from a unique characteristic of the communication channel that also distinguishes it from illegal listeners. This process involves two stages: first, legitimate parties measure and estimate the channel characteristics to generate a rough model, or "sketch," of it. In the second stage, one party transmits a carefully designed test signal through the channel, and the other party compares the received output with their own sketch to make a confirmation decision. Traditionally, both parties need to exchange encryption keys to communicate securely. In contrast, our study presents an innovative, keyless verification system that leverages the unique noise present in communication signals to achieve this. Our method utilizes an unsupervised learning algorithm to generate highly accurate, low-bit sketches of Gaussian noise channels, and a corresponding test classifier that uses these sketches for confirmation. Our results show that these sketch-based tests are highly effective, often outperforming similar methods that analyze the full signal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these tests can be customized to meet specific performance requirements by adjusting the size of the sketches.

We investigated the flat-band surface plasmon polariton in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides, and discovered that its frequency can be adjusted through rotation angles and chemical composition. For certain twist angles, the plasmon polariton mode transforms into a two-dimensional electron gas, whereas modes with other angles remain trapped and do not participate in interactions with light. Additionally, we found that these structures support multiple flat-band plasmon polariton modes simultaneously, where the interaction light-matter results in Rabi splitting. Our study provides design principles for plasmonics devices based on flattened surface plasmons in twisted dichalcogenides.

This research focuses on semi-homothetic transformations of a Ricci soliton defined on a Sasakian manifold and subsequently examines how such transformations relate to the conformal structure of the manifold. Additionally, this research explores scalar curvature properties of the manifold in connection with a 1-form and investigates the harmonic characteristics of the soliton when certain conditions are met.

The nature of magnetospheres in celestial bodies with intrinsic magnetic fields is significantly influenced by the solar wind. A comprehensive analysis of Gusts and their effects on these magnetospheres is presented, including their characteristics and distinctions from Steady solar wind conditions. The underlying physics of both scenarios are examined and compared, particularly in terms of magnetic reconnection and shock reformation cycles. Simulations reveal distinct reconnection rates and cell thicknesses arising from both conditions. The analysis is extended to include the potential reformation of the standing reconnection X-line and its reformation cycle. Furthermore, the reformation of the downstream cell is examined through simulations and theoretical models, including the role of ion and electron diffusion regions, as well as the energy sources of sound waves and Alfv\'en waves. The potential for both conditions to generate Alfv\'en waves is explored, as well as their possible commonality. The reformation of the standing reconnection X-line and its cycle may have implications for the origin of auroral kilometric radiation and Io plasma torus on Jupiter. Additionally, differences in ion and electron diffusion regions may have different effects on the generation of Alfv\'en waves in both scenarios, as well as on the magnetospheres of Io and Jupiter.

Spin-orbit proximity effects result in enhanced spin-orbit coupling in heavy metal layers adjacent to a thin film of adjacent material. Recent studies have shown that increasing the number of heavy metal layers can significantly improve these effects due to spin-flip scattering at the interface. However, in thin films with low net magnetization and large magnetic anisotropy, an additional term arises from the heavy metal/heavy metal interface that depends on the electron mean free path and the magnetic anisotropy. This term can become dominant beyond two heavy metal layers and may inhibit effective magnetic control via electric fields in devices utilizing these effects. Our model incorporates this competition within a Bi/Co multilayer stack and demonstrates how magnetic anisotutoring varies based on the number of Co/Bi interfaces, impacting the efficiency of electric field-induced magnetic control.

This study utilizes the Jumarie type fractional derivative to analyze the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in the presence of a generalized Mie-like potential in multiple dimensions. By applying the semi-analytical Elwish method, researchers aim to obtain approximate solutions to the resulting time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation. The core objective of applying the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in the presence of a Mie-like potential is to determine the energy eigenvalues and associated eigenfunctions. The validity and accuracy of the obtained results are confirmed through graphical representations and comparative analyses with existing methods such as the variational iteration method and He's fractional iterative quadratic scheme. The successful application of the Elwish method demonstrates its efficacy in solving the given problem.

We have developed a novel perspective on training neural networks through the lens of consistency. Our work demonstrates that networks capable of accurately predicting outcomes under slight perturbations in input data exhibit superior performance. We formulated an optimization problem to select a neural network capable of maintaining consistency between its outputs for data and its averaged fuzzy representation. We established a theoretical link between this optimization and regularized regression. Furthermore, we modified the network's ability to model this distribution by analyzing a specific class of neural networks. This modification led to a simplified cost function characterization and a characterization of the network's structure. Notably, our analysis reveals that the network consists of two components: a linear part that embodies the network's ability to model the distribution and a highly constrained non-linear part that embodies the network's ability to regulate this distribution. This modular design enables more efficient end-to-end training by leveraging pre-trained nonlinear components from data.

Neural machine translation models are sometimes hindered by data noise, which can be difficult to acclimate to and capture due to the absence of explicit supervision. In Basque, a language characterized by complex agreement patterns that rely on multiple factors, we investigate whether neural translators can master this aspect of the language. Our analysis, focusing on the development of the recent Basque corpus (MCBv2), reveals that the model's improved performance is primarily a result of more accurate input encoding rather than its ability to capture the agreement accurately. To overcome this limitation, we propose a practical solution by providing the model with explicit information about the agreement, thereby enabling it to acclimate to this challenging feature.

A globally coordinated network of telescopes, known as the CHANTO program, tracked the complete orbit of the planet HD 8066 b by continuously monitoring its host star for increased brightness due to the planet reflecting more light as it approaches. This observation took place between 2015 and 2017 and included the use of small, large, and space-based telescopes to ensure optimal viewing. By analyzing data from this observation, the team derived a precise orbital period of 110.0028 days and an average distance from the star of 0.446 AU. Additionally, they calculated the brightness received from the planet at closest approach and greatest distance as 16.68 days * 10^-3 and 18.81 days * 10^-3, respectively. These results can be used to effectively schedule observations for the James Webb Space Telescope to maximize its ability to study this planet in greater detail.

Virtual environments are effective tools for assessing and enhancing upper limb motor skills in individuals with stroke. Various studies have utilized force-feedback robots within stroke-induced virtual environments to provide therapeutic benefits. These systems typically consist of two components: a control module that processes user input, generates environmental feedback, and applies force through the robot; a assessment module that analyzes and evaluates user performance. A significant aspect of the control module is the baseline play model, which significantly impacts stroke patient performance. In this study, we evaluated the effects of different line play styles on patient performance by analyzing data from existing research on force-feedback robots within stroke-induced virtual environments. Our statistical analysis revealed that environment design, prior training, and force-feedback robot use have a more substantial impact on patient performance than control strategies. However, when participants were subjected to the same environment, training, and robot, their performance varied based on the line play model. Specifically, it was observed that when confronted with a counter-intuitive environment, patients' performance was worsened by the presence of the force-feedback robot, yielding a poor therapeutic outcome. Furthermore, our research suggests that virtual environment-based rehabilitation systems should be designed with intuitive line play models to optimize the recovery process for patients.

This paper offers a variational approach to reconstructing severely degraded 3D objects or deformed rigid bodies from multiple 2D viewpoints, a process known as phase-field estimation. The approach combines elements of variational reconstruction and the Bhattacharyya-based stiffness penalty, enabling it to handle objects with holes or multiple disconnected parts. By directly modeling 3D objects using rough approximation methods, the model avoids the need for hyperparameter calibration often associated with brittle fractures models like the Stefan-Payne polynomial. We prove convergence results for the proposed approach and present both numerical experiments and applications to reconstruct objects from limited data, including objects with substantial damage.
