Optical systems with PT-symmetry maintain their parity-time invariance under specific conditions, typically resulting in the conventional phenomenon where light is partially reflected and partially transmitted when a PT-symmetric network is illuminated from outside. In this paper, we analytically and numerically investigated the impact of PT-symmetry on a type of periodic network where each unit cell comprises two coupled waveguides that exhibit either PT-symmetry or reflective symmetry. Our results show that for both types of periodic networks, light is mostly transmitted through when there is no phase mismatch, leading to high clarity in both directions. Additionally, we demonstrate that PT-symmetric periodic networks with no phase mismatch can support the occurrence of coherent perfect absorption-lasing under the right transmission conditions.

The majority of current network representations solely focus on pairwise connections, disregarding the prevalence of multi-node interactions commonly seen in real-world systems like neural circuits and technical setups. Such multi-node interactions can significantly influence system behavior by combining effects across interconnected nodes. In this study, a novel model is created to analyze the dynamics of sparse, binary logical networks featuring multi-node interactions and self-interactions. Our findings demonstrate that such network states typically evolve in discrete stages, with various internal configurations deemed equivalent due to their shared external properties. An analogous reduction technique is introduced to examine the complexity of these networks' boundary behaviors. Notably, our theoretical analysis and numerical evidence indicate that the boundary dynamics of such sparse, binary logical networks generally exhibit chaotic characteristics.

The precision of various methods used in nuclear physics depends crucially  
on the reliability of evaluating matrix elements of one- and two-body operators  
between different HFB wave functions.  This work derives general expressions  
for calculating the matrix elements of one- and two-body operators constructed  
from quasiparticle creation and annihilation operators, and provides an overview  
of computational approaches, including manual computation and a newly developed  
automated algorithm, which will be demonstrated using the quadrupole operator in  
case studies involving HFB calculations for ^24Mg and ^24,26,28Si.

Point cloud denoising addresses the removal of noise from imperfect 3D point clouds acquired by depth sensors, which often suffer from inaccuracies and incompleteness. Due to their general applicability, point-based representation methods are prevalent in tasks such as scene reconstruction and object recognition. Nonetheless, these approaches typically struggle with fine textural details as a result of their representation mechanisms. We propose a point cloud smoothing technique called TPC that utilizes hierarchical voxel grids to represent points. By employing a volume rendering process, TPC prevents unnecessary point deformation and ensures stable, accurate rendering. To avoid unnecessary computational costs, we restrict the voxel volume and hierarchy, focusing on critical areas of the point cloud. For real-world applications, we train a point cloud reconstruction network using synthetic data generated from Mono-TCV and ScanNet datasets, which contain rich annotations and real-world scans, respectively. TPC achieves superior performance in point cloud smoothing, outperforming existing methods in both noise removal and point preservation.

We're investigating medium access methods, like ALOHA and CSMA, for low-rate radar networks where multiple users share a limited number of measurement opportunities. In this paper, we focus on coherent frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar systems and evaluate how different network configurations impact network throughput. Specifically, we examine the performance of network protocols by considering various FMCW operation modes. Our analysis shows that in networked radar systems, medium access techniques can lead to significant variations in network throughput. By leveraging the additional information available in FMCW radar measurements, we propose a method to enhance medium access control that results in a more stable and improved network performance.

Predicting the evolution of a fact-aware temporal knowledge graph is a crucial task for a variety of applications. Despite temporal knowledge graph representation learning being the natural framework for addressing this problem, most current evaluation methods are operator-dependent, as they rely on comparing the generated triple with alternative triple candidates. In this study, we introduce two dependent-free evaluation methods: one assumes a low-rank structure for the time-dependent representation and the other is operator-independent by directly evaluating the generated continuous representation. Our experimental results, conducted on real-world temporal knowledge graphs, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods and their parity with traditional operator-dependent approaches. Building on this foundation, we leverage our second method to compare different representation models and their components, which their level of sparsity, without necessitating competition with other triple candidates. Our findings provide novel insights into the evolution of temporal knowledge graph representations in a manner that is sensitive to model design choices and the temporal time.

Within the RPA framework, Jost functions are constructed using the RPA kernel and amplitude, from which scattering energy and amplitude can be derived. Notably, the product of Jost functions associated with different isobaric states yields the scattering eigenenergies. As RPA amplitude incorporates both particle-hole excitation and dressing components, this approach effectively rectifies the common overexcitation flaw inherent in standard RPA theory. By applying this theory based on Jost functions to the 16O nucleus, our method successfully replicates the scattering eigenenergies of single and double RPA states, especially those related to the energy distribution density of the Giant Dipole Resonance. This indicates that including two-body correlation within the RPA amplitude significantly impacts scattering eigenenergy.

Identifying groups of similar systems within a diverse collection helps focus research efforts on common patterns and variations within specific subgroups. In this work, a novel approach is presented to separate systems exhibiting distinct typical behaviors from those with atypical trajectories. Our method finds similar systems by examining typical trajectories and distinguishing between typical and unusual trajectories using kernel-based tools and an optimal smoothing parameter chosen through data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with multiple examples of artificial and real-world datasets involving systems from diverse fields such as mechanical, biological, and chemical domains.

Text generation models based on sequence modeling often struggle with copying long functional phrases due to the inherent limitations of N-gram-based methods. Deep learning-based generative models, including GANs, have been widely used for text creation, but they typically rely on sequence modeling techniques like RNNs which can be inefficient at copying lengthy substrings. Our proposed model, SparseGAN, combines the strengths of zero-shot learning and GANs to overcome this limitation. By training a descriptive encoder that captures the semantic structure of input text and using it to guide the generation of control codes in an unlabelled training set, our model can efficiently copy substrings corresponding to real-world entities and functions. By leveraging both a discriminative decoder that distinguishes between real and generated text and an adversarial decoder that mimics the behavior of real data, our model produces high-quality text with complex patterns. By adding a model that copies text based on the control codes generated by the descriptive encoder and the control codes manipulated by the unlabelled training set, our model achieves efficient copying of substrances. Our model outperforms current state-of-the-art generative text creation techniques, particularly in terms of model efficiency and quality of generated text.

The hypothesis of interstellar pansomophyta, which suggests life's travel between stars, could explain the rarity of life in the solar system and its quick emergence, yet it's a theoretical concept with significant speculation. To assess its plausibility, a model combining interstellar travel with ejection from stellar systems is developed, considering the diverse environments of the Galactic disk. This model predicts detectable signatures, such as population fluctuations, changes in planetary system statistics, and localized anomalies. However, discovering pansomophyta remains challenging due to their location on planets closest to their stars. Nonetheless, such environments may be observable with upcoming telescopes.

Disturbance theory is utilized to forecast HI intensity mapping power spectrum coefficients based on the dark matter spectrum, incorporating various nonlinear corrections up to one-loop. Specifically, we consider a primary perturbation in the neutral hydrogen number density with elliptic and vector modes remaining unchanged, which allows us to consider HI clustering at redshifts between 1 and 5. For a typical disturbance spectrum, linear HI-clustering effects dominate within a comoving scale range between 10-30 $h^{-1}$ Mpc, where moderate nonlinear clustering can be predicted by the dark matter spectrum with the help of the typical disturbance. However, extreme cases of primary perturbations, such as primordial black hole clusters, can lead to considerable additional clustering (exceeding a factor of ten) within the same scale range, due to their gravitational influence. Simulations are used to validate our predictions and further explore the effect of a typical surrounding gas environment, which can be effectively modeled using the typical disturbance. These simulations indicate that the predicted clustering patterns can be accurately represented by a typical disturbance, with a match exceeding ninety percent. Conversely, they also reveal that the distance between the primary perturbation and surrounding matter can be effectively probed by analyzing the clustering of HI around such perturbations, with significant potential for cosmological application.

Like the spontaneous symmetry disruption that preceded the present era, a newly emerged phase with the same or greater vacuum expectation value for the bosonic boson could give rise to a disruptive transition in a higher-dimensional space.

Combining spatial capture-recapture (SCR) with state-space models has the potential to significantly improve our understanding of how animals utilize space and collect valuable information that is typically elusive. Nonetheless, current SCR frameworks struggle to effectively utilize external covariates in modeling detection probabilities. We've developed a novel method that integrates SCR with state-space models, enabling the incorporation of environmental variables and an increase in detection data by up to 50% in our simulations. In actual field studies, this combined model can: (1) utilize imperfect environmental covariates in modeling detection probabilities, (2) effectively utilize spatial point process data of resources (such as vegetation or animal scat) by integrating latent states, and (3) estimate the collection and detection biases of observed environmental covariates. The combination model offers a robust statistical solution to address limitations of the current SCR models in collecting and utilizing spatial data, especially when study detectors are imperfect. Combining SCR with state-space models can provide more efficient and accurate estimation of animal density and an improvement in collecting space utilization data that is typically elusive.

In the Minimal Power $k$ Edge Disjoint $st$-Paths problem, the task is to find the smallest possible power $ \lambda $ such that we can identify $ k $ paths between nodes $ s $ and $ t $ in a graph $ G $, with each edge having a associated cost (or 'lambda') and no two paths sharing the same edge. Although this problem seems straightforward for even values of $ k $, developing an efficient algorithm to solve it approximately has been a longstanding challenge. So far, the best achievable approximation factor has been $ O(\sqrt{ k \log^{5} { k } } ) $. We present a novel algorithm that can estimate power $ k $ with a outcome of $ O(\sqrt{ k } ) $.

This study presents a novel approach for controlling swarms of small aircraft in relation to their environment, capping the need for a lead machine. By using probabilistic models and situational awareness systems on each individual UAS, we ensure they can make at least a basic level of decisions on their own and work together through direct communication. Our methods are tested with decentralized Markov decision processes and demonstrated with two swarm control systems, one using collaborative planning and the other using swarming behaviors. Our results show that our approach can successfully coordinate the UAS swarms through communication with each other, not by relying on external commands.

Spatial restrictions significantly influence how networks function in various settings.
To study this, the concept of embedding subgraphs has been developed to mathematically
represent network components. In this paper, we introduce the concept of
dynamic embedding subgraphs and use it to analyze local processes on time-varying
networks. Firstly, we establish a method to reliably measure the stability of
community structures detected in social media data. Secondly, we explore how
community structures in social media evolve over time through the use of
community detection and our newly formulated metric.

Using historical match data from the 2020 UEFA EURO and 2022 UEFA EURO tournaments, a geometric probability model was utilized to evaluate defensive effectiveness in these competitions. A spatial probability distribution, specifically the Stokic-Gold (2020) assessment, provided a framework for analyzing goal-scoring patterns and defensive performance. By estimating model parameters through a non-linear optimization process, a map was created that reflects the relative strength of national teams based on geographical location. A Bayesian approach was then applied to calculate the expected goal averages, taking into account the variance of the estimates and the influence of adjacent regions. A rank system was also developed, incorporating both attack and defense, to assess the overall performance of each nation participating in the tournaments.

This work called Visual Template-less Form Interpretation (VTFI) achieves accurate extraction and calculation of numerical data from complex, disorganized forms without relying on predefined templates. VTFI is further distinguished by its ability to learn the structural elements of novel forms through just a single example, utilizing only a minimal amount of annotation. A novel approach known as Relational Network is introduced in form field detection and field value recognition, learning the unique features of each form while efficiently utilizing global image information. A two-stage process involving selective element learning and field value recognition is also presented, where an innovative selective attention mechanism utilizes only relevant visual elements to enhance performance on challenging fields. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of VTFI over competing methods, showcasing substantial improvements overall and on exceptionally difficult cases, thereby proving the efficacy of the proposed method.

A novel concealed parameter recurrent state space (CPRSS) network is presented, which is derived from the well-established recurrent state space model (RSSM). This new framework allows for the incorporation of hidden parameters that significantly alter the model's latent state and influence its dynamics. The CPRSS model is capable of effectively addressing complex and interconnected problems and yields superior performance compared to the original RSSM model. The proposed concealed parameter alteration mechanism is versatile and can be applied to a diverse range of conditions and systems. The efficacy of the CPRSS model is empirically validated through comprehensive testing on multiple datasets, including those used for forecasting and anomaly detection. The results show enhanced forecasting accuracy and precise anomaly detection accuracy, thereby confirming the model's excellence. The code for the CPRSS model is publicly accessible for further investigation. This framework represents a significant leap forward in latent variable modeling and may pave the way for more innovative solutions in the field of artificial intelligence. The author would like to acknowledge the contribution of the research assistant, whose valuable support enabled the development of this groundbreaking framework. The author also appreciates the constructive feedback provided by the reviewers, which significantly contributed to the improvement of the research.

We investigate free conditional independence and type B freeness, a newer concept. 
First, we establish a connection between free conditional independence and ordinary independence given specific patterns of symmetry. 
We then examine freeness conditioned on type B symmetry, showing that it converges to ordinary independence given that pattern of symmetry as the matrix size increases.

We take a specific type of curve $\tilde C$ and another curve $C$ as its base, with a covering map of type 3. Under the condition that the genus of $C$ is greater than 1 and certain technical criteria are met, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the Prym variety of $\tilde C$ over $C$ to be an abelian surface with a trivial Prym map of genus $C$. Furthermore, we provide examples of these compactified moduli spaces by taking $C$ to be a plane quartic, a rational normal quartic in $\mathbb P^4$, or $C_{12}$ in $\mathbb P^5$.

The significance of structural polarization in comparing organizations remains poorly understood due to the absence of a unified method for measuring it, as well as a lack of clarity in differentiating structural polarization from organization disturbance. This study aims to streamline research on polarized organizations by examining various polarization metrics through the lenses of polarization direction, magnitude, and shape, and proposing a set of standardized measurements. Additionally, we explore the impact of organization disturbance on polarized structures and propose models for measuring polarization within contexts influenced by external shocks.

The dynamics of multiple interconnected layers can facilitate a more stable and flexible operation of networked systems by decoupling different functions within the system. However, not all types of interactions are suitable for forming multilayer systems, as certain interactions may lead to undesirable and unpredictable effects. In this study, we examine a specific multilayer network and identify its capacity to decouple different functions or rather cause different parts of the network to interact in an unintuitive and singular manner. We analyze multiple, interconnected networks of oscillators that are synchronized with one another, focusing on a specific pattern of connection between the layers where each node in one layer is connected to its counterpart in an adjacent layer. We discover that, under specific conditions, these networks exhibit a unique and transient state of synchronization, characterized by distinct, isolated periods of synchronized activity in each layer. The formation of these states is attributed to the creation of effective bipartite interactions between adjacent layers, leading to the emergence of synchronized dynamics on these types of networks. Furthermore, these states become more prevalent as the interlayer connections increase, making them valuable for multiple, distinct tasks performed in separate stages within a single multilayer system.

For a linear, elastic material at a given point with uniform stress and strain characteristics, finding the simplest rotational representation of the Cauchy stress operator is key to various computational tasks, such as the efficient calculation of its eigenvalues and stress invariant values. This paper presents a direct, exclusive, and comprehensive method for determining the most basic representation of the Cauchy stress operator in a specific coordinate system, supported by multiple examples and an exploration of its underlying principles. Additionally, the process is efficiently implemented through an algorithm presented in the study.

In software testing, ensuring the reliability of systems is a key objective. One prominent approach to achieving this goal is through the use of property-based testing, which involves generating test inputs and verifying specific invariants. To enhance the efficiency of this process, we propose a new framework that leverages geometric insights to define and generate test inputs in a more effective manner. This framework can be applied to any data structure that supports geometric operations, providing a basis for efficient random generation and sampling. As a demonstration of its potential, we used the framework to improve the testing process of program slices, a widely used analysis technique. By unifying various slice semantics and enabling more accurate verification of invariants, our framework has been shown to, in combination with existing tools, reduce evaluation times while maintaining the effectiveness of the testing process.

We introduce HyperPrompt, a novel architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention HyperBlocks within the Transformer framework. Specifically, HyperPrompt allows us to easily add new, distinct task conditions, such as unique TaskPrompts, without risking negative task interference common in Multi-Task Learning scenarios. As a result, our model can efficiently utilize TaskPrompts to facilitate optimal task performance and, if necessary, generate task-specific conditions for each application. We demonstrate the hyper efficiency and effectiveness of HyperPrompt in two comprehensive evaluations, including accelerated training acceleration and precise HyperBlocks substitution, respectively.

Let $\sigma$ be a symmetric operator associated with the differential equation $\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + q(x)\cdot I$, where the function $q(x)$ is real and periodic, and the function $q$ has a period of one. Let the spectrum of $\sigma$ consist of discrete values $\lambda_n$ that occur at specific, non-overlapping intervals. Let $P_n$ be the corresponding eigenspaces of $\sigma$ at each $\lambda_n$. It has been proven that for any vector $f$ in $P_n$, the trajectory formed by applying $\sigma$ repeatedly to $f$ remains within or decreases from a certain boundary formed by $\lambda_n$ over time.

In the context of quantum optics, the symmetry of quantum states typically facilitates simplified calculations of light emission. However, despite quantum states evolving over time and potentially losing their symmetry, they still allow for controlled light emission through manipulation of external fields. This study reveals that quantum states whose odd and even components are separated by parity symmetry can still exhibit enhanced light emission when that symmetry is briefly combined with nearby energy levels through a two-photon process. This phenomenon occurs within a three-level system consisting of two symmetric quantum states and an intermediate anti-symmetric state, and as such, it extends the principles of parity protection to include all of a system's properties. Moreover, this setup allows for highly efficient light emission in an entirely balanced manner.

We design a robust network scale estimation algorithm for agents in small-world graphs, which accurately identifies the diameter of the graph even in the presence of malicious actors. The proposed drawfiameter algorithm achieves a precise result within $O(\sqrt{k})$ factors of the actual graph diameter, where $k$ denotes the number of malicious agents. The algorithm's efficiency lies in its distributed nature and randomness, devoid of the need for a central coordinator, while providing the most robust factor approximation thus far in the context of Byzantine failure. The algorithm's mechanics involve the implicit exploration of shortest paths and the use of randomness to circumvent the influence of malicious edges, which are known to distort the network's topological structure. Theoretical analysis of the algorithm is supported by the development of a novel bound on the eccentricity variation in small-world graphs under malicious control, where the bound's secrecy resides in the use of a randomized measure technique. The algorithm's implementation in small-world graphs is completed with the provision of upper and infinite bounds on the estimated network diameter. The development of drawfiameter algorithm is incorporated with a discussion on the context of biological systems, in which organisms depend on accurate network scale estimation for the proper functioning of their underlying networks. The algorithm's name is a play on the words 'draw' and 'fiammeter', where the former denotes the implicit edge exploration and the latter refers to the instrument used for scale measurement. Accurate estimation of travel time and related metrics is crucial for effective navigation systems and road safety. This study aims to provide real-time traffic parameter estimation based on the positions and speeds of unseen vehicles, and specifically, develops a nonparametric method to estimate queue lengths at traffic signals using only the location of the probing vehicles. A key assumption in this approach is linear speed propagation from the first probe to the tail of the queue, which is commonly accepted in traffic operational models. The estimated quantities are then used to derive nonparametric estimators for travel time, speed, and other traffic parameters, with no need for traffic signal data or knowledge of the road layout between the traffic light and the point where the probe exits the queue. Simulation studies and comparison with traditional methods demonstrate the reliability and accuracy of the proposed method.

Einstein's General Relativity theory has been successfully applied in the field of astrophysics for over half a century. The upcoming third-generation gravitational wave detectors will significantly enhance detection capabilities, allowing for more precise data analysis and potential insights into the fundamental aspects of gravity. However, the process of simulating binary compact objects has been hindered by initial data constraints, a problem that may now be solvable with a novel numerical approach. This method, known as CTTK and based on the conformal transverse-traceless decomposition, addresses initial data requirements by utilizing a robust, hyperbolic system of equations that doesn't rely on specific symmetry assumptions. As a result, arbitrary, initial binary compact objects can be modeled with high accuracy and minimal constraint violations, allowing for the creation of evolving, circular orbiting simulations. The efficiency of the CTTK has been demonstrated in various scenarios, producing waveforms that align with the expected characteristics of coalescing binaries.

The $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ process, which can occur through very rare interactions, cannot be fully understood by considering only the intermediate contributions of well-known intermediate particles. 

To gain deeper insights, we studied the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ process in detail, employing effective field theory and quantum loop calculations to calculate form factors within the standard model and various new physics models. 

In addition, we derived theoretical estimates for the branching fractions and relevant variables, and designed a method to thoroughly study the rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ process that can be implemented with the experimental data available at the LHCb. 

To illustrate our approach, we focused on the rare process and estimated its detection efficiency and background interference, and obtained relevant information that can guide future experimental studies. 

To illustrate the feasibility of detecting the rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ process, we estimated its cleanliness and found that it can reach a level of 10%, providing a clear path for its detection and setting a clear goal for future experiments. 

To achieve this goal, we estimated that an upgrade to the LHCb is necessary and that a fully upgraded LHCb can reach a clean sample of around 100 events, providing a clear path for its detection and setting a clear goal for future experiments.

Recent discoveries of colossal Nernst effects in various magnetic materials near phase transitions have sparked significant interest in fundamental research and potential applications.  In this study, we discovered unusually large Hall and Nernst effects in the antiferromagnetic state of thin Mn$_3$NiN layers as small as 2 nm thick.  Our researchers observed that despite the magnetic state's stability to epitaxial sapphire substrate addition添加, the Nernst signal persisted to temperatures as high as 300 K.  Further investigations into the origin of this effect included out-of-plane and in-plane inelastic neutron scattering as well as varying nitrogen content, which led to the observation of an additional carrier contribution to the Nernst signal in samples with lower nitrogen content.  Based on additional measurements of the neutral matter's velocity using X-ray dichroism, the effect was interpreted as resulting from coupled spin-charge dynamics modulated by a reservoir of neutral matter moving as a result of the Lorentz force.

In recent years, automatic medical image analysis has made significant progress, thanks to deep neural networks that have achieved great results. These advancements can be attributed to improved data efficiency and accuracy thanks to multi-task learning and knowledge distillation. However, most current knowledge distillation techniques require teachers to be pre-trained and then combined, which becomes increasingly cumbersome as the number of experts grows. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-teacher knowledge distillation technique called Pairwise Iterative Logits Aggregation (PILE) for both single and multi-teacher scenarios in medical images. PILE is a flexible and iterative process, where labels are automatically created by selecting two high-confidence teachers and combining their outputs, which is done repeatedly until convergence or human intervention. As a result, PILE can converge to a high-performance model without requiring all teachers to be trained beforehand. Notably, PILE has a unique property called latent label balancing, which ensures the implicit labels generated during the process are well-distributed. Experiments on medical images demonstrate that PILE outperforms existing methods, including ensemble and Bayesian model averaging techniques, by achieving superior results with fewer teachers.

Accelerators of low and medium acceleration rates usually operate with several beams simultaneously, often resulting in substantial beam losses that generate excessive heat and radiation hazards, making them unsuitable for modern high-energy, high-intensity applications. To tackle this problem, a proposed methodology involves modeling each beam using an associated "diversity function" which guarantees low coherence between beams, thereby reducing beam losses. This concept was initially proposed in the context of circular devices, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through both theoretical calculations and numerical simulations for a dipole case, including rates of beam decay that match observed trends.

User centers around the world are key in testing and validating emerging technologies across various fields including computer science, engineering, life sciences, and agriculture. These facilities are designed to accelerate groundbreaking discoveries by allowing for large-scale, simultaneous, and even remote experiments. To effectively manage these activities, significant investments have been made in cutting-edge hardware, comprehensive infrastructure, and highly skilled staff in large user centers. However, coordinating and sticking to schedules for complex activities requires substantial investments in sophisticated scheduling systems, which have been further complicated by the additional security safety checks needed in large facilities like synchrotron light sources. These safety checks can take hours to complete, depending on the experiment. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of machine-intelligent scheduling systems, leveraging the potential of machine learning algorithms to streamline scheduling, sticking to schedules, and security safety checks. We outline the challenges and opportunities in this area and provide examples of existing implementations in large user centers.

This study provides comprehensive uniform regularity results for solutions to a class of non-autonomous sub-quadratic expansion hindered functional differential equations. Building on prior research, the abovementioned outcomes can also be applied to uniform regularity in fully non-autonomous harmonic map type systems.

A significant prediction of theoretical models for improved plasma confinement, such as advanced tokamaks and superconducting tokamaks, is the potential for high-energy particle losses due to geodesic acoustic modes (GAMs). Previous studies on GAMs typically assumed symmetric Geodesic Pressure Fluctuations (GPFs) in order to facilitate the cancellation of leading-order terms during the plasma amplitude decomposition. However, in实际情况中, plasma instabilities often exhibit asymmetry between the ion and electron populations. Therefore, the impact of both identical and contrasting temperatures on the GAM growth rate and structure must be considered. A notable increase in the GAM growth rate is observed when there is a contrast in temperatures, in contrast to scenarios where temperatures are comparable or temperatures are measured in units of mass-to-charges ratio. Furthermore, the electron component's contribution to the plasma amplitude becomes more significant in high-GAM frequencies resulting from temperature disparity. Consequently, GAMs with such frequencies may experience enhanced interactions with trapped electron modes, which could further exacerbate their growth rate.

The performance of quantum annealing can suffer significantly from both stochastic nonadiabatic transitions and a phenomenon known as the catastrophic collapse. Although the search for minimum-energy configurations in a Ising model is a basic application of quantum annealing, it's important to consider factors that could impact more intricate models, such as those used in applications. Non-stoquastic interactions in the Ising model can cause an unexpected increase in the ground-state gap during an exponential slowing down of the annealing process, even when initial and final states are local ground states with the same magnetization. This is in contrast to stoquastic evolution, which doesn't exhibit catastrophic collapse. The addition of decoherence, specifically weak transverse and longitudinal noise, can actually hinder ground-state formation and cause a sudden jump to an excited state with a much higher energy during quantum annealing. Interestingly, for a strong decoherence regime, a quantum state that closely resembles the ground state can be achieved by using a stoquastic annealer with a sufficiently strong decoherence strength, provided that certain conditions are satisfied, including the inclusion of non-stoquastic interactions.

The discovery of extragalactic stars by van Rhijn in 1937 revolutionized our knowledge of the universe's structure. This finding formed the foundation for subsequent research into the nature and dynamics of the universe. As director of Kapteyn's Observatory in Groningen, Netherlands, van Rhijn had access to advanced equipment and the opportunity to utilize a vast collection of photographic plates that had been taken since 1910. Although initially designed for research on nearby stars, van Rhijn's significant contributions were made possible by his extensive use of these plates to analyze the content of distant galaxies and nebulae across the sky. Specifically, he utilized a groundbreaking approach of analyzing small, well-documented sections of the sky, or "Selected Areas," to determine the distribution, movement, and dynamics of matter within the universe. By examining numerous "Selected Areas" across different distances, van Rhijn was able to reveal the existence of our Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy, as well as provide valuable insights into our galaxy's spiral structure, movements, and density variations, setting the stage for future research on the universe.

This paper proposes a theoretical framework and conducts an in-depth analysis of 2-power clear Serre weights for GL_2 with respect to an infinite sequence of increasingly large extensions of local fields, focusing on Kummer theory. A key feature of this setup is that there's no need to consider residual characteristics of p. As a key outcome, we establish the existence of clear Serre weights for a vast array of finite extensions.

We establish the existence of optimal volumes within optimal boundary behaviors for collections of equal-volume objects, and their corresponding optimal surface structures as they scale down to the Smollar type surfaces. This development leads to the derivation of an isoperimetric functional, providing evidence for the existence of minimal surfaces that combine mean curvature and curvature. These surfaces, characterized by a decomposition into two parts, represent larger-scale configurations and localized configurations. The larger-scale configurations can be represented by smoothly curved surfaces, while the localized configurations correspond to large-scale optimal arrangements. We demonstrate how these configurations and arrangements relate to the existence of a smooth, curved surface in the mid-range. This surface, however, may not be directly observable due to the influence of external forces and may require theoretical analysis to understand its formation. This analysis is supported by a proof of gradual surface behavior, providing evidence for the existence of a smoothly curved surface in the mid-range. Deep neural network (DNN) training often necessitates model-parallelism, a technique that segments the model into manageable sections and distributes each section across multiple machines. However, coordinating this process is complicated by the need for precise synchronization of gradient updates across each segment during training. Research indicates that decoupling this synchronization can enhance model-parallelism's scalability. This study proposes an innovative approach that introduces virtual reviewers and regional loss calculations to split the DNN training process into independent parts. By doing so, this method not only parallels the model-parallelism technique but also outperforms it by significantly reducing communication overhead and doubling effective parallelism. Further studies reveal that increasing the number of virtual reviewers can reduce training time by sevenfold and yield a 225x speedup over conventional model-parallelism techniques for specific use cases.

To maintain composite aircraft structures, identifying the location and severity of growing cracks is essential. This research uses Self-Sensing Composites (SSCs) that incorporate piezoelectric patches for in-situ damage detection, pinpointing the boundaries between intact and damaged areas within the composite material. By analyzing changes in electrical impedance tomography (EIT) images as damages develop, we aim to pinpoint the damage within the composite structure. This study examines the classification of 2D binary patterns representing possible states of EIT images and explores various optimization algorithms to locate the exact boundary between intact and damaged regions within the composite.

Recent experimental evidence suggests that young children have an advanced grasp of compositionality, which contradicts established developmental theories. Our study seeks to refine the original experiment's design, focusing on the comprehension of non-obvious, compositionally-derived relationships. Utilizing modified tasks, our results indicate that both young children and adults struggle to discern these comparison patterns, aligning with previous findings. However, when the logical structure was altered, our data reveals that adults and even young children can successfully detect these comparison patterns.

Highly complex autonomous machines need simple controls that can learn optimal movements quickly from just a few examples within real-time constraints and use these lessons to master new tasks with zero examples. Feeding an optimal control system rich information from surrounding environment helps it process the surrounding environment. This project focuses on the challenge of optimal control systems learning movements from a single example. It aims to tackle this challenge by using a minimal number of inputs and optimal control concepts to manage the system. It proposes a novel method to reduce the system's requirements to a single optimal movement. It demonstrates the method on multiple models of dynamic systems such as simple walking and flying machines, it learns complex movements within a single trial. Moreover, it uses the method to transfer lessons from one example to another. It uses a simple walking machine, it creates multiple optimal control systems and it transfers lessons and it refines the method.

A novel approach to linear vector and tensor analysis is explored, integrating classical affine geometry with tensor algebra. This approach eschews coordinate usage and vector differentiation, instead leveraging geometric measures within Euclidean space to establish a robust theoretical framework. The implications of this framework include a streamlined derivation of the reciprocal basis, a diverse range of connection coefficient transformation rules, a unifying series of identity equations, a simplified basis for tensor transformation, and the development of the absolute differential calculus. The theory is further expanded to include Riemannian space and the identification of key differential geometric objects like Christoffel symbols, Riemann curvature tensor, and geodesic paths, utilizing an intrinsic differential invariant method.

In the Standard Model, massless particles such as photons are anticipated to modify taste perception by interacting with electrons during biting or chewing. A precise experimental investigation is proposed to determine whether these particles can be detected based on their interaction with electrons, ultimately allowing constraints to be placed on the properties of any potentially massless or nearly massless particles that may mediate a new long-range force between fermions.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced educational institutions to close physically and shift to remote learning via remote education (RE). Research suggests that this sudden shift to RE may negatively impact students' focus and grade retention. Unfortunately, many studies lack consideration of relevant factors including gender, grade level, and socioeconomic status (SES). Consequently, this research fills a crucial gap in existing knowledge. Data for this cross-sectional study was collected from 1,020 public high school and middle school students in Florida between May and July 2020 via an online survey administered by Qualaroo. Results revealed remote education significantly hampers students' ability to stay on track, with in-person learners experiencing less disruption than their remote counterparts. Furthermore, our data showed gender and SES have a diverse influence on how remote education affects students' focus, but grade level did not. These findings provide valuable insights for the AERA audience and have practical applications including the need to consider diverse variables when implementing remote education in the future.

We construct the Toda conformal field theory based on a simple affine Lie algebra and utilize this to develop its holomorphic sector. This development enables an examination of the theory's global symmetry, specifically its bosonic affine Lie algebra. By applying the Ward identities associated with this symmetry, we derive the constraints on conformal blocks and successfully compute three-point coefficients. These computations are then compared to previously obtained results for $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. Notably, our calculations reveal that the corresponding structure constants are rational functions of the background coupling, which asymptotically approach -1 for large values. This asymptotic behavior aligns with the expected unitarity of the theory. Our results also exhibit consistency with the bootstrap equation for degenerate fields and demonstrate asymptotic agreement with the large-$b$ limit.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

In this study, they investigated how charge and the scalar field's charge influence the black hole's outer and inner horizons as well as its small and large black phase regions.  They found that increasing the scalar field's charge expands the area where a certain type of black hole exists, but restricts it in another.  They also discovered that in contrast to mass, both horizons behave similarly, and their relationship with temperature varies depending on which horizon they represent.  They observed that in a certain temperature range, charge has an opposing effect on both horizons.  They found that adding a scalar field is equivalent to increasing the black hole's mass by an amount equal to $q_{\phi }q_{e}/r_{-}$ as seen by a certain type of black hole.  They investigated how charge and the scalar field's charge affect two black hole interaction scenarios, and discovered that in both cases, adding a scalar field results in an increase in energy, complying with a certain hypothesis. In standard Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, several key principles such as replacement, choice, and separation are formulated using first-order logic. This study explores a modified framework based on first-order paraconsistent or paracomplete logic, which differs from traditional first-order logic by altering its treatment of excluded middle, noncontradiction, and consistency principles. As a result, the basic Zermelo set theory is also redefined in this new logical context. The study aims to compare the equational capabilities of the original and modified systems, and ultimately, it seeks to demonstrate that both systems are theoretically equivalent to one another.

A study investigated how different forms of movement, such as walking, running, and walking on a treadmill, affect brain activity. Researchers used an electrocorsogram (ECoG) to scan the motor cortex of nine volunteers while they performed these activities. They found that there are at least five distinct states of movement, including walking and running at gliding states, and that the movement's rhythm plays a key role in these movement patterns. Additionally, the study found that classifying these movement states can be done with high accuracy when combining features of movement frequency and phase.

This paper proposes using nested sampling to calculate Shannon and Kolmogorov entropy for the purpose of classifying and predicting complex systems. Nested sampling is particularly advantageous in this context as it effectively handles high-dimensional problems and naturally incorporates the assessment of prior probabilities. The algorithm's efficiency and reliability are explored, including a method to determine the statistical uncertainty of entropy calculations. The approach is then applied to two test cases: the Little model for magnetization and a dataset from the U.S. National Center for Atmospheric Research for predicting the evolution of atmospheric flow fields. The results highlight the algorithm's capacity for system prediction based on entropy criteria.
We examine how right-angled Artin groups split apart according to their geometric properties, focusing on how these divisions correspond to the structure of associated Cayley graphs.

Structural functional connectivity methods identify individual neural elements that facilitate communication between brain regions, but current approaches fall short in capturing time-varying connections due to excessive computation, lack of interpretability, or excessive model parameters. In contrast, our proposed framework, Dynamic Efficient Gaussian Process Factorial States Space Models, strikes an efficient balance between high model capacity and reduced parameter count while representing latent cognitive states. Our method's 100-fold reduction in parameters over 100 time points enables precise tracking of connections' fluctuations. Applied to fNIR data, it revealed task-related activations and distinctions between individuals in a working memory task, including nuanced differences in the medial prefrontal cortex.

Hybrid networks serve as a comprehensive phylogenetic representation that includes unresolved taxa. Until now, most phylogenetic analysis tools produced hybrid networks from three input trees sharing the same set of leaves, a limitation excludes scenarios where the inputs may differ in the species they contain. In this study, we identify several network construction methods capable of generating hybrid networks and explore their topological properties. Our research reveals that the majority of these approaches necessarily result in specific intricate structures, particularly when dealing with larger network designs. A necessary and sufficient condition for a specific algorithm to produce such intricate structures in a specific way has also been established in this study. A practical application of our theoretical necessary and sufficient condition allows the phylogenetic community to develop tools with features such as optionality and computationally 100% efficiency. Furthermore, our explicit mathematical derivation of the intricate structures's solution contributes to the development of more efficient computational algorithms, with some achieving run times of less than 0.01 seconds for specific configurations. A code implementation of our Option Checker Tool has been made available on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/danieldelgadoa/OptionCheckerTool.

Determining whether a image or video contains actual movement or attempted deception has long challenge researchers in the fields of computer vision and security. This specific task can be particularly difficult when attempting to detect subtle biological movement in video, often used in advertising and other media. To automate this process, a novel approach has been developed that utilizes motion estimation and statistical analysis. This method estimates the biological movement within a video sequence by examining local optical flow. A key advantage of this method, which relies predominantly on established computer vision techniques, is its adaptability to varying input formats. Additionally, it outperforms alternative methods, including ultralight and deep learning models, achieving higher accuracy in detecting biological movement in video.

Delegating computationally intensive tasks to computer graphics processors enables scientists to effectively manage large-scale data sets by balancing CPU workload. However, leveraging GPU potential requires addressing its limitations, particularly insufficient cache size for dense matrix operations. Researchers have developed elevated order techniques to mitigate GPU memory access bottlenecks, but these methods introduce excessive cache pressure. An innovative approach is presented here, integrating elevated order methods with iterative matrix inversion through a novel solver designed for massive parallel computations. By utilizing simple matrix-vector multiplications, this technique reduces GPU memory access pressure while maintaining a balance of computational efficiency. The proposed method outperforms traditional elevated order inverses in benchmarks involving dense matrix operations, achieving at least a tenfold speedup over Gaussian elimination for specific datasets and surpassing the capabilities of previous GPU-optimized algorithms.

Our study derives mathematical relationships for the frequency-dependent absorption characteristics of scattering systems across a wide frequency range. By leveraging Kramers-Kronig relations and optical sum rules, we establish bounds on the average absorption efficiency that varying monochromatic lights produce in relation to the system's total number of resonators. This approach enables the derivation of specific sum rules applicable to systems like cavity-photocatalytic converter configurations consisting of multiple resonators and subject to monochromatic illumination.

A theoretical model has been created to simulate topological Anderson insulators in two-dimensional systems with random disordered interactions. The model specifically focuses on two types of disorder and applies to both large and small system sizes. Using an exact numerical method called the finite-size scaling of the energy spectrum, researchers were able to map out how different disorder levels affect the system, regardless of how much the system was scaled. This allowed for an efficient algorithm to determine the critical disorder levels associated with the transition from ordinary to topological Anderson insulators. The topological nature of the state was confirmed using the Chern number, and their results show that the topological Anderson insulator phase can exist in systems with random disordered interactions of this type.

For a given biordered set $\mathfrak{B}$, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for an isomorphism between trimmed versions of homomorphically equivalent sets to imply the equivalence itself. Additionally, we derive an isomorphism condition for the biordered sets derived from maximal centralizers of irreducible morphisms.

A novel mechanism for reducing the Higgs boson's mass in the MSSM is presented, involving a pheno-physical Higgs that is not a fundamental particle. This additional Higgs degree of freedom, which phenomonologically appears as a 125 GeV particle, is combined with the standard MSSM tadanom Higgs. The model is combined with intricate supersymmetry parameters and is analyzed for a range of multi-TeV super-Drell-Yan cross-section limits at both ILC and HL-LHC.

A new class of linearity tests has been created, allowing for robust assessments of linearity in network autoregressive models. These tests are designed to handle both symmetric and non-symmetric matrices, and the accuracy of the tests' estimates is verified for large datasets. The evaluation of the tests' performance is carried out using artificial data generated from network autoregressive models, as well as real-world examples such as mutual fund networks and in-flight network data.

When applying declarative models to complex systems, under-fitting is a common challenge due to the models' limited capacity to simple, global patterns. This issue has been particularly prevalent in recent studies on declarative neural network design, which have often been constrained by computational power. However, advances in computing have enabled research on high-dimensional, dynamic systems, such as human social interactions, the feasibility of declarative models is now being investigated. To assess these models, we propose an issue framework consisting of five categories: model, data, mechanism, topology, and time. This framework serves a dual purpose: it helps identify potential problems before conducting simulations and provides a structured manner for presenting simulation outcomes. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through comprehensive case studies, utilizing specialized declarative networks called Data Processing Network (DPN).

Our work presents an initial framework for mathematical biology models of cellular processes, including cell detachment, movement, and protein relocation within an Hele-Shaw cell. The model's components interact through complex non-linear connections. A submodel of the Navier-Stokes equation describes cell behavior by incorporating a moving boundary with one or more disconnected areas. The model's accuracy and efficiency are suitable for a typical biology simulation of cell and protein activity. Furthermore, the cell's movement is governed by a parabolic equation, facilitating the application of standard numerical methods.

The rapid adoption of cryptocurrencies in the financial sector has fueled innovation, yet it also facilitates complex money laundering schemes that utilize layered transactions to conceal illicit funds within the blockchain ledger. Our new tool, called FinPath, fills the gap in existing systems by automatically generating easy-to-understand visualizations of cryptocurrency laundering operations for analysts to investigate. Using machine learning techniques adapted for ledger analysis, FinPath identifies sophisticated money laundering patterns such as the mule-based, mixer service, and the triangular money laundering techniques, ensuring users have access to precise detection capabilities through the use of interpretable classification models.

Quantum computing has the potential to revolutionize fields such as drug discovery, cryptography, and scientific simulations, but building large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers remains a significant challenge. Recent advancements in quantum error correction have produced robust logical qubits capable of withstanding multiple failures, making quantum error correction thresholds closer to 20 percent. However, the process of error correction is not fully efficient, as it involves costly error syndromes measurements and results in faulty logical gates that require many physical gates to implement. In search for more scalable methods, researchers are exploring novel approaches to threshold achievement, such as reinforcement learning-based code designs customized for specific tasks and integrated into feedback control systems. A new framework has been developed that applies this type of reinforcement learning code design to fault-resilient computation, enabling the development of custom code codes through reinforcement learning and their use in a code-based error correction framework that combines reinforcement learning and syndrome measurements, effectively creating a quantum computational device that can execute resilient code for multiple iterations.

Precise measurement techniques known as quantum leaps metrology are noted for their ability to detect minute changes, making them ideal for applications like detecting dark matter through axial gauge field fluctuations. A sensitive system is proposed, based on a pair of coupled optical cavities connected to superconducting qubits, where a small change in the axial gauge field can be detected by analyzing the radio-frequency signal resulting from quantum leaps in the system's atomic population. The model demonstrates sensitivity to flux at levels exceeding the thermal noise threshold, and through optimal control, the detection scheme can effectively identify extremely small fluctuations, similar to those expected from the absorption of a single photon.

The PHENIX Collaboration analyzed direct photon-hadron correlation data to compare the energy loss of medium as a result of the interaction between thermalized media and partons. In contrast to parton-parton collisions, which exhibit increased hadron yields due to the energy lost by partons being converted into new hadrons, a reduced hadron yield is observed in the near region due to radiative and interaction energy loss of partons. Our findings show a reduced hadron yield in medium compared to parton-parton collisions, with this effect increasing with photon transverse momentum. Additionally, mass-dependent flow within the medium causes a shift in the hadron spectrum toward lower transverse momenta. Considering both effects, theoretical models replicate the measured data, indicating an enhanced ratio of parton-parton collisions to medium-induced energy loss with rising photon transverse momentum. Furthermore, we found that the measured parton-parton collisions to medium-induced energy loss ratio in d+Au collisions is similar to that in nucleon-nucleon collisions, indicating similar energy loss mechanisms in both types of collisions.

In a universal Smarandache's sigma product, figures are paired such that the length of any figure equals the number of edges accumulated around it. We've established the universal Smarandache's sigma product conditions for four specific graph types: cycle-nest graphs, twisted cubes, prism-cyclic products, and hex-prism graphs. Additionally, we've proven the existence of these sigma products for hex-prism graphs when n is an even number greater than or equal to 4, and we've demonstrated the equality of lengths in the Smarandache's sigma product of twisted cubes and prism-cyclic products.

Cloud deployments of network-intensive applications can experience significant network performance fluctuations due to sharing infrastructure with other users. This dynamic environment leads to a cloud's Mean Performance Variation Ratio (MPVr) exceeding that of a dedicated data center (Dcvr). Traditionally, application designers have focused on maximizing scalability in a single-node scenario, neglecting the broader implications of performance variability. This study reevaluates the scalability (Cvr) of cloud vs. dedicated data center deployments, considering both variability and scheduling losses. Our findings indicate that due to higher MPVr values, certain applications lose their scalability advantages in cloud environments, or require a minimum number of nodes to match data center performance. To address this, we propose a novel clustering approach that groups nodes with similar processing speeds, or clocks (Cvcl), to only compare applications' variability-induced scheduling losses in controlled conditions, or clvrs. This leads to a revised formula for cloud variability-induced scheduling loss ratio (Cvirs). Empirical validation through live experiments on real-world datasets supports the soundness of our approach, or Clvirs.

We know that context-sensitive learning algorithms can achieve optimal performance using a minimal number of experts when dealing with large numbers of possibilities. In this study, we investigate whether these algorithms can be used in settings where participants can't directly communicate with each other, but do have access to the same source of information and can learn from the same general patterns. The results show that while the algorithms can't do as well as in a fully cooperative situation, they still converge to a stable solution and context-sensitive versions can't significantly improve this outcome. However, a modified version of the algorithm, which takes into account the characteristics of the problems being studied, can far exceed the performance limits.

In today's highly adaptable work environments, many organizations are adopting remote work as a permanent arrangement. Despite the advantages of remote work, studies on its impact on agile project performance remain scarce. This hybrid research approach seeks to explore how telecommuting works together with the Scrum process in enhancing the results of software projects. We combine survey data from 244 Scrum practitioners across nine European countries with in-depth interview insights into the results of this study. Findings indicate that telecommuting has a negative influence on Scrum project success but can be countered through the use of face-to-face meetings during the project duration. Additionally, team size plays a part in this dynamic, with larger teams benefiting more from face-to-face meetings in achieving successful project outcomes when working remotely.

We appreciate the interest shown by Rao, Zhang, and Hu our research on robust, distributionally optimal personalized treatment guidance throughout various regions simultaneously. Our guidance consider the cost structures of multiple regions while accounting for potential probability model discrepancies. Acknowledging the importance of Hoeffding inequalities in guarenteeing optimal cost in multiple regions, we emphasize the significance of learning the Hoeffding inequalities through data, given the cost functions are known, which is typically the case in policy learning scenarios involving the generalization of optimal distributions across multiple regions.

Our analysis of the inclusive transverse momentum (p_T) and transverse impact parameter (r_T) spectra for charged hadrons in Pb-Pb and pp collisions at a cross-section of 2.76 TeV reveals that an accurate fit can be achieved using the Wigner-Eisenberg event formalism. By incorporating the impact parameter, we reevaluate previous proton-proton findings and observe a high degree of consistency. Furthermore, this approach allows us to obtain the one-dimensional probability distribution for the nuclear entropy as well as the elliptic motion parameter (epsilon_2), which can be linked to the geometric properties of the collision region. Introducing a hadronization threshold of 1 GeV/c for nucleons, we examine its influence on the hadron spectra and related quantities, discovering a direct correlation between the hadron to nucleon ratio and the entropies of hadrons and nucleons. The hadron hadronization threshold also impacts our analysis of the charged hadron average transverse momentum as a function of the collision impact parameter, with considerations of this threshold leading to an apparent phase transition at certain proton-proton collisions and influencing nucleon residual free motion.

This study introduces the concept of invariant points within the domain of the four-variable quaternion linear canonical S transform, specifically focusing on unit norm functions. Furthermore, it derives a necessary and sufficient condition for a non-zero function to have a specific behavior under this transform, namely, if a function meets this condition, then its transform will have a specific property. An additional, alternative sufficient condition is also provided. These conditions ultimately lead to an explanation of the functions that remain unchanged under this transform. Additionally, a derived formula known as the Bessel inequality will have a corresponding, refined version.
