Autonomous mobile robots depend on path planning systems to move from one location to another. These systems utilize various navigation methods, including laser radar and sonar blending. While blending multiple sonar readings is typically done to enhance the performance of laser radar, there has been little research on using this technique independently. Our proposed approach involves a novel sonar blending module that can independently blend sonar data in real-time. This approach overcomes the limitations of single-sonar sensing by seamlessly integrating data from multiple sonar sensors. Our module employs the DTS method to smoothly blend the trajectories of objects detected by each sonar sensor, resulting in precise object and boundary tracking even when using just one sonar sensor. We have integrated this approach with the ROS navigation stack, enabling layered navigation management. Our system has been successfully applied to guiding service robots through narrow corridors and around corners, where the sonar data is processed in real-time.

Social engineering threats pose a significant risk in identifying and preventing fraud. One method of social engineering is crafting deceptive news articles by replicating legitimate headlines and stories. Due to the vast number of online news articles, manually analyzing them to identify fraud becomes an insurmountable task.

To tackle this problem, we explore the potential of using machine-generated summaries to aid in identifying deceptive news. By leveraging automatic text summarization machines, we can efficiently analyze the content of deceptive news stories. We built and assessed multiple summarization models over several datasets, ultimately achieving an F0.5 score of 0.537 in identifying fraudulent news through their summaries.

Furthermore, analyzing the effectiveness of summary features along with sentence embeddings led to a significant performance boost, yielding an F0.5 score of 0.600.

This research investigates a new phenomenon known as the bending influence in random fields, specifically how a change in one component can influence the probability distribution of unrelated components as a function of their spatial separation. The study focuses on Gaussian random fields in two dimensions and derives a new inequality, showing how the bending influence on two components can be limited by the interaction between them and their neighboring components. The derived limit becomes more restrictive in flat geometric settings and loosely related in scenarios where the change and observation are separated by a significant distance. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the practical application of the inequality in understanding how an externally imposed deformation could potentially facilitate a biological decision-making process in neural networks.

The implementation of Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) increases signal efficiency but also amplifies interference within 5G systems. To mitigate this risk, Physical Layer Authentication (PULA) has emerged as a potential solution by validating both users and base stations through deciphering shared secret information hidden within their transmitted signals. However, a critical issue arises when an untrusted NOMA user deciphers the secret information, potentially compromising the authentication of other communicating parties. In response, a novel approach is presented where the Base Station encrypts distinct bits of the secret key for each user using their individual channel states, enabling each user to retrieve their respective portion of the secret key. A new analysis is proposed to assess the authenticity of the transmitted signals, accounting for the information leaked to an untrusted NOMA user. Furthermore, a performance evaluation is conducted, determining the minimum signal-to-noise ratio required for successful authentication (by the Base Station and User to User) in the presence of the untrusted NOMA user.

Inforeferencing systems are increasingly utilized in various sectors, with their applications spanning from political and religious figures to celebrity and political commentary programs. Given their growing importance and potential for misinformation dissemination, detecting and flagging inforeferencing has become essential, a complex task due to the common employment of rotation-based inforeferencing techniques. This study presents a novel approach to identifying such information by leveraging the symmetry of rotation-based inforeferencing and an adjusted $\ell_1$-norm to enhance interpretability. By leveraging this symmetry, the proposed method efficiently reduces search space, enabling the use of sampling techniques for solving the modified norm examination. However, earlier attempts to leverage symmetry have resulted in information distortion and misleading conclusions. This study proposes an innovative application of $\ell_1$-norm to maintain accuracy and detect information reliably. The proposed approach guarantees a fixed efficiency in examining the revised problem, an uncommon trait for $\ell_1$-norm-based methods. The examination of synthetic and real-world data sets demonstrates the proposed method's superiority over baseline methods.

Despite their success in various NLP tasks, current question answering systems still face challenges in accurately capturing human intent due to the difficulty of properly annotating question semantics. The rise of emotionally-driven online interactions has emphasized the need for robust semantic annotation of questions, yet existing methods tend to underperform in this area. To address these limitations, this study proposes a new dataset called EMBA, which contains a rich set of emotionally-labeled datasets for real-world questions and answers. Building on the limitations of existing annotation techniques, this study presents a new method that leverages the BERT model to automatically refine the semantic marks of questions, yet even with this approach, human expertise remains essential for ensuring the quality of annotations.

We examine the effectiveness of basic strategies in infinite, monotonic games played on ordered sets of numbers. Our research indicates that within this category of games, there are two significant limitations: first, no universal universal game can be constructed that is homeomorphic to the real numbers; second, the existence of such a constructible game even with two universals implies a contradiction with the axiom of countable compactness. These conclusions are derived from the principle of effective monotonicity.

Over the last decade, new observations of magnetic white dwarfs in polars have revealed asynchronous precession of their magnetospheres. This phenomenon, observed in multiple stars, offers a new area of study, whereas other rotating magnetic white dwarfs, such as gigahertz pulsars and spin-precessing dwarf planets, are well-established. Understanding asynchronous precession's relationship to its counterpart, conventional precession, is essential before proceeding with further investigations. By analyzing the X-ray spectra of multiple polars during various orbital interactions, researchers found that the hard spectral component in these systems correlates significantly with the inclination angles. This previously unexplored relationship between the hard X-ray flux and the white dwarf's inclination in polars could imply that the white dwarf's spin-axis precession is connected to its orientation, similar to quasar precession.

This research presents an innovative method to resolve Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems through the integration of reduced-order models. By decoupling the temporal and spatial components of the reduction process, we utilize precomputed, partitioned reduced-order models for both fluid and structural components, which can be designed independently. Combining these models results in a highly efficient, unified reduced-order model that provides real-time solutions and accurate predictions of non-linear phenomena such as wave generation. Furthermore, the framework is flexible, incorporating a variety of partitioned reduced-basis techniques, and includes methods for handling interface issues, mesh transformation, and coupling strategies, as demonstrated through the simulation of wave generation and the Benneyon problem.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate independently, they need an effective map representation that shows the spatial arrangement of rooms and corridors. Current state-of-the-art methods focus on generating room and corridor layout representations using various techniques, but often overlook the hierarchical nature of larger environments. Existing approachs typically produce a flat layout that Straps them to larger spaces and makes them generate excessive unnecessary rooms. To tackle this issue, we present HiTMap, a new method that uses a hierarchical representation to capture the structure of large environments efficiently. HiTMap uses a grid-based approach to create a detailed semantic map, then applies an iterative clustering process to develop a hierarchical layout representation. The result is a compact, tree-structured model that accurately reflects the room and corridor layout of any given environment, regardless of its size or complexity. Our method also includes a process to refine and generate virtual sensor data to improve the layout representation, leading to high precision and recall scores in evaluating the accuracy of HiTMap's room and corridor layout representations.

This document reports on our team's approach to the 6th SemEval-2019 Task on Classifying Offensive Language, which required detecting derogatory speech. We focused on a specific subset of test data during the challenge. For the baseline, we used an LSTM model with character-level embeddings as described in the challenge guidelines. We developed two primary solutions: one involved a linear SVM with Descriptive Twitter embeddings, while the other combined multiple LSTM models to create richer embeddings before feeding them to the SVM. Additionally, we created an improved LSTM by training it on a customized dataset that gave more weight to the majority language, which enhanced its performance on the challenge test set. We ranked 13th out of 65 participating teams during the competition.

Employing a pulsed atomic interferometer in the presence of superconductors can take advantage of the Meissner effects to precisely measure local magnetic field changes. The interference patterns produced by the atomic interferometry are highly sensitive to linear velocity shifts induced by the time-varying magnetic field under the superconducting surface as it transitions from normal to superconducting or vice versa. By taking the derivative of this sensitive measurement with respect to the duration of the interference sequence, we can effectively cancel out the impact of unpredictable atomic initial conditions and central bursts that often pollute atomic interferometric readings. This technique is projected to achieve a precision of approximately $10^{-12}$ T/s for magnetization rate sensing when utilizing a one-meter-wide superconducting coil and a Rubidium atomic interferometer.

The distinctive properties of two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals crystals can be modified by altering their atomic arrangement into moiré patterns, a process known as superlattices formation. Leveraging this, we propose using atomic closure strain to induce localized spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect (MPMCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. Through a theoretical analysis combining tight-binding models and density functional theory, we found that twisting two layers of MoS2 creates superlattices with strain-induced localized states near Fermi level. Applying an in-plane magnetic field causes these states to experience the magnetocaloric effect and results in anomalous magnetoresistance due to localized states' differing resistance changes as temperature varies, a process referred to as closure-induced spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect. Due to the absence of long-range order in moiré patterns, this effect occurs within nanometer-scale length scales, a characteristic of two-dimensional materials that benefits from the intrinsic quantum fluctuations, a crucial difference from bulk systems. Additionally, we demonstrated closure-induced localized states can also be induced by applying an in-plane magnetic field, a process known as strain resonance. These findings offer a promising avenue for strain resonance-induced quantum sensing and provide a foundation for developing low-power magnetic sensors based on two-dimensional materials.

The behavior of gap-plasmons in nano-capacitors is investigated numerically as the separation between two electrodes approaches zero. Increasing the gap thickness relative to the wire radius significantly alters the energy dispersion and group velocity of gap-plasmons, slowing their velocity and creating a minimum in the dispersion curve. A significant electron spill-over effect, resulting from the overlap of electrons between the wires, also plays a crucial role in determining the geometry-induced changes to gap-plasmons. The simulation model incorporates this effect to better understand the interaction and formation of gap-plasmons.

The addition of normal forms to the Calculus of Constructions with Inductive
Types, as done by Coquand and Castagna, enables the development of
efficient normalization algorithms and proof search methods. Nonetheless,
this approach is compromised by pathologies such as non-terminating
reduction sequences that result in normal forms. In this paper, a modified
definition of normal forms is introduced, which excludes such pathologies.
The defined structure is demonstrated to be robust under the extension of
the Calculus of Constructions with Large Eliminations, and it is proven that
a normal form always corresponds to a closed term with the same type.
Furthermore, normal forms can be efficiently described in CNF, allowing for
an efficient algorithm to transform assumptions into a robust normal form.
This algorithm's correctness and termination are clearly proved, and its
effectiveness is shown through multiple numerical examples.

The rise of machine learning techniques for analyzing complex systems has underscored the necessity of a meaningful interpretation of extracted concepts. To achieve this, a methodical framework called Topological Quantum Occurrence Decomposition (TQOD) was developed, leveraging simple theoretical models such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. In this model, a variation in a coupling parameter triggers the formation and movement of boundary modes within a system. By subjecting multiple random ensembles of matrices to a scanning process around this critical point and subjecting resulting states to dimensionality reduction, a visual representation known as a "Carter diagram" can be generated. When the algorithm's hyperparameters are optimally set, it becomes evident that certain features such as winding numbers, occupation numbers, and phase signs play a significant role in interpreting the observed boundary mode behaviors. Furthermore, the formation of these modes can be attributed to the elastic property of bands and the attraction to potential wells, while their localization near specific system edges can be explained by their respective phases. The proposed TQOD method holds the potential to provide a deeper, physically relevant interpretation of the concealed structures and mechanisms at play within machine learning models when applied to more intricate systems.

In simple probability distributions, the mean and entropy are often used as key descriptors. However, in more complex systems, these quantities can provide insights into the system's overall behavior and structure, making a link with probability distributions through geometric methods known as Choquet theory. Mixture models are then utilized to represent relationships between subsystems.

Using dual-loop methods, we re-examine four-loop glueball supergravity amplitudes in AdS5 x S5 and find discrepancies with previous calculations for two of the three relevant dimensions, which start at eight loops in the original context. These discrepancies may be attributed to an incorrect count of supergravity multiples in the spectrum, as the dual CFT spectrum includes an additional two multiples in the relevant range. Furthermore, the analysis at four loops is found to be deficient due to an incomplete treatment of threshold effects, specifically the contribution from two-particle cuts across the boundary of the AdS bulk. A framework for computing these missing contributions within the AdS context is established in the study.

High-performance object allocation on GPUs is crucial for developing efficient, concurrent applications using programming languages like Java and C++. However, existing GPU memory allocators fall short in supporting a large variety of memory sizes effectively, as they either focus on generating live objects without considering memory access patterns or are limited to specific types of allocations. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel, size-class-based concurrent memory allocator called DynaSOAr, which is designed to be both adaptable and optimized for runtime use. By drawing on the strengths of reference counting and garbage collection, along with a custom error-handling approach, our allocator delivers on safe memory management, efficient runtime performance, and a high level of adaptability, all while outperforming the leading alternative allocators in a variety of real-world benchmark scenarios.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse class of sublinear operators along with their commutators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, sufficient conditions for the boundedness of these operators and their commutators on these spaces are established.

Using a first-principles approach based on the Liouville equation and initial conditions, we model the drift current of electrons around magnetically active sites, such as isolated transition metal atoms or clusters on a superconducting metal surface. Specifically, we examine an Mn atom and various Mn configurations on the Nb(110) surface and compare our results to existing experimental and traditional density functional theory data. Our simulations reveal the formation of sub-Bang electron halos and streams in multiple locations, with drift currents in some areas exceeding 0.1e, a current that is many times larger (approximately 10^3 to 10^4 times) than those obtained through magnetization or superconducting pairing in standard electronic structure calculations. Notably, the magnitude of these electrons' drift currents surpasses the experimental detection threshold. As a result, our results indicate that current experimental setups may be capable of detecting these currents.

Recently, implicit functional mapping has gained traction in instance segmentation due to its versatility in representing continuous scenes. Typically, parameters are learned for a specific parameterized representation, such as Fourier features, to achieve this. Building on this, we propose FourierMask, which also utilizes Fourier features. As an improvement over previous methods like DM-Mask and NeRF-Seg, FourierMask predicts instance segmentation masks directly. We demonstrate that Fourier features allow the model to focus on mask-relevant details rather than the entire scene. Furthermore, FourierMask achieves state-of-the-performance in zero-shot generalization, matching NeRFSeg on challenging instances and exceeding DM-Mask's results on average.

Let $M$ be a compact, oriented surface with the boundary consisting of $k$ disjoint components in the plane. If $M$ has a smooth, orientation-preserving Hamiltonian immersion into $S^3$, then there exists a smooth, Hamiltonian embedding of $M$ into $S^3$ with the same homotopy type as $M$. Furthermore, any smooth, Hamiltonian immersion $\phi\colon M \to S^3$ can be deformed through a sequence of operations - smooth Hamiltonian immersions with fewer critical points of type $z$-height - into a smooth, Hamiltonian embedding $e \colon M \to S^3$ while maintaining the same Hamiltonian minimax invariants. Any Hamiltonian minimal immersion $M \to S^3$ with non-zero minimax invariants has a range that fills $[0, R]$ where $R$ is strictly less than the minimal area of any essential loop in $M$. If $M$ has a non-empty set of essential loops, any Hamiltonian minimal immersion $M \to S^3$ with a minimal area loop tracing its boundary is a graph over its $x$-axis projection and has a non-zero minimax invariants.

Our research employs satellite data from multiple scattering lidar MISR and broad spectral radiometer MODIS to investigate the complex internal structure of optically thick convective clouds. By analyzing 450+ cases, we've identified a veiled core within these clouds, characterized by an optical depth exceeding 10 which obscures the cloud's topological features using MODIS but can be precisely measured using MISR's multiple angles of scattering light. Within this veiled core, we've discovered that the cloud contains optical depth gradients, structural formations such as rolls and cells, as well as thickness variations. These features are likely generated by the cloud's internal dynamic interactions. Moreover, we've discovered that multiple scattering lidar increases effective path length of light within these clouds up to 3 times, significantly enhancing their imaging resolution compared to single photon detectors used in radiometers. This enhanced effective path length means that even extremely thick clouds contain regions where dynamic interactions play a crucial role in multiple scattering events, effectively processing an abnormal amount of time over relatively long periods within a large three-dimensional volume, resulting in significant effective path lengths compared to the cloud's overall thickness.

To counteract gradual radiation that builds up on a spacecraft as it travels through space, a novel concept called self-induced relativistic translucency has been proposed to mitigate radiation absorption by utilizing reflective forces. This new approach suggests using transparent conductive materials and generating heat internally through high-power laser or microwave sources, such as ion propulsion systems with gradually increasing power outputs. By analyzing the combined effects of these systems under various conditions, a model incorporating chirp-driven heating and reflection was developed and solved, revealing the conditions necessary for translucency and the benefits of using variable power sources. Specifically, it was found that an superhydrophobic coated spacecraft with an increasing electric power output has the potential to fully achieve this translucency state before reaching a significant relativistic speed.

Planet $Planet_b$ of the system TOI-712, which is similar to the Sun, stands out as the first comprehensive case study of a young exoplanet system under 1 billion years old. This discovery includes four planets, notably $Planet_d$ and $Planet_c$ with masses of approximately 0.6-0.8 $M_E$ and 0.9-1.2 $M_E$, respectively. The system's age was ascertained through X-ray analysis of the star, which also yielded a rotational period of 0.7 days and characteristics matching 90% of the parameters through astrometric simulation. Although there's a discrepancy in age estimation based on the star's features (around 400 million years) and metallicity (similar to the Sun) with literature values suggesting a younger age, we place greater emphasis on the former. Based on the accumulation of geologic evidence, we believe these sub-$Hubble$ planets to be in their juvenile stage of development. Notably, $Planet_b$ exhibits a low eccentricity (0.13 $\pm$ 0.05), and its semi-major axis places it at the inner boundary of the habitable zone. Considering the star's high temperature and brightness, as well as its habitable zone location, we conclude that $Planet_b$ has the potential to support liquid water on the surface if it's a rocky planet. However, we also predict

A first-principles study explores the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within TiO2's rutile structure, using a variety of computational methodologies including GPOT, RPA, and GGAP. Unlike previous studies that used an oversized simulation box and neglected electronic and magnetic ordering, this research models monomeric defects and various dimeric defects with different spin configurations. Comparing total energies provides a more accurate electronic and magnetic arrangement for these defects. Carbon defects exhibit localized states within the TiO2 electronic gap, forming distinct C-derived subbands. N defects, however, introduce states that overlap the TiO2 valence band maximum, potentially altering its optical properties. Some dimeric defects display uncancelled magnetic moments and wide spin bands, making TiO2 potentially active in spin-dependent light absorption. These findings enhance our understanding of the electronic and magnetic behavior carbon and nitrogen defects within the TiO2 rutile structure may have on its optical properties.

The primary method of top quark production at the LHC, known as "W-boson mediated," includes minor contributions from the LHC's unique features, such as the elliptical path of colliding beams and forces between protons. For a more thorough investigation of top quark generation, we introduce the concept of fully elastic top quark production. This process, although seemingly complex, can be broken down into two main components: the first being the interaction between protons and the second involving the creation of top quark pairs. We demonstrate the feasibility of identifying fully elastic top quark production through elastic W-boson mediated channels using simulated data from the ATLAS experiment for center-of-mass energies of 13 and 14 TeV. Our findings also reveal that top quark production via forces between protons, specifically diagram v in Figure 1, cannot be considered negligible, in contrast to other diagrams representing quadratic contributions.

To accurately measure the turbulent fluctuations in the intra-cluster medium, a precise understanding of structure functions is crucial. In this study, we analyze the impact of various measurement inaccuracies on the determination of these functions. Our simulations indicate that volume-averaging and boundary corrections can distort the true turbulent fluctuations, and therefore, alternative methods need to be developed. Moreover, the accuracy of estimating power spectra from structure functions is limited, particularly at higher spatial frequencies, where the errors become significant and难以区分 from the actual turbulent spectrum. This limitation implies that a precise reverse calculation of the structure functions from the power spectrum may not be achievable. Furthermore, the inclusion of Gaussian smoothing, commonly used to regularize structure function measurements, leads to an artificial increase in lower-order structure functions, particularly for n=2, which plays a key role in estimating turbulent motion shifts and pressures. This effect also impacts the derived properties of turbulent cascades and power spectra. A crucial factor in understanding these issues is the comparison between noisy and noise-free data structure functions and their corresponding power spectra. This raises questions whether structure functions derived from the power spectrum of noisy data will accurately reflect both the true turbulent fluctuations and its associated power spectrum.

The concept of $p$-colorability for graphs divided by $p$ colors has long been studied, focusing on graphs with upper $p$-richness and graphs comprising an upper $p$-rich component. This paper explores graphs that are both Ramsey-$p$ choice choosable and possess $p$-rich upper richness, particularly those with a single, upper $p$-rich component. Although some initial findings date back to the 1990s and 2000s, a general theorem was elusive. Our work fills this gap by presenting sufficient conditions for a graph to be both Ramsey-$p$ choice choosable and upper $p$-rich with a single component, alongside several corollaries that were previously unknown.

Located at the heart of the Galactic Center, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) contains numerous dense star formations.  In these areas, massive clusters and individual stars are unstable over time and constantly mix their gases, which may impede the process of star creation.  Analyzing how gases are distributed and structured in various regions of the CMZ is vital in understanding the interaction between formed stars/clusters and gas.  However, assessing shape, structure, and distribution in three dimensions is more difficult than in two dimensions.  This study introduces a technique to examine two-dimensional shapes and structures using visual data, applying it to gas in four fields within the CMZ.  By integrating this technique with numerical modeling, we are able to measure dimensions, elliptical shapes, and orientation of a three-dimensional ellipsoid that encloses a specific mass in CMZ regions.  Results show that gas configurations in four observed fields are mostly symmetrical in two dimensions but exhibit notable asymmetry in three dimensions.  This study's recommendations on describing two-dimensional gas configurations using visual data can be utilized in studies on star-gas interactions in various cosmic environments.

A significant number of stroke victims experience Bell's palsy, which impairs one side of the face, making it droopy and difficult to close the eye.  By analyzing videos of stroke patients, we can detect Bell's palsy with reasonable accuracy.  To do this effectively, it's crucial to focus on eye-specific features affected by the condition.  Our proposed method, which centers around the eyes being examined, uses deep learning to classify videos as either positive or negative for Bell's palsy.  We found that extracting frames from video at a lower rate and using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to do this eye-centered analysis, resulted in lower computational costs and better efficiency.  When tested on a dataset of 104 videos, our method achieved a 0.11 F-score for identifying persons with Bell's palsy.  We also optimized the code to run 4 times faster than the initial version.

In our investigation, we examine the role of initial state and numerical noise in generating sound-like artifacts in lattice simulations of sQED using qutrits, and propose a method to eliminate these enhancements via a noise-cancellation technique. Our findings from scalable simulations on up to 57 qutrits demonstrate that sound-like patterns persist even in the absence of numerical noise and with precise initial states, indicating their origin lies within the qutrit-based simulation framework itself. Furthermore, our research reveals that an adjusted protocol which sets the extra degree of freedom for each qutrit's phase space to zero through controlled initialization significantly reduces the spurious enhancement of these sound-like patterns in the electromagnetic field. Our approach is directly implementable in the BQUAP simulator using the available qutrit interface. Our study thus provides crucial insights into understanding and controlling numerical noise in qutrit-based simulations of sQED, and our proposed noise-cancellation technique may have broader implications for optimizing the performance of future scalable simulations.

Our analysis suggests that circularly polarized laser interactions with thin, dense, and heated foil produce a dense stream of spin-aligned positrons in the path of the intense laser beam. This phenomenon arises when considering tightly bound electrons within holes in Fermi seas, extending beyond the basic three-dimensional theory. The interaction between high-intensity lasers and relativistic plasma produce a dense polarization-aligned electron-positron plasma. The required conditions for this phenomenon to occur in a QED regime can be met with current technology using high-power lasers and aluminum or copper targets, and simulating these scenarios in the lab has the potential to replicate the conditions of neutron star magnetospheres.

Building on previous research, several scholars have explored the concept of finite groups with algebraic diameter by examining specific types of components like simple, abelian, nilpotent, or solvable parts. In this study, we focus on splitting a finite group into its interaction of a simple component and the rest, and establish the algebraic diameter for groups that consist of a single maximal composition. Moreover, we provide details on groups with algebraic diameter equal to one or two. Notably, these details were previously known but had not been explicitly stated in literature, including cases where a finite group has algebraic diameter one or, when the maximum index of a subgroup is at least three, where the group has algebraic diameter two.

This research develops a compact and low-power temperature sensor suitable for application in battery-managed systems, based on the intrinsic property of bipolar transistors whose gain changes with temperature. Variations in collector current in a biased differential pair are then used to create two distinct voltage references through 0.6V and 1.8V level circuits. An incremental binary comparator ensures the efficient use of dynamic power in the sampling process. Simulations performed with TSMC 18nm process show that the sensor's dynamic power consumption during conversion is as low as 0.6pW at the minimum voltage of 0.6V. The temperature detection range spans from -40{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C, with a resolution of 0.24{\deg}C and an error margin of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C. Furthermore, tests demonstrate the sensor's robustness against common process, voltage, and temperature fluctuations caused by dynamic voltage scaling, requiring only static trimming for optimal performance.

The stability of magnetic fields in stars has long intrigued researchers. Previous studies examined the conditions under which these magnetic fields could remain steady, assuming they were confined to specific stellar zones. In these studies, a magnetic field that maintains its shape over time within a defined region was considered stable. However, this definition of stability is not always the most beneficial, as some previously thought unstable configurations were later found to produce lasting periods of quiescence in real stars. This work explores alternatives to stable equilibria, specifically focusing on dynamically isolated systems where magnetic fields remain trapped due to rapid decay into neutral particles as they attempt to move across boundary layers. This concept of dynamic isolation is applied to stars that preserve their magnetic fields for extended periods, including those with equatorial magnetic fields.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) has emerged as a primary tool for studying the scale-dependent behavior of quantum field theories in various dimensions. Despite its success, a thorough understanding of the FRG in a pandas-perturbative framework remains elusive. This study seeks to clarify the dynamics of the FRG by analyzing the evolution of effective degrees of freedom and symmetries in quantum field theories. A key focus lies on zero-dimensional models, specifically $N$ scalar variables, which exhibit distinct behaviors in the infrared due to IR cutoffs. A detailed analysis of the FRG equations for these models reveals the existence of multiple stable fixed points, both under specific and generalizations, of the renormalization group transformations. The nature of these models leads to the development of distinct phases, potentially exhibiting order parameters, vacuum condensates, or topological defects, as well as broken symmetries. A key finding is that the dynamics of the renormalization group transformations lead to the topological defects annihilations. This process leads to the evolution of topological defect numbers, which can be related to topological susceptibilities. The topological susceptibility arises from the defect number squared. As the models lead to phase transitions, topological susceptibility can be understood as measuring the amplitude of topological fluctuations around a particular topological sector. Musical exploration, arrangement, and creation are laborious and time-consuming processes for a human. A human listener's ability to pinpoint discrepancies between two musical recordings within a short timeframe is remarkably precise. Leveraging this human capability, we introduce the Pied Piper system, consisting of a customizable interface and a meta-level acoustic inquiry mechanism that utilizes two musical recordings to identify notes, tempo, and key. Through evaluations and arranger-friendly guidelines, we demonstrate the system's potential to significantly enhance productivity and musical output. Furthermore, we explore the potential of employing this system to facilitate collaborative projects between multiple musicians.

We examine various geometric structures, including connections, connections 2-functors, and principal bundle morphisms, within the context of Lie groupoids and smooth stacks. A unifying approach is proposed through an adapted version of Saavedra's classification from gerbes to Lie groupoids and smooth stacks. Notably, this approach reveals that connections 2-functors correspond to Riemannian metrics on underlying Lie groupoids.

A new observation from the SubMillimeter Array reveals an unusual feature 
near the center of a molecule-cloud core called Dragon NDB, located in China. 
Dragon NDB exhibits the characteristics of a star-forming region, yet it remains 
undetected in observations of carbon monoxide gas. Instead, millimeter-sized 
molecules of hydrogen cyanide indicate the presence of a molecular outflow, which 
also points to an invisible bubble inside the NDB cloud. These features set the 
NDB cloud apart from typical molecule-cloud cores, where star formation occurs 
readily. Further inside, small clusters showing signs of infalling motion seem to 
be developing at the edge of the NDB cloud, which may eventually lead to new 
stars. As a result, dragon-like dark nebulae appear to be a vital stage in the 
formation of stars in starburst galaxies.

Godel modal logics can be divided into two main categories based on their algebraic and Kripke semantic frameworks, and this paper explores these two types of algebras and relational structures for a given signature and further considerations for the logics in question. 

For the first category of Godel modal logics, we identify the corresponding algebraic frameworks and present important results regarding their subalgebras and generative relational structures. 

In the second category of Godel modal logics, the associated algebraic frameworks exhibit discontinuities; and some of these results are extended to incorporate higher-dimensional and many-sorted Godel type theories. 

We also discuss the connections between these two categories of Godel modal logics and the corresponding algebraic and relational frameworks.

LiDAR, or Light Detection and Ranging, uses laser technology to generate 3D point clouds for the safe and efficient collection of spatial information in various fields, including urban planning, the automotive industry, and environmental monitoring. However, working with LiDAR data in its raw 3D point cloud format can be challenging and computationally demanding. To mitigate this, researchers often convert LiDAR data into voxel grids, which simplify the data while preserving key 3D spatial relationships. This conversion enables more straightforward and reliable classifications of objects within the dataset, such as identifying trees, buildings, or other features. Despite these advantages, there are still significant drawbacks to using voxel grids, which our proposed method aims to overcome. By developing a novel approach that leverages specialized machinery to efficiently process and analyze LiDAR data, we can accurately detect and classify objects within the dataset while avoiding the need for data conversion.

A key issue in geostatistics is predicting values at unmeasured locations using a spherical random field defined over a given region. A common approach to this problem involves calculating the covariance between measured and unmeasured points, assuming the random field is stationary. Our study derives closed-form expressions for the autocovariance between observed and unobserved points, as well as the autocovariance between unobserved points, when the measurement set is symmetric on the unit sphere. These formulas are written in terms of the SODP coefficients, which have significant applications in geostatistics. Our work provides the foundation for developing new, efficient numerical methods to solve the spherical Laplace equation.

The Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina has the capability to pinpoint the origins and locations of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and has operated in neutrino detection mode since its completion three years ago. A one-year simulation utilizing the VAIANcE code, which mimics the characteristics of active galactic nuclei and bursts from gamma-rays, along with the accurate representation of the observatory's performance over a significant energy range, reveals that the Auger detector can detect high-energy neutrinos with energies above $10^{19}$ eV in specific sources up to distances of $100$ Mpc. Furthermore, analyzing the spatial distribution of energy cutoffs indicates that the detector has the capability to identify spatial correlations between high-energy cosmic-ray cutoffs and neutrinos generated by active galactic nuclei and some $\gamma$-ray burst sources. The outcomes of this study imply that the Auger detector can also distinguish between different types of sources of gamma-rays and active galactic nuclei based on neutrino flux.

We measure the friction within liquid foams as they flow through narrow channels, discovering that their friction is not consistent and does not change with velocity. This irregular friction appears to result from the uneven distribution of liquid within the foam, creating an internal framework that must be deformed for the foam to move. By analyzing the foam's behavior, we find that its internal stresses relate to its friction in a specific way, identified through a ratio that remains constant and matches the foam's yield stress when measured over a range of saturations and channel widths.

Approximately three billion people around the world are at risk of developing skin cancer, with melanoma being particularly aggressive and difficult to treat due to its rapid progression and resistance to treatment. Distinguishing between numerous clinical samples can be a challenging and time-consuming process, often exacerbated by the presence of difficult-to-classify outlier cases. This study overcomes these obstacles by integrating a Range-ResNet-50 network with two entropy-based metrics to automatically categorize borderline skin cancer samples and improve overall classification accuracy. Our skin cancer detection method not only outperformed 11 existing approaches in accuracy, but also surpassed them in handling skin carcinoma samples that lie between categories. Moreover, this breakthrough enables clinicians to rely on an efficient and robust classification tool, potentially reducing the need for invasive biopsy procedures.

As molten material is injected at room temperature, cooler boundaries cause it to cool down and solidify at a certain depth, forming a layer. A rotating Hele-Shaw cell, shaped like a cylinder, is used to create this layer and examine its stability. A series of overlapping frames can provide a coherent view of air and the solid layer's movement in this setup. In our research, we used this technique to study the behavior of flexible structures, like a set of fingers spinning at different speeds and with varying amounts of initial movement. As the structure begins to rotate, the centrifugal force causes it to press against the cell wall, potentially deforming or even blocking the injection of new material. We observed that under certain conditions, the flexible structure in response to this phenomenon exhibits a set of finger patterns. By analyzing these patterns, we were able to derive a map that connects specific rotational speeds and initial movements to the resulting patterns, like the sets of fingers observed.

Research on attention mechanisms in Neural Machine Translation has primarily relied on volunteer-based evaluations. To address this limitation, our study focuses on assessing the potential for look-forward attention implementations to be applied in a production environment. Initially, we examined how different smoothing strategies impact training performance for attention with look-forward inputs. Subsequently, we tested the validity of training models with look-forward attention using real user data. In addition, we evaluated a model with look-forward attention against a model with backward attention using real user data. Our findings demonstrate that look-forward attention can deliver comparable or superior results to volunteer users and can be successfully deployed in a production setting for translation tasks.

Computer scientists have long used the translational method to tackle complex design challenges. This approach involves combining existing solutions to address a significant, overarching problem. While primarily discussed in English, its concepts apply universally. A notable grid computing architect brought this method to the field by first creating a simple, functional prototype, and then gradually developing a translational framework. This framework included a core system and a range of auxiliary tools, each using the prototype as a building block. As a result, the project's progress has been highly transparent, with all grid computing innovations essentially experimental in nature. To demonstrate these benefits, a specific implementation of this translational framework will be explored in detail.

In the realm of educational research, there is a significant lack of empirical studies dedicated to the examination of curiosity as a cognitive process that enhances learning. Our work seeks to bridge this gap by introducing a pioneering approach for analyzing curiosity in learning contexts that utilizes self-report data and incorporates a set of social network metrics. Our study involves 48 university students who worked in groups of three and engaged in science-based learning activities for a set period. Our research methodology involves the use of a newly developed measurement tool for curiosity, which was first introduced by Kim et. al. in 2019. By combining this tool with data on group interactions, our study enables us to explore the complex nature of curiosity as a process that influences learning. Our multilevel modeling results reveal a nuanced relationship between curiosity and various factors that include emotional support, communication patterns, and group status. Our study also reveals that curiosity varies significantly among individuals within learning groups and over time. Ultimately, our work offers valuable insights for the design of learning systems that take curiosity into account.

Spatial statistical data are frequently analyzed using a flexible class of covariance models known as Matérn, which can be divided into two main groups: those based on characteristic functions and those based on physical densities. Characteristic function based models, though computationally straightforward, face limitations in interpreting regression models and suffer from incomplete feature coverage, particularly for small $
u$ values. On the other hand, density based models offer full flexibility in $
u$ but suffer from complicated computation due to non-rational Fourier transforms. This research introduces a class of Matérn covariance models based on graph-connection functions that model the relationship between nodes, which unifies the two groups of Matérn models and provides a valuable alternative for spatial data analysis. The proposed models incorporate an interpolating spectral density formula whose limit as $
u$ approaches any positive value results in a non-negative definite matrix, thereby overcoming the feature limitations of characteristic function based models. In contrast, density based models are restricted to specific $
u$ values due to their transform properties, which disadvantages them in the context of spatial data that is modeled by graph Laplacian matrices. These models are evaluated using computational simulations and a real-world dataset, which demonstrate their comparable accuracy to Matérn models but offer substantial computational advantages.

The effectiveness of a well-maintained road network relies heavily on timely and accurate monitoring systems. In this study, we propose a novel two-stage method for optimal detection of urban road networks, leveraging the data generated by a large number of ridesharing vehicles as natural sensors. The first stage involves the real-time estimation of traffic speeds and traffic flow rates on roads, while the second stage uses a specially designed system to adjust the positions of ridesharing vehicles in order to minimize the number of vehicles required for accurate road network monitoring. Unlike traditional methods, our approach explicitly takes into account the complexity of the road network and the availability of ridesharing vehicles in each stage. The proposed method results in the direct observation of network states and structure variables at the minimum number of vehicles required, while also ensuring the stabilizability of the system and minimal cost of vehicle repositioning. The effectiveness and adaptability of our method is demonstrated through the efficient monitoring of a complex urban road network in Shanghai, China, with a high level of accuracy and low cost of vehicle repositioning.

We investigated J/ψ decays into visible photons and unseen particles to gain insights into neutrino masses, mixings, and possible interactions with Lorentz-breaking symmetries, as well as dark energy. Assuming a valid effective field theory, we evaluated strict constraints on neutrino mass differences and mixing parameters from experiments such as J/ψ decay observations, cosmic microwave background radiation, and neutrino oscillation tests. Moreover, we compared the resulting limits to those derived from other sources. The experiments into J/ψ decays provided extremely stringent bounds, surpassing existing limits by up to seven orders of magnitude. Consequently, we discovered that such experiments are most sensitive to very heavy neutrinos with masses spanning from 10^-11 MeV to 10^-9 (10^-7) times the J/ψ mass. Furthermore, we found that the effective field theory generates additional sensitivity to dark energy parameters, specifically to its interaction with symmetry-breaking Lorentz forces at energies around 10^-9 (10^-7) times the J/ψ mass.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the order consistency approach, and this study extends that work by directly controlling the local truncation error, following the approach established by Hairer and Wanner. We introduce similar direct local error control methods for SDIMs and prove their convergence at first order for standard differential equations. A numerical experiment demonstrates the theoretical results and shows the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

Our proposed method, Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Examination, adapts kernel PCA to handle multiple continuous variables and performs harmonically different tasks across various dimensional spaces.

Automated Evaluation (AE) has long been critical in developing reliable systems for computer assistance, yet the rising use of Machine Learning (ML) requires a more robust approach, as current methods are susceptible to both exaggeration and sensitivity. Recent studies have examined these issues individually, mainly attributed to imbalanced data, which creates a hidden bias against minimizing errors over time, especially in scenarios where events constantly evolve. In this paper, we address this issue comprehensively by introducing a unifying evaluation method that accounts for stability and responsiveness, then experimentally assessed the effect of incorporating weights on stability over time, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, we propose a simple yet effective solution to adjust the balance between the two aspects of reliability.

In one-dimensional simple random walk, a pivotal moment arises when the walk shifts from staying positive to becoming negative, marking the end of an extended positive period following numerous fluctuations across the time axis. This extended period is not isolated, as the walk can remain confined within a bounded area without interacting with its boundaries for increasingly long periods as time progresses. Conversely, there is an equal and opposing phenomenon to consider.

The IShTAR facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is an advanced test chamber designed to mimic the conditions of a magnetosphere. To study and prevent the loss of plasma in the Earth's magnetosphere, IShTAR uses various systems such as a large helicon plasma source, a set of magnetic coils, and a set of guns. The IShTAR source is capable of producing high-density plasma which can be directed toward a target and create a type of current known as Field-Aligned-Current. This current can also be found in space near the Earth's magnetosphere. To study this phenomenon, researchers need a reliable plasma source, and the helicon source is ideal for its ability to produce a plasma that is easy to measure and control. However, implementing this source required significant modifications to ensure its optimal performance. To ensure the source is operating correctly, a series of tests and modifications were conducted, which ultimately led to a stable operation of the source. To further validate the source, a series of plasma measurements were performed, and the expected results were confirmed, leading to its optimal use in a series of experiments, such as those aimed at studying Allee thresholds and plasma disalignment in the Earth's magnetosphere.

To mitigate the spread of vector-borne diseases, several control strategies have been employed, including the use of biopesticides. This study presents a microbial biopesticide model designed to prevent vector-borne diseases, incorporating a control mechanism to model the biopesticide's supervening effect. The model's optimal control is analyzed through the application of Pontryagin's minimum principle, while its implementation is supported by numerical solutions. Features of the system's optimal control are also examined.

In pathology, accurately detecting cancer cells within histopathology images can be significantly time-consuming and labor-intensive. In some cases, a single image may contain hundreds of nuclei that need to be found, identified, and located, contributing to increased workload for pathologists. To alleviate this burden, automated methods have been developed to locate and find nuclei within histopathology images. However, existing approaches often struggle to achieve optimal results due to vast scale variations, background interference, and overlapping nuclei in such images. To address this challenge, a two-stage network called W-Net is proposed to utilize histopathology images for efficient and accurate nucleus detection, identification and localization in H&E stained images. In the first stage of the proposed network, histopathology images are preprocessed to extract meaningful features and guide the second stage in locating nuclei within images. To minimize the computational cost associated with using a heavy computational unit in the first stage, a lightweight computational unit is designed, called the histopathology preprocessing module (HPM). In the second stage of the proposed network, HPM modules are utilized to detect and identify features of nuclei within localized bounding boxes, resulting in efficient and effective performance, as evidenced by its superiority over state-of-the-art methods on the CAMEL30 dataset.

We establish a novel connection between the pluckability of a symplectic or special orthogonal matrix $Q$ and the validity of an integral equation that defines a function matching the beta integral of that matrix, where this matching function also satisfies a specific functional equation. This relationship enables us to derive the converse theorem for the Fourier-Laplace transform for special orthogonal and symplectic matrices in complex symmetric spaces of rank one.

This research investigates the existence of a tour within a graph that visits every edge in the graph multiple times, particularly in relation to connectedness properties of the original graph. A key criterion for determining whether a graph has this property is presented, and this criterion is also applied to an index that measures the graph's potential for having a hamiltonian cycle. Furthermore, we provide a bound for this index for graphs that are subgraphs of a specific type. All relevant proofs and derivations are included in the paper.

Epidemiological data indicate rapid worldwide spread of the novel coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). While extensive research has been conducted both computationally and physically, the virus's intricate biological mechanisms remain poorly understood due to limited available data. In contrast to earlier studies that focused solely on infection, death rates, and transmission patterns, our investigation delves into cell-level interactions. Through a solitary-cell lens, we utilize pyroptosis, a form of inflammatory cell death, as our starting point for analysis due to its documented infection by the virus. Our mathematical examination encompasses several aspects of pyroptosis, including the cellular inactivation, inflammatory cytokine and gas production induced by the virus, and the impact of anti-inflammatory interventions investigated in experimental settings. Notably, our research reveals that, unlike other types of cell death, pyroptosis can be halted via appropriate anti-inflammatory medication administration, an observation with potential implications in infection-controlled public health policy. Furthermore, we obtained the necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing the system's long-term stable state, as well as an explicit equation describing its trajectory in a two-dimensional plane.

External influences can unintentionally hinder learning and generalization in reinforcement learning agents by leveraging exogenous state variables and rewards. This paper introduces a framework for identifying such variables and proposes an elimination method to counter their negative effects. Our approach, Leverage-Driven Dynamics (LDD), modifies the environment by simulating varied leverage conditions. This allows the identification of exogenous variables and rewards through comparison of the resulting state spaces. A reinforcement learning policy is then trained to achieve good performance across these conditions, making the solution robust. Moreover, levers can be seen as catalysts that accelerate and enhance the transferability of learned behaviors. In experimental evaluations, our approach significantly reduces the performance gaps in transfer learning scenarios, surpassing baseline methods.

The blockchain platform of smart contracts relies on correct implementation to prevent financial loss. To ensure reliability, a new approach combines higher-order logic in a specification language with a type system in a validator. This method, utilized in projects like Kealra and Helmholtz, incorporates a co-inductive invariant to handle stateful blockchain validators. A case study on a Refinement Typed Contract in the Tezos blockchain demonstrates the approach's effectiveness. Furthermore, this method's applicability extends to other blockchain platforms utilizing smart contracts.

Deep learning techniques have been effectively applied to node, edge, and graph classification tasks by leveraging Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs). We've introduced a novel GCNN model based on the matched filtering theory that leverages pre-trained node feature embeddings and utilizes filtering kernels to capture local graph structures. Furthermore, we've derived a mathematical equation linking matched filtering to data normalization, which reveals the normalization process as a method of matching filtered signals. Experiential evidence from multiple experiments supports the validity of our approach, which has yielded superior performance compared to leading GCNN models in node, edge, and graph classification experiments. We've also launched an open-source GCNN toolkit, accessible at https://github.com/hjwang2/MatchedFilteringGCNN, and initiated the 'Node Feature Embedding Evaluation (NFEE)' campaign on OpenCompass to fairly assess the performance of node embedding models within the context of graph neural networks.

In a model combining Einstein's gravity, a scalar field, and a $U(1)$ gauge field, we found a large set of "hairy" black hole solutions using a specific action that includes the Chern-Simons term for the gauge field. Our model is closely aligned with the $U(1)$ sector of Einstein's General Relativity coupled to $N=4$ Super-Yang-Mills theory in three-dimensional spacetime. We discovered that a particular value of the Chern-Simons level, $k=\pm1$, enables a simpler form of the hairy black hole solutions, characterized by an essential singularity at zero radius. We inferred from the path integral approach that these solutions represent the dominant contribution to the integral, accounting for the majority of radiation emitted from these objects. Interestingly, for all other values of $k$, the corresponding levels of "hair" rapidly decline in emitted radiation. We also found a set of soliton solutions corresponding to the same Chern-Simons level, described as rotating disks of matter spinning at angular velocities $-\omega/r^2$. For soliton solutions with Chern-Simons levels other than $\pm1$, the corresponding "hair" becomes concentrated in an infinitesimally small, singular core.

We explore a general framework for reversible and irreversible changes in systems that possess membrane-like structures and exhibit symmetry. This framework is applied to explore how systems with moving boundaries can self-organize, with a focus on the role of symmetry in this process. Specifically, we examine systems with moving boundaries that exhibit $Z_2$ symmetry, which can be found in photonic and polar materials. By utilizing a Landau-Ginzburg-Beljaev approach, we create an effective field theory for fluctuations near a critical point, which helps us to identify multiple types of state transitions. These transitions include both organochemical and purely chemical phase changes. Organochemical phases are characterized by distinct values of order parameters in different "wells," which represent disorganized fluctuations of the system's symmetric state. These phases are connected by a barrier, which signifies a more organized state of the system. This organized state is known as an "domain wall" or "membrane," which has a specific thickness and energy. We derive a steady-state equation for this membrane, which can be used to understand its shape and stability. This analysis is used to understand the characteristics of the membrane in system with moving boundaries and materials properties, with a focus on the shape of the membrane in system with polar materials. This membrane can be understood as a minimal surface, which seeks to organize itself into the most efficient shape. In ultrasound elastography, accurately estimating tissue movement in the lateral direction is crucial for high-resolution elastography images. A newly proposed technique called Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) was recently introduced to improve lateral estimation by combining data from multiple beamforming methods. Although initially applied to B-mode imaging, this method is now being adapted for elastography imaging. By leveraging the advantages of VOSA in beamforming, the new VOSA-based elastography method allows for millisecond frame rates and utilizes all available data in the Matched Filter Demodulation (MFd) method, resulting in enhanced lateral displacement estimation. Studies indicate that VOSA MFd achieves a significant improvement in lateral estimation accuracy, exceeding the VOSA method with a direct-based demodulation (VFMd) approach by a factor of 1.9 when processing elastography data. Furthermore, the frame rate can be increased by 1.9 times for VFMd, whereas VOSA MFd delivers a 2.2-times improvement in lateral estimation accuracy compared to the conventional method (OSAdem).

Algorithms and corresponding pseudocode are frequently analyzed in computer science research and instruction. Recently, algorithms augmented with demonstration-based feedback have shown significant potential across various applications including robotics and artificial intelligence. However, the conventional method of representing algorithms through pseudocode lacks clarity for a wide range of readers due to its abstract and formulaic nature. This study aims to establish a user-friendly approach to describing algorithms using "rational pseudocode", which incorporates both human-readable actions and underlying mathematical principles. This format is illustrated using a search algorithm as a case study, thereby providing a foundation for the development of rational pseudocode in algorithm-based systems.

A poset $P$ is considered $r$-colorable if there's a way to color its edges with $r$ different colors such that a large, identical, monochromatic poset exists within each color. This property, which indicates the presence of a large structure in each color, is contrasted with the concept of a poset appearing with the same color throughout a specific range of a Boolean algebra. The notion of a monochromatic ideal is then explored, where an entire monochromatic ideal exists within each color, even if the colored poset doesn't appear identically. It is proven that certain $r$-partite posets, consisting of chains and $V$-shaped posets, have a threshold where they contain a large, identical monochromatic poset or an entire monochromatic ideal of a specific size. The proof provides a lower bound for this property, specifically for chain-decomposable posets, showing it holds for all posets within a certain range containing $n$ elements. A corollary follows, stating that $V$-shaped posets, containing two chains, also possess this characteristic and can be found as monochromatic posets or ideal-containing posets of a specific structure in an $n$-element Boolean algebra colored with $r$ different colors.

In response to the persistent challenge of organizing massive amounts of multimedia and text data, supervised methods like image classification and text labeling often run into performance bottlenecks and substantial initial costs. Unsupervised clustering, in contrast, typically delivers robust results without needing labeled data, yet most existing techniques fail to cope effectively with dynamic data sets and complex, high-dimensional spaces common in multimedia and text domains. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new supernetwork-based clustering framework called N^2-CDP that incorporates contrastive learning and operates without labeled data, allowing for efficient clustering of dynamic, high-dimensional text and image sets. By representing newly added items as network extensions and using an unsupervised contrastive loss to identify relevant data pairs, our method seamlessly integrates new data sets while delivering state-of-the-art clustering performance on dynamic RGB images and live Twitter updates, even as the number of images and data dimensions grow.

In the dynamic, hierarchical system of competing entities, our research explores a novel variation of the classic stochastic pursuit-evasion game, adapted to incorporate multiple levels of organization. To achieve this, we expanded the standard model to reflect both subordinates reporting to immediate supervisors and higher-level leaders who receive reports from immediate supervisors. A specific two-level setup was developed, consisting of a central pursuer aiming to capture one or more evaders, with an intermediate layer of evaders reporting their positions to the pursuer, who then commands a central evader. We analyzed a game with a central pursuer and evader, governed by an intermediate layer of evaders who make decisions to minimize their capture probability. Notably, we discovered that, in order to evade detection, the intermediate evaders will seek the help of the central evader, whose role becomes that of an optimizer trying to avoid capture by the pursuing leader. We then explored a numerical example of this hierarchical game, providing insights into the effects of reporting costs and participants' information.

Inspired by a longstanding concept in psychology, we introduce a circular probability model. This new model maintains the fundamental properties of nonnegative numbers and adds a distinct feature: its structure mimics the continuity found in human perception. Contrary to established round-robin formats, our circular probability system does have a feasible solution. A specific function is now available to generate this circular arrangement. We observe that as the system's parameter approaches certain values, it exhibits both transitivity and easiness properties. Additionally, we present a circular Ising spin model derived from our circular probability model. This circular Ising model displays ergodicity in line with our maintenance conditions, and unexpectedly, it also shows a coexistence of phases and a sudden coil-uncoil transition, despite being simplified. Finally, we discuss how our circular probability model can be applied in both theoretical research and practical scenarios.

Recently, deep learning techniques have made significant advancements and
have been successfully applied to various tasks in medical imaging such as
segmentation, diagnosis, and image reconstruction. In particular, deep learning
methods for CT dose reduction in 2020 have produced substantial improvements and
have been applied to various models such as auto-encoders, generative adversarial
networks, and convolutional neural networks, achieving successful results.
However, it is crucial to note that these models are highly sensitive to changes
in low-dose training data, particularly when utilizing a single generator for
dose reduction. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called the
AdaIN-switchable GNPI model, which employs multiple low-dose encoders and a
single generator that is coupled with an noise-to-image network. We also integrate
Adaaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) to facilitate the transfer of low-dose

Recent dialogical language model pre-training methods have achieved impressive results, however, most of them rely heavily on large-scale annotated dialogue datasets which are often corpus-specific and cannot fully capture the intricacies of conversational language modeling. In addition, the quality of pre-trained models is limited by the lack of semantic supervision in head-to-tail dialogue connection. To address these issues, we introduce a novel pre-training framework for dialogue that utilizes a semi-supervised contrastive loss function. Our approach connects model-generated responses with high-quality annotated dialogue datasets, while also ensuring semantic consistency between connected turns. Furthermore, we integrate this contrastive objective into a hierarchical tree structure to leverage the benefits of both division and merging strategies in language models. The results show that our method significantly outperforms recent dialogical language models across a wide range of natural language understanding tasks, even without the need for extensive dialogue data. Our code is available at the provided GitHub URL.

We establish a mean curvature flow for a ideal fluid spacetime and prove that the scalar curvature evolves over time under certain conditions. Additionally, we investigate conformal Ricci-Yamabe solitons on semi-spray metric spaces and prove an expansion condition under a specific inequality. Furthermore, we prove that the metric coefficient in an ideal fluid spacetime satisfies a differential equation when undergoing a flow and showing that the pressure is constant under certain constraints. Finally, we obtain the geometry of an ideal fluid spacetime when it is conformally related to a Yamabe soliton.

Research on the spin dynamics of distorted halo nuclei is explored, with an emphasis on theoretical theories related to spin response. Recent theoretical studies suggest that in certain scenarios, the intrinsic and spin degrees of freedom of nuclei can act independently, particularly in open-shell, superfluid nuclei. This concept is referred to as spin uncoupling. Within a theoretical framework based on relativistic halo-core interaction models, this theory is applied to spinning distorted core-halo systems. By incorporating interactions between core and valence nucleons, as well as considering the deformation of both components, this study investigates spin response in such halos. As an example, it examines the properties of spinning ^11Li core-shells, exploring how different core-shells combinations, core-shells spins, and angular momenta influence the nuclei's low-energy excitation properties. Results suggest that spin uncoupling may emerge in these nuclei when specific conditions are met, involving the intrinsic distortion of nuclei and specific core-shells combinations.

A common strategy in video super-resolution involves using information from adjacent frames to fill in the transformed pixel values in video super-resolution, but this approach can be negatively impacted by motion estimation errors in video super-resolution. We introduce a video super-resolution model called BasicVSR++ which involves two main aspects: improving the flow field estimation between neighboring frames and ensuring better alignment of the incoming low-resolution frames with the predicted flow fields. Specifically, we utilize an end-to-end trainable propagation alignment network to correct the discrepancy between the source video and the predicted flow field. By utilizing this model, we achieve a video super-resolution performance that surpasses the video super-resolution performance of the widely adopted video super-resolution model BasicVSR on several video super-resolution data sets, including SVIDR, Live Video Super-Resolution, and Video Super-Resolution Testbed video super-resolution benchmarks.

The precision physics potential of a muon collider is largely dependent on the development of robust vertex detectors and advanced triggering systems. To fully exploit its potential, processes with initial-state photons must be effectively identified and measured at energy levels of 10 to 100 times that of the designed vertex detector. Furthermore, efficient measurement of these high-energy quanta is crucial due to their substantial impact on the distribution of final-state particles. To address these challenges, the characteristics of typical $\ensuremath{W\ensuremath{W}^{*}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}\ensuremath{\ell}\ensuremath{\nu}\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{\gamma}}$ processes at a muon collider have been investigated. A novel algorithm named Gluon has been introduced to mitigate the substantial growth of multiplicity associated with initial-state photons. With this method, most events yield only two high-energy photons in the final particle distribution. With an ideal Gluon, a significance of 4.5 sigma can be achieved for $\ensuremath{W\ensuremath{W}^{*}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}\ensuremath{\ell}\ensuremath{\nu}\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{\gamma}}$ processes at a center-of-mass energy of 10 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 10 $\mathcal{L}$. The model-based reinforcement learning approach is known for its versatility, adaptability, and efficiency across various applications. Building a single, generalized model for multiple tasks is a natural idea, yet the model's output must remain accurate for each specific task, which can be difficult to achieve. Our analysis reveals that without proper management, models trained on diverse tasks may result in incorrect predictions due to interference between tasks. To address this challenge, we propose an anti-undoing assumption that prevents one task from negating another. Tasks that adhere to this assumption are called modular, which allows us to utilize techniques from the modular reinforcement learning community. The key contribution is the introduction of a modular error term that guides the learning process towards creating a separate, task-specific modular system. Our experiments demonstrate that these systems can learn efficiently and robustly, even from noisy data, and handle previously unseen tasks with ease.

The construction of discrete approximations for the porous medium equation and its related nonnegative Laplacian equation on a complete, non-compact metric measure space with a compact boundary is undertaken in this study, using a time-discrete scheme. It is shown that as the approximation parameter tends to zero, the solutions converge in the $L^1$ norm to the solution obtained through continuous formulations. These discrete solutions can also be viewed as minimizers of either the discrete p-Normal 1-slice variation or the discrete p-Ripserd variation, providing an alternative discrete perspective to the minimal energy interpretation. This offers a novel approximation method for solutions with finite p-energy on these specific types of metric measure spaces.

We explore the Godel-Carnap Theorem, a comprehensive theory of recursion that encompasses and extends classical results. This framework enables the development of expanded systems of enumeration with corresponding proof systems. These systems have the capacity to generate basic arithmetic operations within any given number. Furthermore, we examine several distinct notions of provability relative to gathering systems, proving the existence of unprovable statements that signify the absence of gathering in both single and non-single systems. This research extends previous work by Rosser and Tennenbaum on directed quasi-recursive systems.
